TCL is right to question Samsung’s use of the term “Mini LED”

Ars Technica Long form October 02, 2026

Can it be Mini LED without a FALD backlight?

What makes a display a Mini LED display?

It’s a question that sounds like it should have a simple answer. But it’s now at the center of a lawsuit between two of the biggest names in TVs, with TCL accusing its longtime competitor Samsung of falsely advertising budget LCD-LED TVs as Mini LED sets.

TCL may have a point. Samsung’s M-series TVs, which range from $300 for a 43-inch model to $2,300 for a 100-inch model, do raise some legitimate questions about what should qualify as Mini LED. More broadly, though, the dispute highlights a problem for shoppers: Without agreed-upon standards for what “Mini LED” actually means, manufacturers have plenty of room to define the technology for themselves.

In a lawsuit (PDF) filed in the US District Court for the Central District of California in late August, TCL accused Samsung of resorting to “fraud” to compete with TCL’s QM-series of Mini LED TVs. Samsung’s M70H, M80H, and M90H are “merely recycled… pre-existing, low-end, standard LED televisions, [which are Samsung’s entry-level] Crystal UHD line… re-labelled… as ‘Mini LED,’” TCL’s suit says.

“Samsung’s M Models contain none of the technological advancements associated with Mini LED technology, including [full array local dimming],” the complaint reads.

Samsung didn’t respond to questions I sent about specific claims in TCL’s lawsuit. Instead, a spokesperson shared a statement noting that it intends to vigorously defend against the lawsuit.

TCL argues that M-series TVs don’t have backlights capable of true full array local dimming, or FALD, the most advanced type of backlighting technology available in LCD-LED displays.

A FALD backlight uses dozens to thousands of small LEDs, or Mini LEDs, grouped into different zones, each with individually controllable brightness levels. This helps boost contrast, which is critical for image quality and essential for delivering quality HDR on an LCD-LED display.

According to a specification line titled “Micro Dimming” on the M-series TVs’ product pages, the devices use “Supreme Mini LED Dimming.” The spec sheets (PDF) available for download from those pages include a tiny footnote that clarifies: “Supreme Mini LED Dimming is Software-based (not full-array hardware-based) technology.”

Samsung also uses the term “Supreme Mini LED Dimming” on product pages for its Neo QLED TVs, which TCL accepts as true Mini LED TVs. The Neo QLED spec sheets don’t include the footnote, though.

Software-based dimming without individually addressable LED zones differs from the FALD technology described above. With software-based dimming, a TV typically analyzes each frame of a video, breaking it into different zones and determining each zone’s ideal brightness level. Using that information, the display modifies the frame’s brightness to boost perceived contrast. Critically, though, the display’s brightness level remains uniform across the panel, unlike in a display using a FALD backlight.

Software-based dimming was more common on TVs from the 2010s, such as TCL’s P6-series and LG’s UH8500-series. But even then, software-based dimming paled in comparison to FALD, as Reviewed noted in 2016.

Software-based dimming “will never be as effective as a well-designed, hardware-based local dimming solution, especially in scenes that are more susceptible to blooming artifacts,” Guillaume Chansin, associate director of displays and XR at Counterpoint Research, told me.

“However, the software plays an important role to get the most out of the hardware, with some brands able to achieve comparable image quality with fewer LEDs or dimming zones,” he said.

Because displays that support software-based dimming work differently from those that use a backlight with individually addressable LED zones, they’re not what people typically think of when describing “FALD.”

Eric Virey, principal displays analyst at Yole Intelligence, considers FALD a hardware feature first and foremost. It requires a “2D array of LEDs uniformly distributed across the entire area of the display,” along with a good algorithm to help reduce blooming, he said, adding, “To me, a ‘software-based’ Mini LED dimming just doesn’t make any sense if you don’t have that full, 2D-array of LEDs or Mini LEDs in the backlight.”

An LED display with FALD should have better contrast than an equally specced display without it. But experts I spoke with took things further, suggesting that a display shouldn’t be considered Mini LED if it doesn’t support FALD.

“I think that is broadly agreed across the industry that FALD is a key and mandatory feature in Mini LED backlights,” Virey told me via email.

Bob O’Brien, Counterpoint’s research director, also equates Mini LED with FALD.

“Mini LED was originally introduced as an improved FALD technology, with more dimming zones. So among those in the industry, it has always been assumed that a Mini LED TV has FALD capability,” he told me.

Even Samsung’s own website describing Mini LED suggests that local dimming is essential. “Mini LED is an advanced backlighting display technology that uses tiny LEDs, smaller than standard ones, for more precise backlight control through local dimming zones—a technique where backlight zones are controlled independently,” it says.

In its complaint against Samsung, TCL says it disassembled an M70H and M80H, both Samsung sets, and confirmed they can’t perform local dimming because they lack the necessary LED control chip and circuitry and use the same processor as Samsung’s entry-level Crystal TVs.

Although FALD support is key to TCL’s argument, a more obvious question might be whether M-series TVs use actual Mini LEDs. Again, though, there’s no industry-wide rule for what makes an LED “mini.”

I’ve seen Mini LEDs referred to in various size ranges over the years, including 50-300 µm (0.05-0.3 mm), 100-200 µm (0.1-0.2 mm), 100-300 µm, and “typically below 200 µm.”

TCL’s lawsuit claims that Mini LEDs “are generally .1 mm to .3 mm” and that the LEDs in Samsung’s M-series TVs are 0.5 mm. I’ve been unable to find a reputable source that refers to an LED as large as 0.5 mm as a Mini LED. I have even seen LEDs measuring more than 0.2 mm or 3 mm be considered a traditional LED in some cases.

TCL further alleges that M-series TVs have a few dozen LEDs, while some Mini LED displays have thousands. Those LEDs aren’t arranged in an array on a panel; instead, they’re “arranged on two aluminum strips,” the filing says.

A teardown video from YouTube channel AP Tech also shows an M-series TV’s backlight consisting of two rows of LEDs.

The industry hasn’t established standards for how many LED zones or Mini LEDs a display needs to qualify as Mini LED. That can leave shoppers confused about what they’re actually buying. It also creates a gray area where manufacturers can set their own standards.

“There are no organizations with authority to make and enforce such standards. TV brands have historically exploited the lack of clear standards to be more creative in their marketing,” O’Brien said.

“I think that [TCL’s] claims are legitimate and raise some important question[s] for the entire industry, which lacks a clear definition of what a Mini LED display is,” Virey told me.

The problem can be seen elsewhere in the display panel industry with technologies like QLED.

The industry could try to create standards, but Virey thinks it would lead to “an endless race.”

“Each time there are new technologies, new marketing terms are invented and can easily be abused,” he said.

While enthusiasts may delight in digging into the complex underpinnings of backlight technology, most people just care about performance. So how are Samsung’s M-series TVs?

There aren’t many reviews. RTINGS found that the M80H had “low” contrast (6,440:1, according to the review site’s testing) that makes “dark scenes look washed out in a dark room.” Regarding HDR performance, RTINGs said, “Content mastered at 600 or 1,000 nits, which is most HDR content, cuts off rapidly at the TV’s peak brightness. This lets the TV get as bright as it can, but there’s less gradation in bright parts of the scene, so highlights can seem to blend together.”

By comparison, Samsung’s $1,200 Mini LED Neo QLED QN80H, which uses individually addressable dimming zones, reached a contrast of 80,000:1 after calibration, according to RTINGs. That translated into visible improvements during actual use. RTINGs reported that the QN80H “looks good in a dark room thanks to its high contrast ratio and great black uniformity, making it a good choice for a home theater room.”

The AP Tech video below shows how an M-series TV and one with FALD handle dimming differently.

TCL’s budget QM6K ($550 MSRP as of this writing), meanwhile, reached a contrast ratio of 118:059:1 after RTINGs’ calibration. But even this set falters in areas where you might expect Mini LED to shine. Its HDR performance, for example, is reportedly lacking.

“Visually, the TV doesn’t impress, although its black levels are quite good due to its impressive contrast and good black uniformity. Unfortunately, there’s more haloing around bright highlights than you’d like, but it’s alright. Its HDR brightness is mediocre at best, so the TV doesn’t provide an impactful HDR experience overall,” RTING’s review says.

TCL has an obvious stake in challenging Samsung’s marketing. The companies are longtime rivals, and casting doubt on Samsung’s claims could help TCL sell more TVs. But the underlying question is still worth asking: What should consumers expect when a TV is marketed as Mini LED?

I’d argue that a TV with slightly smaller LEDs than average but without local dimming shouldn’t be considered Mini LED with local dimming. The important distinction isn’t simply the size of the LEDs; it’s how they’re used to deliver improved contrast and HDR performance.

But even that definition has limits, as small LEDs and local dimming zones aren’t enough to guarantee good performance. TCL’s own budget line of Mini LED TVs can disappoint in areas where the technology should have an advantage, such as HDR support. And compared with Samsung’s more expensive Mini LED TVs, the M-series has worse HDR performance and black levels and is harder to use in a dark room, according to RTINGs’ testing.

That leaves shoppers in an awkward position. Terms like “Mini LED” or “QLED” are now used liberally, but they don’t always tell you how a TV will perform. Manufacturers often fail to disclose basic details, like the size of the LEDs, the number of dimming zones, or accurate contrast and brightness measurements.

For shoppers, then, it’s important to remember that comparative pricing and independent testing are ultimately much more useful than a label on a box.

How student went from YouTube to Bake Off

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 05:08:54 GMT

A student taking part in the new series of the Great British Bake Off says he taught himself to bake after "stumbling across a YouTube video".

When Mo Mahir, 22, from West Bromwich, was nine years old, he "found a video of a guy making a mug cake in a microwave", which he said ignited his passion for baking.

"I feel like as a Bengali, we don't really have a lot of cakes or baking in our cultural background," he said. "It started with me mixing a bunch of random stuff. My mum used to always be shouting at me saying 'stop, that's making a mess’."

As part of the Channel 4 series, Mahir, a student at Birmingham City University, has been competing against 12 other bakers.

"Growing up, I've always loved cakes and cookies and stuff and I've always wanted to eat them, but it's just that we never always got the, like, freshly baked stuff. So I kind of had to teach myself," he said.

"Nothing turned out right because I wasn't measuring anything, but it slowly just progressed from there."

On week one of the competition, Mahir landed star baker after he stunned TV judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood with his peanut and caramel chocolate stout cake.

On week two, viewers watched him bake a biscuit mosaic. His newfound TV fame means he has been spotted while out and about in Birmingham.

"It's been really positive, just like all the DMs [direct messages] I'm getting on Instagram is very supportive and kind.

"When I'm going to town to do a bit of shopping, I do get recognised and people are like rooting for me, and it's just nice to see and hear that."

Mahir's former teacher Sam Hayes, from George Salter Academy, previously said: "When I found out he would be going on, I knew he would do really well.

"I'll always remember being brought some of the delicious treats Mo had baked at home, a very welcome perk of having such a talented student.

"He always was an absolutely amazing baker while he was at school," he added.

Other contestants competing to win the series include a paediatric doctor, a competitive sprinter, a hairdresser and a drag artist.

We're saving £100 a month for our kids but they won't get it until they're 57

BBC News Tue, 06 Oct 2026 08:16:11 GMT

Richard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them.

The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules.

So the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083.

Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing.

"Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow."

Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council.

He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended.

In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18.

The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life.

Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past.

"We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain.

"And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids."

Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600.

The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show.

One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open as in the same period a year earlier.

Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023.

While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more?

Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years.

"The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help."

Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says.

For parents who can afford it, the money can grow substantially before the child can access it, says Jemma Slingo, a pensions specialist at Fidelity.

"Paying in £50 a month from birth, including tax relief, the family would contribute £10,800 over those 18 years. The pot could grow to around £135,000 by retirement. That's the real power of starting early - relatively modest amounts can have an exceptionally long time to compound."

It's not just British parents that are opening long-term investments for their children.

In July this year, US President Donald Trump launched a new retirement investment scheme for children called Trump Accounts.

Families, friends and employers can contribute up to $5,000 (£3,800) per year per child. The difference with the UK is that the children can access the funds from when they turn 18, although withdrawals are subject to taxes and a possible 10% penalty if made before the age of 59 and a half.

Wally Luckeydoo, a personal finance teacher at Smyrna High School in Tennessee, has opened Trump Accounts for his two children, aged four and three.

"My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally.

"For much of my adult life, I have felt like I was trying to catch up financially, particularly because of significant student loan debt.

"I don't necessarily think of this as specifically saving for my kids' retirement. I think of it as giving them a head start and helping change the trajectory of our family financially."

Scotland's 'Chornobyl' housing scheme takes starring role in new horror film

BBC News Tue, 06 Oct 2026 04:57:00 GMT

A short film has captured some of the last images of a derelict housing estate nicknamed "Scotland's Chornobyl" before demolition crews moved in.

The tenements at Clune Park in Port Glasgow were built a century ago as housing for shipyard workers but most of the buildings lay empty for years.

Glasgow-based filmmaker Alessio Avezzano shot scenes for his post-apocalyptic sci-fi horror comedy, Behind, on the estate before bulldozers moved in last May.

"It's the last film to be made there. It was announced it would be demolished the day we were filming - we managed to get in there not a moment too soon," said the Scottish-Italian writer and director.

Redevelopment of Clune Park had been delayed for years due to a stand-off between private landlords and the local council, leaving the site frozen in time with just a handful of tenants remaining.

Large parts of the site became run-down and comparisons were made with the Ukrainian city of Pripyat, abandoned after the 1986 explosion at the Chornobyl nuclear plant led to a huge radiation leak.

The plot for Behind was inspired by "butt dialling", accidentally calling someone from a phone placed in a back pocket.

In the film, it has devastating consequences.

Avezzano said he come up with the idea while trying to write a script.

"That week my cousin, who hadn't done this before or since, just started to butt dial me every day and by the fifth day the light bulb moment came," he said.

"It is basically taking the idea of butt dials and what if they were a symptom of something more deadly."

Avezzano added: "It's got elements of how we responded to the pandemic and it's got elements of phone addiction and social media addiction."

"It's post-apocalyptic satire."

Avezzano said Clune Park gave him the ideal backdrop for the short, and scenes were shot in areas accessible to the public.

Scenes for 2013's sci-fi horror Under the Skin, starring Scarlett Johansson, were also filmed at the estate.

"The idea it was described as Scotland's Chornobyl has always been fascinating." said Avezzano, who is working on his first feature - Midgies - a horror film set in Scotland and due to be released next year.

The film was entirely self-funded.

The lead character is played by Jade McDonald who was in the female run of Singin' I'm No a Billy He's a Tim, a play about a Celtic fan and a Rangers fan locked in a prison cell together on the day of an Old Firm match.

Behind has been taken on a tour of international film festivals, including in Italy and Argentina, following its premiere at Glasgow Film Festival's Frightfest.

It was nominated for the best editing prize at Basingstoke's Exit 6 Film Festival and won best international short at Roswell Shorts Festival in New Mexico.

'My donated Brummie accent gives me confidence'

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 12:32:16 GMT

A man who appealed for help to no longer sound like a "character from Star Wars" says he has found his calling.

Christian Wilson, from Bromsgrove, has verbal dyspraxia - a difficulty in placing muscles in the correct position to produce speech. He uses text-to-speech software in order to communicate, but said he wanted to sound "like a man from Birmingham".

The 24-year-old's dream was made possible in 2024 when he selected two voice donors that blended a Birmingham accent and a Warwickshire accent, which he hoped would help him sound more like his father.

Since May, Wilson has worked at Worcestershire County Council as a SEND Peer Advocate. He said his new dialect had given him "the confidence to voice [his] opinion".

Speaking to BBC Hereford & Worcester on Thursday, he told presenter Tammy Gooding: "There was a moment where I thought, this is really what I'm meant to do.

"I was really excited about it, because as long as I can remember I've always wanted to be an advocate, plus I have always been passionate about education."

According to the NHS, verbal dyspraxia is a speech disorder where the muscles have not been damaged, but the messages from the brain that tell the muscles what to do have been affected.

The condition caused Wilson to start his search to find his voice.

Previously, he said: "I'm from Bromsgrove and I was born in Birmingham.

"I want to sound like a man from Birmingham, not a character from Star Wars or a cyborg from Doctor Who."

And now as a SEND Peer Advocate, Wilson said he now had the confidence to challenge Ofsted representatives to "do more" for children and young people with disabilities.

He said: "The representatives said they would definitely feed back what I had said. My hopes for the future are that I continue to use my voice as an instrument to do good.

"I hope to continue to advocate for disabled children and young people by sharing my expertise and experience with whoever necessary to improve the lives of others in Worcestershire."

In 2024, he described feeling emotional when he listened through to the voice submissions with his family.

"As I was listening to them, I knew I was getting closer to my dream, something that I thought never would happen," he said.

"I hope to use my new voice to share my experiences with other people - that would be great."

Wilson's sister felt an instant connection to the Birmingham accent he selected for his new voice.

He said: "I liked the voice originally, but when my sister heard it she said 'that is you.'"

Wilson's Birmingham voice donor, Martin Brennan, said: "It's such an emotional journey and even sitting here, I'm welling up now.

"I just thought why not - it was a no brainer and it was a joy to get involved."

Fellow donor, Stephen Robotham, from Warwickshire, said: "Having a voice is so important and especially having your own voice, it's integral to your identity."

Boos, anguish & fading belief -'worrying day' for under-pressure Carrick

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 20:54:46 GMT

This video can not be played

Solanke scores in added time as 10-man Spurs draw with Man Utd

For the second time in successive home Premier League games, Manchester United failed to beat opponents reduced to 10 men.

For the third time in as many seasons, a United manager finds himself under severe pressure before the clocks have gone back.

Four weeks ago, Manchester City needed an incorrect video assistant referee (VAR) decision to take advantage of an ineffective United performance after Phil Foden had been shown a red card in the 23rd minute for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes.

On Saturday, the damage was self-inflicted as a Spurs side, who had given every indication of being unable to score before Rodrigo Bentancur's headfirst charge at Luke Shaw just five minutes after Bryan Mbeumo's opener, came up with an injury-time equaliser.

Centre-back Lisandro Martinez was outmuscled embarrassingly easily by Dominic Solanke, with goalkeeper Senne Lammens failing to read the striker's deft touch that crept in at the far corner.

The anguish on United faces told its own story.

"A worrying day for Michael Carrick," observed former United skipper Gary Neville on Sky Sports.

Late Solanke strike salvages 10-man Spurs draw at Man Utd

Tottenham grab a draw but who got 1/10 - Ratings for Man Utd v Spurs

Michael Carrick after Manchester United's 1-1 draw with Tottenham at Old Trafford

First, a couple of sorry statistics.

Manchester United have just six points from their opening six games of the Premier League season, their fewest at this stage of a league campaign since 1986-87, when they amassed four under Sir Alex Ferguson.

They have failed to win five of their six Premier League games this season (D3 L2), already as many as in 17 league games under Michael Carrick last season (W12 D3 L2).

United have collected two points from their last two games, both of which were against teams who began the match at the bottom of the Premier League.

In points terms they are closer to the relegation zone than the Champions League spots.

Carrick's side are now winless in four league games and face an always tricky trip across the Pennines to face old rivals Leeds at Elland Road on Sunday, 18 October. Either side of that are daunting Champions League trips to Atletico Madrid and Como.

United officials have repeatedly offered their backing to Carrick in recent weeks.

However, no fan needs reminding that two seasons ago a run of two wins in nine games in all competitions put Erik ten Hag under severe pressure before the axe fell after a defeat at West Ham on 27 October.

Last season, a combination of a shocking EFL Cup exit at the hands of League Two Grimsby and an insipid 3-1 loss at Brentford on 27 September did so much to undermine confidence in Ruben Amorim before he was sacked on 5 January.

The start to this campaign is starting to look increasingly familiar.

This video can not be played

'We've got to do better' - Carrick calls for improvement after Man Utd draw with Tottenham

"I'm not happy with he amount of points we've got so far, for sure, you know," said Carrick.

"I'm not hiding, there's no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we've got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that's pretty plain."

The 'little things' Carrick talks about are the defending for Solanke's goal, the lack of pressure put on Everton's Ainsley Maitland-Niles when he smashed another injury-time equaliser at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on 6 September, and the preventable Martinez own goal that nearly gave Fulham victory at Craven Cottage just before the international break.

"We've got to be a little bit more streetwise in moments, a little bit more stubborn and a little bit stronger in seeing out certain things," he added.

"It doesn't change my belief or the confidence in the players, you know. We're a really good team and capable of being a really good team, but we've obviously got to start getting more points on the board, that's for sure."

The problem is with each disappointment, the belief of United being 'a really good team' starts to ebb away.

Yet again, a post-match focus centred on how much Carrick's team ran, even though running for the sake of it has proved to be of little benefit.

"The stats don't lie when every time the other team runs more than you," said Sky Sports pundit and former Spurs captain Jamie Redknapp.

"Tottenham ran 5km more than Man United. OK, they had 10 men but that is every game. If you outrun your opposing number, you will win games. I'm not saying they are not trying. It is that physical battle they are losing though."

It feels as though some fans are losing faith already, judging by the way they reacted at moments during the game, aside from the boos that accompanied the end of each half.

Forward Matheus Cunha - one of a number of Carrick's squad who have failed to reproduce the form he showed in the second half of last season - gestured to the crowd during the opening period. It wasn't clear whether he was responding to a negative comment or urging more noise, but the Brazilian clearly wasn't happy.

Carrick's family are season ticket holders. He knows what it is like to watch United struggle at Old Trafford.

"Obviously, it hurts," he said. "It hurts a lot. It's not nice to go through. I care as much as anybody about this place. Sometimes you could say too much because then it overspills. But it's coming from a good place, really, and so I understand it."

It is in moments like this that Carrick, who presents such a calm front in public, must be churning inside.

He knows how the pressure can mount around Old Trafford and how fierce the debate around the club in the search for answers can be.

As he said, Carrick cares. And he is certain his players feel the same.

"I don't feel let down," he added. "You can make mistakes.

"We've all got standards; we've all got levels. The players hold their hands up at times when something goes against them.

"It's not like everyone walks off into the distance tonight like everything's fine and it's left on me. It's not that at all. The players care, for sure.

"I don't feel let down by them for making a mistake. We've just got to all help each other be better, and it's on me to help them and guide them through it."

Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 20 people

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 20:51:12 GMT

Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 20 people including four children, local officials said.

The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the southern city on Saturday morning. At least 32 others were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks on Zaporizhzhia were Russia expressing "its thanks" for a deal announced by US President Donald Trump last night easing sanctions on Moscow to import Russian diesel.

He added that 13 other regions had come under attack overnight, arguing this demonstrated Russia took "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting".

Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes in Zaporizhzhia show an apartment block mostly destroyed.

"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Harchenko told Ukrainian television from the scene.

She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.

The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.

Harchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."

Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles.

Zelensky was quick to criticise Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Analysts view the deal as an attempt by the US president to allay domestic concerns about high fuel prices ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

Zelensky wrote on social media on Saturday that Russian attacks on energy facilities in the capital, Kyiv, demonstrated Russia's "true intentions".

"Russia's choice is war. And they will be ready to end it only when they feel that their ability to drag the war out is diminishing.

"Unfortunately, the signals Russia received yesterday were entirely different – signals suggesting that it could simply keep attacking. And this needs to be corrected."

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as Moscow's full-scale invasion, launched in 2022, drags on.

On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region.

The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.

The number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55% in the first eight months of this year, according to the UN.

Russia has also stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as winter approaches, a strategy it has undertaken in previous years. Kyiv has repeatedly accused it of targeting Ukraine's civilian population, which Moscow denies.

For its part, Ukraine has increasingly adopted a policy of striking infrastructure often deep inside Russia that is crucial to its economy, including several oil refineries and terminals.

Several strikes on data centres owned by Yandex have left the tech giant struggling to maintain services.

Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at curtailing revenue streams for Russia's war machine.

Ceremony marks return home of kiwi feather cloak

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:37:20 GMT

A ceremony has been held to mark the return of a Māori kiwi feather cloak to New Zealand by a British museum.

The kahu kiwi was one of the farewell gifts presented by Māori leaders in 1900 to Dr George Cleghorn, a medical doctor who had been working in New Zealand.

It was loaned to the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford by Cleghorn's widow in 1913.

The Homebound Project, a charity which funded the return, said the cloak was "crying to come home".

Dr Lorraine Eade, chair of Ngāti Rārua o Te Wairau Society, which now owns the item, said its significance was "beyond measure".

She said its return was an opportunity to acknowledge Cleghorn's work for Māori people.

The doctor advocated for their right to attend a local hospital instead of being required to travel further afield for medical treatment, Pitt Rivers Museum said.

He also spent time educating families at their homes on the importance of taking public health measures, it added.

Shane Graham, chief executive of Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Rārua, a Māori authority, said the return was a momentous occasion.

"It restores mana [prestige] and honours the deep emotional and cultural significance of our living connection to this taonga [treasure]," he said.

Prof Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum, said: "We are very pleased that the day has come for the Kahu Kiwi to return home."

A ceremony was held in Oxford earlier to mark the cloak's departure.

'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:28:28 GMT

US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.

The Ukrainian president warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his nation, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday that Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.

"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".

Global fuel supplies, including diesel, have been severely limited by the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel, which led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil products usually flows.

Russia - a major producer - and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes on each other's energy infrastructure and transport facilities, further straining energy markets.

"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump continued.

"He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."

Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev described Trump's intervention as "iconic and historic", saying that Ukraine "needs leadership actually focused on peace".

The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.

Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.

He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" following deadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.

The Ukrainian president spoke to several allies on Saturday to discuss the latest developments, calling for "real decisions to protect lives in Ukraine" and to protect European security.

A Downing Street spokesperson said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Zelensky and offered his "complete solidarity".

The pair had agreed Russia should acquiesce to "an immediate energy ceasefire" and end its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea, the spokesperson said, as "this would immediately release more energy and food supplies into the global market".

News of the US-Russia diesel deal was also met with criticism by EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas, who echoed Zelensky in saying that suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."

She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.

The deal with Russia is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.

The average price of diesel is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA – up from last month's $5.94 average, and $3.68 last year.

Under the deal, Russia would release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace" followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November.

A further million would follow, Trump wrote on Truth Social, and then another 3m tonnes "within a short period of time" – but he noted that this delivery will be "based on the condition of their diesel refineries".

In the past 10 months, Russia experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country due to Ukrainian drones strikes on its oil refineries.

Diesel production in Russia dropped by an estimated 30%, according to the International Energy Agency.

Trump had already called for new elections in Ukraine last December, saying Ukrainian voters should have the choice to replace Zelensky.

Since the war broke out in 2022 Ukraine has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.

Man dies after tiger attack at wildlife park

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:09:59 GMT

A man has died after being attacked by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, police have confirmed.

South Yorkshire Police said it had been called at 13:35 BST to reports of a man entering the tiger enclosure at the attraction near Doncaster. The tiger then attacked the man and he died at the scene, the force said.

His family had been informed and were being supported by officers, it added.

A park spokesperson said: "We are deeply saddened by today's tragic incident. Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies are with the family and loved ones of the person who has lost their life."

They added: "We are working closely with the police and relevant authorities and would ask that the privacy of those affected is respected at this extremely difficult time. The park will remain closed tomorrow."

Police said the tiger was uninjured, remained in the enclosure following the incident and there had been no wider risk to the public.

The park was evacuated and officers remain at the scene.

The force added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."

Earlier, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, had been enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated.

She said she had heard what sounded like "gunshots" and an air ambulance had circled above.

Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure."

She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it had been "very, very well organised".

Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with its Land of the Tigers area opening in 2011.

The purpose-built two-acre reserve is home to Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with around 500 left in the wild.

Photos of the enclosure on the park's website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.

Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:08:17 GMT

Four people have died and hundreds of thousands are without power after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern US with powerful winds and heavy rain.

Officials reported two deaths each in the states of Alabama and Florida, which included people who were killed when trees fell on their houses.

At least 600,000 people were without power in several states as of Saturday afternoon, according to tracker PowerOutage.

Isaias made landfall in Florida late on Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105mph (168km/h) before being downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone.

The storm felled trees and ripped the roofs off buildings. Alabama, Florida and Georgia all declared states of emergency ahead of its arrival, while both Florida and Alabama issued mandatory evacuation orders to thousands of people.

Two deaths were reported in Florida's Escambia County. A woman was killed when a tree fell on her house, local Sheriff Chip Simmons said.

Joey Williams told NewsNation his wife had died in the storm. He said they went outside to snap pictures of the damage but, when they went back into their home, a tree fell through the roof and trapped them.

"I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn't make it," Williams told the outlet.

Simmons later reported that a man had died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a garage that was not properly ventilated. Four other people who were in the same house were taken to hospital.

Officials had to rescue people in vehicles that became submerged by floodwaters. The Florida National Guard shared pictures of a truck stuck in a flood ditch, saying soldiers "stopped, swam to the vehicle and pulled its occupants to safety".

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said flooding was a continued risk and warned of a "very hazardous situation".

In neighbouring Alabama, a sheriff was injured when a tree fell on him as he was responding to a car crash.

"Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives," Governor Kay Ivey said in a post on X, without giving further details on the circumstances of the deaths.

She also said officials were concerned about "spinoff tornadoes" in the state from the strong winds and heavy rain.

"As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop," she said.

In Charleston, South Carolina, officials asked people to stay home on Saturday night as high tide is expected to reach 7.5ft (2.3m).

"After dark, floodwater is much harder to see and it's impossible to judge how deep it is from behind the wheel," the city said.

The storm is expected to continue to weaken as it travels to the north-east, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) warned that the Carolinas and Georgia could see floods from up to 10 inches (25cm) of rainfall.

In addition to Isaias, Tropical Storm Rachel is expected to hit southern California later on Saturday, and Hurricane Simon will hit the Pacific coast of Mexico on Sunday.

Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.

Several injured in attack on airport in Saudi capital Riyadh

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 18:37:10 GMT

Several people have been injured in another attack on an international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, authorities say, days after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have carried out similar strikes on the hub.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were suspended on Saturday after the attack, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said in a statement.

More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to news agency Reuters, citing an eyewitness.

The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport" and urged American citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.

The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudis including a pilot were killed in two attacks on the airport by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior. Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.

A source at a local hospital told AFP that dozens of people had been wounded in Saturday's attack.

An eyewitness who said they had been in the domestic terminal told the news agency that they had seen gate 401 hit and "injured [people] in front of my eyes", adding: "Everyone was running."

Western embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens away from the airport, while the UK Foreign Office told British nationals to stay away "until the airport is secure and to monitor the advice of the Saudi authorities".

Several Gulf airlines said they had cancelled their flights to and from the airport, with Kuwait Airways citing the "security situation" there.

All flights to Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled, aviation tracker Flightradar shows.

Doctors had been asked to report to hospitals to address the situation, a medical source told AFP.

"We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'," the medical source told the agency.

The suspected attack comes during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.

The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.

The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

But the informal truce began to unravel in July.

The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

Expedition hopes to find aviator Amelia Earhart's plane on remote island

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 18:22:29 GMT

A team of researchers are on their way to a remote island to inspect what they think could be the wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart's plane.

The group, from the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University, are expected to arrive at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean by Monday in the hopes of solving the mystery of her disappearance.

The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation on her fate.

The team are aiming to find what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020.

Purdue University said the object had since been confirmed to have been visible in aerial photography of the area dating back to 1938.

The researchers are currently roughly halfway through their journey to the remote atoll aboard the Marin Mainiku, a Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel.

They departed the capital of Kiribati on Wednesday to begin the 830-mile journey to Nikumaroro, which is also part of the multi-island country.

When they eventually arrive, they will have to navigate through a narrow gap created in the atoll's reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.

"Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the ALI and the expedition lead, said.

Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.

From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.

But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.

Earhart's disappearance spawned numerous theories - from a simple crash due to fuel exhaustion to more elaborate claims of interference.

The official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems while the two struggled to find the island, and Earhart eventually crashed into the ocean when she ran out of fuel.

While this version of events is largely accepted, no physical evidence has ever been recovered.

One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.

Images of the so-called Taraia Object show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.

But some - including rival explorers - have expressed scepticism that this could be a plane, let alone Earhart's.

Ric Gillespie, who specialises in recovering historic aircraft wrecks, told news agency Reuters that the object looked like a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the nearby water.

"I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," he said.

The researchers en route to the island credit Gillespie with previously finding evidence of a human presence on the atoll in the 1930s and forensic analysis of skeletal remains found there in the 1940s they say lend credence to their theory.

But Gillespie suspects Earhart's plane had likely broken apart and its fragments carried into the depths of the Pacific long ago.

Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.

In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.

Similarly, an expedition in 2019, conducted by the marine archaeologist who discovered the Titanic wreck, to investigate a photograph of what might have been a landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

The rock behind Chelsea's entertainers: Midfield duo key for Blues

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 18:09:37 GMT

This video can not be played

Highlights: Henderson stars as Chelsea put five past Bournemouth

Moises Caicedo and Jordan Henderson were paired in midfield for the first time as Chelsea produced their most complete performance of the season.

In a 5-1 victory over Bournemouth on Saturday, manager Xabi Alonso finally found the control and stability required behind his free-scoring attacking trio of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers.

The Blues have had no problems scoring goals this campaign, with 15 goals from six matches, but no team has conceded more than their total of 13.

Against the Cherries though, Caicedo and Henderson provided the balance to suggest Alonso could finally have found an answer - despite still having to wait for their first clean sheet of the league campaign.

Henderson stole the show by scoring his first two goals for the club. He opened the scoring with a curling effort after 66 seconds before adding a 25-yard free-kick to complete the victory.

Having also set up Rogers for the second goal after just two minutes and 30 seconds, the 36-year-old became the third-oldest player to score and provide an assist in the same match for Chelsea, behind only Didier Drogba and Gianfranco Zola.

Henderson's performance came after a shift in Chelsea's summer recruitment strategy. He arrived on a free transfer from Brentford to add experience to what had been the Premier League's youngest squad.

Alonso said: "We signed him for everything. If he's able to score two beauties like today, we are more than happy for him.

"But apart from the goals, he's done many, many good things. I think today was a very complete performance. We were in control for most of the game, so I'm happy with that. We had good stability in defence as well."

Having not signed a player aged over 30 since Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang in 2022, Chelsea recruited three this summer, with goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez joining from Aston Villa and striker Danny Welbeck also arriving.

Now, recovered from a broken arm sustained while jumping over an advertising hoarding during celebrations following England's win over Mexico at the World Cup, Henderson is showing he is more than just a vocal leader behind the scenes.

Caicedo made his first start of the season for Chelsea in all competitions

There is a strong argument that Chelsea find it easier to cope without the creativity of Cole Palmer than without Caicedo's ability in possession and his knack for breaking up play in midfield.

In his 150th appearance for the club, Caicedo lasted 72 minutes.

His withdrawal for Romeo Lavia was planned, but the Ecuador international still made a significant impact.

Alonso deployed him in a deep role, dropping into the middle of the back three when Chelsea were in possession and allowing young defender Josh Acheampong to push forward.

He misplaced just two passes and recorded the highest pass-completion rate of any Chelsea starter. He also made and won more tackles than any other Chelsea player on Saturday afternoon.

With Caicedo in the side, Chelsea have won 48.1% of their Premier League matches. Without him, that figure drops to 25%.

Alonso said: "You always want to have Moises on the pitch. With him, we have a better midfield area and when you are better in the middle, you have a more complete team.

"I think that is something to build around. With the players that we have up front, they are solid in defence as well. So, I'm happy that Moises is feeling better because he's going to be a key player for us. We knew that."

The alternative options in Chelsea's midfield include captain Reece James, who is able to play in defence, along with substitutes Romeo Lavia and Valentin Barco, who did not make the matchday squad.

It is most likely James who will be attempting to re-take his place from Henderson when back, but the diagnosis on his knee issues remains uncertain.

Chelsea remain a work in progress and conceded again through poor set-piece defending for Evanilson's goal.

However, if Henderson and Caicedo can help eliminate the defensive lapses, Chelsea can begin to look up the table, with Pedro, Rogers and Palmer already helping to make them the Premier League's top scorers.

Alonso said: "I think that they help each other well and they give presence, they give stability.

"You know that they are going to be the ones that are going to be helping the rest, not just for their qualities because they understand the game. They can play in shorter spaces but as well defensively they give good balance."

Former England striker Alan Shearer told BBC Sport: "Caicedo makes a difference. There's no doubt about it. He gives Chelsea a bit more solidity and stops the ball getting into the back four.

"He and Henderson have worked really well, the opening goal being a good example. He definitely makes them more solid, I've been really impressed."

Verstappen building major momentum as 'no-one very happy' at McLaren

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 17:46:36 GMT

Sunday's race will be Max Verstappen's 250th in Formula 1

Max Verstappen is too far behind, and Kimi Antonelli too far ahead, to consider that Red Bull's revival might create any real jeopardy in the championship fight - but the Dutchman is certainly building some major momentum as the Formula 1 season moves into its closing stages.

Verstappen finished Saturday in Singapore with pole position for the grand prix to add to the sprint-race victory he had completed in tricky wet conditions earlier in the day.

And that gives him a great opportunity to complete a second grand prix victory within a week if he can convert on Sunday.

Verstappen has two eager Ferrari drivers right behind him, after Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton both felt that they had just missed out on a pole position that was possible.

He also has concerns about Red Bull's inconsistent starts - he lost the lead off the line both in Malaysia last weekend and in the sprint.

If he does drop back at the start in Singapore, it is the sort of track where overtaking is at a premium and he will not find it as easy to get back in front as he did on his way to his first victory of the season.

And he is, as one would expect, not getting ahead of himself.

"It was a good qualifying," Verstappen said. "It was always very close and we got ahead when it mattered and we are very happy with that.

"All weekend the car has been in a good window and that makes it a lot easier to find your rhythm. Incredibly happy to start first. Still a long race ahead, a lot of things can go wrong but we have done everything up until now well so hopefully we can continue that tomorrow.

"It's been a really positive last few races and we want to keep that momentum going."

Verstappen beats Ferraris to Singapore pole

Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out

Verstappen's maiden win of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last weekend came after a run of three podium finishes in Italy, Spain and Azerbaijan, the last of which might very well have been a first victory had he not had problems in qualifying that left him eighth on the grid when he could have been on the front row.

His upturn in form has come as a result of steady work from Red Bull in improving their car and getting it into a position where he feels he can predict its behaviour and therefore push to the limit.

When a Red Bull is in that spot, Verstappen can be close to unbeatable.

He proved that in his remarkable comeback last year, when he gave McLaren and Lando Norris nightmares with a quite brilliant second half of the season that saw him eat into a 100-point deficit to the championship lead and ultimately miss out on taking a fifth title by just two points.

This year, Verstappen's deficit to Antonelli is even bigger than that.

He is 129 points behind the Mercedes driver with only 175 still remaining, assuming the two end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi do actually take place in the context of the war in the Middle East.

It would take some kind of miracle - involving not only a non-stop stream of wins for Verstappen and a highly unlikely run of poor form and bad luck for Antonelli - for him to turn that around. So the prospect can be realistically dismissed.

But he certainly looks as if he will be a contender at the front for the remainder of the season.

The McLarens of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris before they came together during the Singapore sprint race

If that is not a major concern for Antonelli, it certainly is for McLaren.

They had their own purple patch in the summer, when Lando Norris took consecutive wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, and would have won in Madrid had it not been for the unfortunate timing of a virtual safety car.

But the world champions have slipped from competitiveness in recent races, and before the Singapore Grand Prix they lie in third place in the constructors' championship, only 11 points ahead of Red Bull.

Saturday in Singapore was a bad day at the office for McLaren.

Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were heading for fourth and fifth places in the sprint when Norris made a dive down the inside of his team-mate at Turn Five on the final lap.

This is not a common overtaking spot and from a McLaren point of view it was a move with no reward, only risk.

The move might have made sense if it had come earlier in the race and enabled Norris to challenge Leclerc, struggling in front of them, for third.

But on the last lap, Norris was not going to have a go at Leclerc even if he had got through - the only remaining overtaking place was at the end of the following straight into Turn Seven.

If the McLaren drivers swapped places, it would make no difference to the team in terms of a collective points haul, but if it went wrong, the cost could be high.

And so it did. Norris was in a position to make a legitimate move, but they came together, pirouetted in tandem, Piastri into the barriers and out of the race and Norris slipping down to eighth. Nine points had become one.

The stewards took no action, feeling that "both drivers had contributed to the incident".

Piastri had explained in the hearing that he did not expect Norris to try a move there, and attempted to leave space when he saw him.

Norris argued that his his car was in a position that, according to the rules, entitled him to make an overtaking attempt, so expected to be left space and had braked and gone over the kerb when he realised he was not going to get as much as he expected.

He said: "There are two sides, one is what the stewards say and that's a fair reasoning, no-one's to blame. But I did apologise because it was still me attacking, as I had the right to do. If I just sat there and was boring like I should be, nothing would have happened. So really it's still my fault but I deserved to go for the space and I still believe I had the right for it."

Norris added: "As you probably expect, no-one's very happy. I'm not happy, Oscar isn't happy. None of us wanted it to go that way. There was things both of us could have done better and, yeah, we spoke about it and we moved on."

Singapore Grand Prix

Sunday, 11 October at 13:00 BST

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

Team principal Andrea Stella is a measured man who chooses his words carefully, but his displeasure was clear.

"It was a very long, tiring and challenging day," he said. "Very simply, it is unacceptable that two McLarens ever come together on track. This is a fundamental principle of how we go racing, and something both drivers are very well aware of.

"As always, we discuss these incidents as a team in a constructive and productive way as there is always something to learn and take forward to emerge stronger. These are not conversations we need to have in public, but we have reminded our drivers that the interests of the team must always come first, and that did not happen today."

The context for the collision comes after two seasons where Norris and Piastri have had a number of incidents that created tensions, especially in their title battle last season. Lessons do not appear to have been learned in the way Stella might have expected.

Stella said he was "disappointed" more than anything, pointing out that this was far from the first conversation he had had with the drivers on the need to put the team's interests first.

"We as a team need to reflect as to how we make sure that these situations do not happen any more," he said.

"It is serious. It is serious because the damage for the team is material. We are in a close fight in the championship.

"We had the ambition to challenge Ferrari and this is a problem in the challenge for the second position, and we have an ambition to finish ahead of Red Bull, and this is a problem to finish ahead of Red Bull.

"And it is also serious because we come from a few seasons in which we have reflected together, team and drivers, as to how we approach racing together and how we make sure that the interest of the team is protected.

"It is serious, but at the same time we approach it with a very constructive mindset because there is only one outcome, that the team will be more united and the team will be stronger in the way we pursue our quest, which is the drivers' and the team's quest, together."

US murderer Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after failed execution

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 17:44:26 GMT

US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.

Pike, 50, has been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years and is continuing to receive medical care, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.

She survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition.

Pike regained consciousness earlier this week and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.

Her case is now in uncharted territory as she is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

Pike's lawyers said in their statement that she was "grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances".

It is unclear what medical care Pike is receiving now that she is back in prison but her lawyers previously said she faced a "long road to recovery".

The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.

At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he did not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again.

The judge ordered the state to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.

Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.

Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.

Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Tennessee Governor Bill Lee declined to block the execution.

Since it failed, Pike's lawyers have renewed their calls for her sentence to be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Pike lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital following her botched execution. Her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.

Pike eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyer Randy Spivey said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"

At a press conference on Wednesday, her lawyers said she was shackled to the bed and suffering from pneumonia and significant swelling on her arms, while also being unable to swallow.

"We don't know the toll all of this will take" Spivey said of her mental health, adding that Pike felt "angry and confused".

Timely recognition or long overdue? How Gross is proving all-time bargain

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 17:07:02 GMT

Only Joao Pedro has been involved in more top-flight goals than Pascal Gross this season

Brighton midfielder Pascal Gross may be one of the best value-for-money signings in Premier League history.

In fact the 35-year-old has effectively cost the Seagulls minus £3m - and been involved in 86 Premier League goals over two spells.

Already in this campaign, Gross has been involved in seven Brighton goals in six games.

His latest provided the opener in his side's 2-0 win at Sunderland on Saturday, a slide-rule pass finding Maxim de Cuyper to slot home.

Gross became the oldest player to provide an assist in three successive Premier League games since a 38-year-old Ryan Giggs did so for Manchester United in February 2012.

In 2026, only Bruno Fernandes and Dominik Szoboszlai have created more chances than the German.

Gross was Brighton's first Premier League signing in 2017 for a reported £3m from Ingolstadt.

He left for his boyhood club Borussia Dortmund in 2024 for £8m - but in a surprise move he returned to Albion in January for about £1.7m.

So has Gross been underrated all this time?

Former England midfielder, and BBC pundit, Danny Murphy doesn't think so.

"The Premier League is shown worldwide, and he has been a part of that for so many years during a time when Brighton have been a shining light," he said.

"You don't have to play for a big-six team to be appreciated in the Premier League. Gross is not under the radar, because people know how good he is."

This video can not be played

Highlights: Brighton beat Sunderland despite controversial Struijk red card

Brighton win at Sunderland despite controversial red card

This video can not be played

Pascal Gross is 'showing the Premier League's elite how it's done'

A little-heralded German from relegated Ingolstadt, nobody could have anticipated the impact Gross, nor Albion, would go on to have.

"There's an argument Gross is pound-for-pound the best value player in the Premier League over the last 10 years, especially when you look at his goal involvements," said BBC Radio Sussex commentor Johnny Cantor.

"However, he also drives standards in training, sets a high bar and is a huge influence in the dressing room.

"Technically he is excellent, has superb delivery but also possesses an awareness, popping up in spaces all around the pitch. Managers have leaned on him, team-mates respect him, and fans of all generations adore him.

"He will surely be remembered as one of the best Albion players of the modern age."

Since joining Brighton, Gross is seventh for Premier League assists with 52 to go with his 34 goals in 253 league games.

All the more remarkable when you consider his journey with Brighton appeared over two years ago when he went home to join his beloved Borussia Dortmund.

Albion supporter Maz Mirzadeh said: "When he left for Dortmund, it was like going through a heartbreak and seeing an ex go back to their childhood sweetheart.

"He's outrageously good and massively underappreciated.

"If you watch him play, you would think someone's put him in slow-motion settings, but what he lacks in pace, he makes up in superior football IQ, technical brilliance and working harder than any other player on the pitch."

Subscribe and listen for everything you love about the Seagulls

Gross has been key in Brighton climbing to third in the Premier League

Gross played 66 times for Dortmund, scoring one goal and assisting 17 times, but on 2 January 2026, he came back to Brighton.

Aged 34 at the time, many wondered if it was more of a romantic career swansong.

"There may have been concerns that he may not have been able to recreate the impact of his first period at the Amex but that has been dispelled already," added Cantor.

Only Chelsea's Joao Pedro can better Gross' goal contributions this season in the top flight. Pedro has five goals and three assists, to his former Brighton team mate's three goals and four assists.

The midfielder - who retired from international football after the World Cup - has also played every single minute for Brighton in all competitions, nine games so far.

Former Liverpool and Fulham midfielder Murphy said: "He's an intelligent footballer, with a great football IQ.

"You can see that he has grown into that version of himself over the years. That happens in football - it happened to me - when you know what you can't do, as much as you know what you can do.

"So, you don't see him trying to beat people on the outside with his pace. Instead he loves a little chop, or a Cruyff turn to give himself space and time, or to play a quick first-time pass around the corners. That's why he always seems to be in space.

"His versatility tells you about his intelligence as well. He is able to play as a full-back, central midfield or, recently, as more of a 10. He is scoring and making goals.

"I am sure this won't be his last season with Brighton but, even if it was, he is already going to be remembered as one of the Brighton greats by their supporters for what he has given so far to the club, especially with him coming back and doing what he is doing. It is nothing short of remarkable."

This form led to Gross being the sixth oldest player to be named Premier League player of the month, for September.

Seagulls fan Mirzadeh added: "Even in his 'unc' era, he's showing the Premier League's elite how it's done.

"If he was called Pascal Silva and played for a top-six club he might get the recognition and respect he truly deserves."

Danny Murphy was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan

Northampton outgun Bath in 119-point thriller

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 16:07:54 GMT

Ollie Sleightholme scored three of Northampton's 11 tries

The Prem

Northampton (26) 71

Tries: F Smith, Sleightholme 3, Freeman 2, Dingwall, Pater, Kemeny, Mitchell, Coles Cons: F Smith 8

Bath (29) 48

Tries: Carr-Smith, C Griffin, A Griffin, Green 2, Carreras, Bayliss Cons: Russell 5 Pens: Russell

Northampton came out on top of a high-octane 18-try thriller at home to Bath, the second highest scoring game in English top-flight history.

The two sides had surpassed 100 points on the scoreboard with 15 minutes remaining and continued to showcase unstoppable, attacking flair as the play went end-to-end.

Northampton eventually streaked clear in the second half, with Ollie Sleightholme scoring a hat-trick and Tommy Freeman scoring twice as they finished with 11 tries and bounced back from defeat by Bristol a week ago.

The loss is the first of the season for Bath, who made 12 changes for the match, with Arthur Green getting two of their seven tries and Charlie Griffin also scoring one on his Prem debut.

The 119 points scored falls short of the record in the English top flight - the 127 points shared in Saints' 94-33 win over Bristol in May.

Caluori scores as Saracens too strong for Bristol

Leicester battle back to beat Gloucester

Rory Hutchinson fed Fin Smith to cross first for Saints and while Bath arrived with a younger-looking starting XV there was no evidence of inexperience, as a moment of world-class Finn Russell skill opened a gap for Green to break through and Tom Carr-Smith to cross.

Bath hit Northampton again through 21-year-old Charlie Griffin before Saints slickly whipped the ball between their backs until it reached Sleightholme for their second try.

Tommy Freeman dived under the posts for Northampton's third right after Bath's Josh Bayliss was shown yellow for repeated infringements but, again, there was nothing to separate the sides as Archie Griffin rolled over under two tacklers for the visitors' third.

Kepu Tuipulotu barged through midfield and found Green to make it 26-19 to Bath, which was quickly cancelled out by Fraser Dingwall's score at the other end, leaving Russell's penalty on the stroke of half-time the only mark of difference.

Arthur Green was making his first appearance of the season for Bath

Green doubled his tally quickly after the restart, but Saints full-back James Pater pounced on Santiago Carreras' dropped ball to steal possession and sprint the distance to the line.

Carreras made amends with a try of his own although Northampton started turning the screw despite Bath unloading their bench of big-hitters.

Josh Kemeny scored in the corner, Alex Mitchell followed - collecting his own grubber kick in a solo showpiece - and Sleightholme capped a superb move that saw Saints turn the ball over by their own line and sweep up the field.

Sleightholme completed his hat-trick four minutes later and while Bayliss kept Bath in touch to close the gap to 57-48, it did not last as Saints had more in the tank.

Alex Coles barged over before Freeman rounded off a blockbuster day in the closing stages.

Northampton Saints head coach Sam Vesty told BBC Radio Northampton:

"Both teams took opportunities pretty quickly and I think both teams will be slightly disappointed in how they exited their end, in terms of when they've got the ball and got control of it.

"We gave it up quite a lot to them and put ourselves defensively under pressure We're not happy with the 48 part of that scoreline.

"We don't want it to be basketball. Obviously lots and lots of very good stuff but there's a good couple of areas for us to focus to be better - a more ruthless Bath and that's a very different game.

[On the attack] "We were so clinical with our execution of what we were doing. Absolutely fantastic.

"I thought our breakdown was very good, lots and lots of positives but we need to be better coming out of our end."

Bath head of rugby Johann van Graan told BBC Radio Bristol:

"It's dsappointing if you score 48 points away from home and lose the game.

"I think we lost control between minutes 50 and 60. The back end of both halves we conceded a yellow card and against a team like Saints it's difficult to contain them.

"But look at the positives, we played some fantastic rugby today."
