King warns malicious online actors are evolving tactics

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 15:56:32 GMT

King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

The letter from the King to NCSC came after he spoke to AI executives at Dumfries House in Ayrshire last month on how the tech can be used to benefit security.

The meeting followed a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

For the second time in three Premier League matches, Bruno Guimaraes has come to Arsenal's rescue.

Having sparked their 2-0 win at Sunderland in September with the crucial first goal, the £75m summer signing came off the bench again to have a pivotal impact against Leeds on Saturday.

This time it was the winner as the Gunners came from behind for a 2-1 success in a testing encounter at Emirates Stadium.

But Ecuador international Piero Hincapie was carried off during the warm-down, raising concern the defender has suffered an injury.

He came on as a late substitute against Daniel Farke's side but completed extra running after the final whistle - a practice most clubs use.

A fifth win in six league games put Mikel Arteta's side level on points with leaders Manchester City, but their title defence has certainly not been without its scares so far.

Following on from their comprehensive 3-0 defeat at Brighton last time out, Arsenal fell behind in a league match for a third time in four league matches - and only a David Raya penalty save stopped them from trailing at Sunderland as well.

For large parts of the game against Leeds, they were nowhere near their best but, after going behind in the 55th minute, Riccardo Calafiori and Guimaraes - on his full home debut - secured an important three points.

"It was a great game of football. Leeds were brilliant for one hour." said Ally McCoist on TNT Sports.

"Mikel Arteta made changes when he needed to and the substitutions gave Arsenal what they needed. That's what champions do. Leeds can hold their heads high."

By getting wins when below par the mark of champions or are there reasons for concern for Arteta and Arsenal?

Coming into the season as defending champions, Arsenal were looking to make a statement signing to make their rivals take notice.

They did not bring in the attacker they wanted but Guimaraes looks like he could be that key arrival to help Arteta's men build on their success.

The 28-year-old midfielder is a 'win-now' signing in the peak years of his career.

He responded well to a disappointing performance in the defeat by Brighton, where he made his full league debut.

The Brazilian international has now scored two goals that have helped his side to valuable points and justified the decision to spend big on Guimaraes, even if the Gunners are inundated with top quality options in midfield.

Arteta said: "He wasn't at that level against Brighton, and this is the level for Arsenal. Every week, every game, every minute, every action, you have to be at that level.

Guimaraes was the first player to score twice from the bench this season and both goals have been from outside the box.

Arsenal won the league last season in part because of their excellent defence.

The Gunners conceded the fewest goals in the league but have already conceded five in six games.

The partnership of Gabriel Magalhaes and William Saliba is one of the best in the world and Arsenal look to be missing the injured Frenchman's calmness.

Ezri Konsa was brought in from Aston Villa for £55m and, despite his quality, is still getting used to his new surroundings.

Hincapie has suffered from muscular issues this term and now faces an anxious wait to discover whether he requires another spell on the sidelines.

"So if you don't want it more than the opponent, you are not able to cope emotionally with certain situations, you're going to suffer.

"And we all suffered and we didn't enjoy that game, but then you have to learn the lesson and we certainly done that.

"We speak about it and you could sense that there was something in those tummies."

Arteta made some big calls when naming his starting XI.

He opted to start with German Kai Havertz up front despite the forward returning early from international duty after picking up a hamstring issue, leaving Viktor Gyokeres on the bench again.

Gyokeres had scored four goals, registering in every match for Sweden, in the last international break, but looks to have work to do to win his manager round.

The 28-year-old has yet to start a Premier League game and in his cameos this season has looked far from the level required as a striker who could fire Arsenal to back-to-back titles.

The forward line did not click against Leeds and, with Havertz looking like he lacked match sharpness, thoughts turned towards whether Arsenal missing out on an elite attacker in the summer would haunt them.

Winger Christos Tzolis, who has shone at times this season following his summer arrival, suffered a hamstring issue with Greece and, with Eberechi Eze out of form, Arteta used Noni Madueke on the left wing.

Madueke was left out of the last England squad due to a lack of minutes with Arsenal but, after "being the best player in training for the last 10 days" according to Arteta, now could be the chance for him to prove his worth.

Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 15:23:47 GMT

Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".

The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.

The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.

"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.

The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.

The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.

It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".

The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.

Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.

Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure María Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.

Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway".

He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

Sara Sharif's grandfather granted guardianship of her siblings in Pakistan

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 14:27:43 GMT

Sara Sharif's paternal grandfather has been granted guardianship of her siblings by a court in Pakistan.

The decision comes after years of legal limbo following the murder of 10-year-old Sara by her father and stepmother in 2023.

All five children, who are now aged between 16 and four, have been living in Pakistan since 2023. They were asked to speak to the judge in court, where the eldest said they were comfortable and the siblings were settled.

Sara's grandfather, Muhammed Sharif, told the BBC he was relieved to be granted guardianship after three years of legal battles, saying his hope is that the children "stay healthy" and receive "a good education".

"It is my responsibility to ensure they get the best possible education and care," he said.

When told by the judge that the grandfather would become their guardian, the eldest child responded saying "that's all good".

The five children have been in Pakistan since August 2023, when they were brought to the country by Sara's father, stepmother and uncle after Sara was killed.

The family was in hiding for weeks before the children were discovered by police at the grandfather's house. They were initially put into state childcare.

The adults flew back to the UK and were arrested at the airport. Sara's father Urfan Sharif and stepmother Beinash Batool were found guilty of Sara's murder. Sharif was sentenced to a minimum of 40 years in prison and Batool received a minimum of 33 years.

Her uncle, Faisal Malik, was found guilty of causing or allowing her death and given a 16-year sentence.

Sara had been hooded, burned and beaten during a "campaign of torture" that lasted two years before her body was found at the family home in Woking, Surrey.

In Pakistan, Sara's grandfather was given temporary custody of her siblings in October 2023. All but the youngest are now attending school in Pakistan, the grandfather has said.

Speaking following Saturday's decision, their grandfather said "we will help them to return to a normal life".

"Hardships can happen to any person at any time, at any place," he said, adding "we will move forward".

Muhammed said that he speaks to his son Urfan once a week or every second week. "Not with the children, not regarding the case. Nothing else, just to ask about each other's well-being".

When asked about allegations that he had helped hide the three adults, Muhammed said they had left soon after arriving in Jhelum and that at the time he had told them to return to the UK.

The children's grandfather added that the siblings will keep their British passports and go back to the UK "when they reach the right age".

The children were made wards of court in England, and Surrey County council had been trying to bring them back through the courts in Pakistan.

Their grandfather has been fighting for them to stay with him. Surrey withdrew from the case in June, saying it had no ability to pursue the application in Pakistan, as English proceedings are coming to an end.

A final decision on their guardianship had not been made in Pakistan's courts until Saturday.

Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 11:09:16 GMT

A Green Party MP has said her party needs to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism.

The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups.

Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the Green Party.

It comes after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said it was not being protected from entryism - where people sign up to a party to try to change it.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists."

The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country".

Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights.

She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."

Appearing on BBC Radio 4 programme Any Questions on Friday, Lucas said she was not putting any blame on the party's current leader, Zack Polanski, who she said had done "great things" for the party.

"Our constitution was written decades ago, well before we had MPs, before we had mayors, before we had anything like the number of that we have today," the ex-leader said.

Lucas, who was for years the face of the Greens as its first and sole MP until 2024, added the party needed to be made "a welcoming place for Jewish people."

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Green Party membership has increased since Zack Polanksi announced his leadership bid in May 2025. Unlike other political parties, our members can bring and set policy.

"This is one motion alongside dozens of others that was discussed at our biggest-ever party conference. Every motion submitted to conference undergoes debate and no single interest group drives policy. "

Polanski, who is Jewish, previously told the BBC he would not have voted for the motion and instead would have voted for an amended version.

However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious".

Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

Ashok Kumar, a Green Party member and part of the Greens for Palestine group, voted for the motion and told the BBC last week it was about "Palestinian liberation."

He said he didn't feel the vote was harming the image of the Green Party, and that a growing number of people see this as a core issue.

"They see the violence that's (been) occurring over the last three years," he told BBC Politics Live. "So, I think the Zionist position is actually the marginal position.

Following Polanksi's by-election defeat in Holborn and St Pancras this week, the leader of the Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said he should resign.

She added it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on the motion or amendments. He left early to campaign for the north London by-election, which Labour won on Thursday with Greens coming second.

Following his defeat, Polanski told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.

He lost out to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.

Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 10:06:23 GMT

An artificial intelligence (AI) agent developed by Anthropic went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the 18 July tip was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation - but the force criticised the tech firm for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

It said the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".

It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.

Citing Anthropic, the police department said its AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites when it had sent the fake tip.

The company behind the Claude chatbot discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.

But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.

"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media.

"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."

The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.

But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide", the force said.

Anthropic this week published a report detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.

Organisations that had been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.

The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.

US President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will co-ordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers and religious groups.

Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, OpenAI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.

In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating, leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face.

Volunteer police chief fired after Palantir probe

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 09:19:53 GMT

The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman.

Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday.

The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller.

Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing."

Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone.

The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened.

He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone.

The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met.

Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again.

Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust.

"That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe.

"They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives."

In April, the Metropolitan Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, urged officers to be "extremely cautious" about carrying Met-issued devices while off duty after the force upgraded its Lawful Business Monitoring software.

The federation's general secretary, Matt Cane, said staff had not been told the upgrade included the introduction of Palantir's artificial intelligence technology, appearing to mark its first deployment to monitor Met systems.

In May, Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes told the London Assembly's Police and Crime Committee that officers were not under any "additional surveillance in the workplace" after the force began using AI in a bid to root out bad behaviour.

He said the Met had considered the reputational risks of using the "divisive" technology, but added that it helped identify "unacceptable, dishonest, corrosive behaviours" among officers.

The London Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac) blocked the Met from signing a two-year contract with Palantir to provide artificial intelligence technology for criminal investigations.

Mopac said the force had failed to set out its procurement strategy, describing this as a "clear and serious breach" of procedure.

Palantir is now suing Mopac, alleging it unlawfully blocked the deal after taking the company's "values and ethics" into account, which it said was an "irrelevant consideration".

Palantir, founded by controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel, holds contracts with a number of UK public bodies, including the NHS and the Ministry of Defence.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is currently facing growing pressure from Labour MPs and trade unions to end government contracts with Palantir.

Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, who recently joined the company, warned against "mob rule" in government procurement.

Lord Watson told BBC Radio 4's Political Thinking With Nick Robinson: "One of the things I'd say to my former colleagues is, 'Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule lead procurement practices?'

"Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one."

Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 09:17:36 GMT

They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.

It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to spectators.

By the execution time of 05:00, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.

That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.

The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.

Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner". The local sheriff had died four months earlier and his widow had become his unlikely replacement.

She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was a hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.

That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in the US. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.

By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.

A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.

The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be livestreamed.

"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked.

"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC.

He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining - it was at 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%.

"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.

It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in.

With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment... bring your popcorn, invite your friends".

Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream.

"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up... to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."

Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's death in 2002, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.

The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution.

"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said.

"Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."

But the polarisation and rhetoric in US politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University.

"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said.

"So it's not like they're cheering a public execution - they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"

Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.

Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said surveys point to a declining appetite for violence in the US.

"This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people."

"I think it's this: a public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."

The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday.

US Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned and said he would not watch it if it were livestreamed.

Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.

He did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution.

"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?

BBC News Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:22 GMT

When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer.

But because she had been removed from her biological parents at the age of seven months and later adopted, she had no way of accessing her family medical history.

"Not knowing anything about yourself genetically is terrifying," says the 26-year-old, "you can't even begin to imagine it."

The lump turned out to be non-cancerous, but it was one of many occasions when she found herself unable to answer questions about her biological family's health.

Aaliyah, now a trainee solicitor, spent years trying to source information from local authorities and eventually made an official data access request to Bradford Council, which removed her from her biological family as a baby.

She says the whole process took its toll.

"I would say bureaucratic hellscape is an understatement," she admits.

Days before Aaliyah's 25th birthday, a large unmarked envelope landed on the doormat of her home, in Birmingham.

"I rip it open, thinking it's an early birthday present," she says.

But what was inside was the response to her data request - pages and pages of her family history, including some medical details she had been painstakingly trying to track down for years.

The documents contained upsetting information alluding to the reason she was taken into care, alongside court records and a personal letter from her social worker.

"They were just given to me in a completely nondescript pile, and they contained completely earth-shattering information, of which I don't think I have ever recovered from," she says.

Aaliyah says knowing about her biological family's health could have helped her understand her own medical concerns.

"My biological mother struggled with eating disorders all her life," she says. "I had very severe anorexia in my teens and that would have been incredibly useful to know."

When a child is adopted in the UK, their NHS number - or equivalent health service identifier - is changed to protect their anonymity.

Their existing medical records should be merged with their new record, but this does not necessarily include their wider family medical history.

And while some local authorities offer specialist support for adoptees up to 21 or 25, the ease of access can vary across the country.

The BBC contacted Bradford Council, which said: "We are genuinely sorry that when Aaliyah received sensitive and personal information through her subject access request, we did not offer the support or signposting she needed. We recognise that we should have done more.

"Following Aaliyah's experience, we are strengthening our approach so that adults accessing their records are given clear information about the support available."

Bradford Children and Families Trust has now offered Aaliyah a meeting to further discuss her experience.

For Dr Chris Tennyson, a delay in getting information about his birth father's health could have put his life at risk.

The 40-year-old clinical psychologist, from Belfast, was adopted as a baby in the 1980s to "a really loving mum and dad, [in a] really comfortable family home".

But in his 20s, he became increasingly curious about his biological origins. He met his birth mother, but his attempts to find out about his father stalled after social workers warned him off asking questions.

Eight years later, Chris tried to trace him again, but it wasn't until he was 33 that a meeting was finally arranged.

Then, on the afternoon the father and son were due to meet, a social worker approached Chris.

"There's something that I need to share with you," the social worker told him. "Your father wants me to let you know that there's a genetic medical condition within your family."

A member of Chris's biological family died in 2000, when the condition came to light. At the time, other members of the family were offered testing. But Chris, who was then aged 14, was not contacted.

The condition, called malignant hyperthermia, causes a potentially life-threatening reaction to certain drugs used during anaesthesia.

While genes linked to it can run in families, not everyone who inherits one of these will necessarily experience a reaction with anaesthesia.

After undergoing genetic tests, Chris discovered his potential risk at the age of 37 - some 23 years after the condition had become known in his wider family.

He says a lack of understanding of how to support adopted adults resulted in the delay in him getting tested.

Chris, who now works with adoption and fostering services in Northern Ireland, says the lack of available information for adoptees is "a huge blind spot".

"There needs to be some kind of mechanism where adopted people's care records can be updated with family information that becomes available throughout the lifespan."

First-time mum Courtney-Grace says she is relieved her baby daughter, Tine, will have access to the crucial family medical history she lacked when she grew up.

Now living in the North of England, the 28-year-old was adopted as a baby and spent time in foster care as a teenager.

"The only thing we knew about my medical history is my biological mom was mentally ill, and had depression."

In her mid-20s, Courtney-Grace was diagnosed with a genetic mutation, which can be inherited and is associated with an increased risk of tumours.

Her symptoms had previously been misdiagnosed as asthma and anxiety, which she says was based off the little doctors knew about her mum.

Courtney-Grace believes allowing medical professionals access to familial history without interfering with data protection rules wouldn't just benefit adoptees, but the entire population.

"The system needs a bit of an overhaul as a whole," she says.

A government consultation on adoption support was launched in February 2026.

Josh MacAlister, the minister for children and families - who is responsible for adoption and children's social care in England - told the BBC that medical records was one of the issues being looked at.

"Adoption support and how it's set up at the moment isn't working well enough and there are obvious gaps in a number of areas that we're going to be looking at making changes to," MacAlister said.

He acknowledged that the current system did not strike the right balance between safeguarding biological relatives' medical privacy and enabling adopted people to access information relevant to their own health.

"We do need to change how we keep, retain, and share medical records," he said.

Authorities in England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all make provisions for adoptees to access their medical history, but the way this operates in practice can vary hugely in the different nations.

None of the four nations gives patients the legal right to that information.

But they advise that when a new clinical record is created for an adopted child, enough information must be kept to support continuity of care.

NHS England said depending on the circumstances of an adoption there may be a need to "protect from disclosure any information about a third party".

But it added that it is important any new NHS records, if created, contain sufficient information to allow for a continuity of care.

For Courtney-Grace, her own diagnosis means her five-month-old daughter will now be closely monitored.

Cord blood was collected when Tine was born, and it will be tested for the genetic condition when she is five. If she has inherited it, a plan will be put in place.

"She has the medical information," Courtney-Grace says. "She can say, 'My mum has this'".

A list of organisations in the UK offering support and information with some of the issues in this story is available at BBC Action Line

Ashe was too scared to cancel her wedding - the story became a hit song

BBC News Fri, 09 Oct 2026 23:01:22 GMT

No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day.

Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck.

As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark.

She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive.

He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean.

In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself.

On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true.

"I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s.

"I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around."

As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away.

Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out.

Its name? Stop the Wedding.

It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts.

"You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt.

"Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says.

"If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used."

What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"?

"I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!"

Released in August, Stop The Wedding this week became one of the 10 most-played songs in the world on Spotify.

On Friday, it broke into the top five of the UK singles chart, while on TikTok, thousands of videos use Ashe's song to highlight red flags in their own relationships.

"I don't think I even let myself dream of this," she says of the song's popularity.

"It's something you hope for when you're first starting out, but when you've been in the business for 10 years, it's a little bit of a shock to the system."

The success is even sweeter because, three years ago, Ashe nearly quit music altogether.

A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations.

It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music.

After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter.

She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words.

The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career.

Her then-husband was not impressed.

"I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'.

"It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time."

It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit.

Moral of The Story (key lyric: "you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You.

Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming.

When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month.

"There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now.

"It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her."

In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness.

"I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music."

For six months, she led a quiet, domestic life. But when pop singer Suki Waterhouse invited her to a session, it rekindled her passion for writing.

She made a tentative return with 2024's deeply confessional album Wilson, then teamed up with Billie Eilish's brother Finneas O'Connell to form The Favors, before signing a new deal with Atlantic Records.

Those experiences mean she's treating the success of Stop The Wedding very differently.

"You can get swept up by all the updates on your phone, but this time I'm navigating the emotions of that, and also going for a four-mile walk and calling my mom.

"There's a real groundedness."

The same can't be said for her new album, Girl of Your Dreams, which is almost deliriously over the top.

Stop The Wedding sets the tone, with abrupt tempo changes that track Ashe's inner turmoil. Lasso The Moon is more whimsical, setting out the star's outlandish requirements for a new partner.

"God forbid I raise my standards," she laughs.

Love Bomb explores the psychology of a manipulative ex (guess who?); while Swan Lake is a comically villainous portrait of Ashe's possessiveness, complete with a Bugsy Malone chorus line.

It's a deliberately maximalist record, recalling the lush orchestrations of ELO and The Carpenters, with a nod to the revivalist pop of Ashe's friend Laufey.

"We were so bored of making music that's boring," she says.

"It scratches an itch for me as an artist to do something different and not meet the status quo."

The album ends back at her second wedding. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada.

"You'll be my Tuesday night and my Sunday drive / And the last speech at my funeral," she sings.

Expanding on that idea, Ashe incorporates the ebullient sound of a New Orleans funeral band in the song's closing moments.

And the person they're burying is the disillusioned girl from Stop The Wedding.

Ashe's album, Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October.

Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you

BBC News Fri, 09 Oct 2026 23:01:14 GMT

If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK.

The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades.

But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an £7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience.

Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.

The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).

What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.

Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.

Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear.

"They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.

A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."

Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".

But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how easy the stores are to navigate.

"You can get everything you need... it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."

Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up.

Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular.

Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck."

The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p.

Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off.

She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with.

Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction".

"I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions."

Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on".

"As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important."

The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment.

The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies.

It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity.

Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals.

"They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says.

While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products.

"When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says.

Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert.

But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results.

Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops.

There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year.

For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area.... Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says.

Additional reporting by Ben Sturt and Anuk Weerawardana

Number of known species of giant waterlilies almost doubles

New Scientist October 08, 2026

Giant waterlilies are not exactly inconspicuous plants. But in the past few years, we have discovered no fewer than three new species, taking the total to five. The latest species to be described was identified with the help of social media, satellite photos and a mad jungle dash in the dark.

“I think it’s incredible that we find something so new, which is so large, in this world where we think everything is already known,” says Maarten Christenhusz at the Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland, who has helped describe two of the new species.

Why rediscovering extinct species can actually be a bad thing

Giant waterlilies are famed for their massive leaves, which grow up to 3 metres wide. For many decades, just two species were known: Victoria amazonica and Victoria cruziana. Then in 2016, Carlos Magdalena at the Royal Botanic Gardens in Kew, London, noticed that giant waterlilies grown from seeds from Bolivia were a bit different, with even larger leaves. In 2022, Magdalena and his colleagues published a paper showing that this was a new species, Victoria boliviana.

Advertisement

Magdalena hasn’t stopped there. In 2021, Jeremiah Harris, who runs a carnivorous plant business in the US, posted pictures online that he took while swimming near the Inírida river in Colombia next to what he assumed was V. amazonica.

Magdalena was struck by the photos because scientists had thought there were no giant waterlilies in this region. “This river is geographically completely separated from the Amazon, and has been for millions of years, and that is why this is such an interesting find,” says Christenhusz.

See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their team examined satellite photos and found telltale green dots confirming there really were giant waterlilies growing there. They then organised an expedition to the region. The team found two plants but neither was flowering – and analysing the flowers is a crucial step in establishing whether a waterlily really is a new species.

At 11pm on the last night of the expedition, with the plane due to leave at 9am, the researchers seemed to have failed. Then one of the guides, Gustavo Melo from the Indigenous Tucano community, said he knew where some more giant waterlilies were growing. The team set off by boat in the dark, and found five plants in a small lake just before sunrise, including some that were flowering.

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues have now published a paper describing the new species, which they have named Victoria colombiana. It differs from V. amazonica in the orientation of the spines beneath the leaves, and in the shape of its flowers and fruits. The spines are a defence against manatees and plant-eating fish, Christenhusz says, so they vary between species depending on which herbivores are most prevalent.

Botanists have finally proved what Charles Darwin was unable to nail down – that a genus of plants known to catch insects also digests them, suggesting the extent of plant carnivory has been underestimated

As far as the team is aware, V. colombiana is found in only one small area. A single event, such as a pollution spill, could wipe out the entire species, says Christenhusz. But the team is planning to try to collect seeds to help ensure the species survives.

Meanwhile, Magdalena also realised that the giant waterlilies growing in the Pantanal region of South America, hundreds of kilometres to the south-east of Colombia, must have been isolated from other populations for a very long time. Sure enough, genetic studies revealed that they are another distinct species, despite looking very similar to V. cruziana. Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues will publish a paper soon to describe this fifth species, which they have decided to name Victoria mattogrossensis.

Phytotaxa DOI: 10.11646/phytotaxa.778.2.1

The big unanswered question about Russia’s ‘plague’ death

New Scientist October 08, 2026

The recent death of a lab worker at a plague research institute sparked fears of another pandemic. But on 7 October, Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it was ending precautionary measures and that most of the nearly 200 people put under quarantine have been released, after tests found no dangerous pathogens.

Was this all much ado about nothing? After all, we still don’t know what caused the pneumonia that killed the lab worker, nor, if it was plague, how she became infected. And the most pressing question of all: why did Russia respond so dramatically to her death? The measures taken went beyond what would be expected for a case of plague. There are two broad possibilities: conspiracy or colossal screw-up.

Nearly 200 people isolated after lab worker in Russia dies of plague

What we know is that Daria Shipilova, a 28-year-old lab worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia, died of pneumonia on 2 October, three days after being admitted to a local hospital. A “DN Shipilova” is an author on an abstract from a conference earlier this year about testing plague strains for antibiotic resistance, suggesting Shipilova worked directly with the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis.

Advertisement

After her death, nearly 200 people who might have had contact with her were placed in quarantine. Around 60 employees at the institute were reportedly locked in for days, and Federal Security Service officers escorted ambulances carrying those quarantined. The head of Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, is said to have travelled to Irkutsk – a 6-hour flight from Moscow – on 2 October for an emergency meeting about “a particularly dangerous infection”, and some local companies imposed mask mandates.

The thing is, there are many plague cases around the world each year and they don’t trigger this kind of response. This is because basic hygiene measures can prevent the spread of the bacterium, while prompt treatment with antibiotics can stop people who might have been infected from developing any symptoms.

DNA evidence shows that plague bacteria devastated a community in Siberia more than 5000 years ago, challenging the idea that there were no major disease outbreaks before the advent of farming and large settlements

For instance, in 2025, a young man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague – where Y. pestis infects the lungs – acquired from sick cats. The 46 people he had potentially been in contact with were given a seven-day course of antibiotics, in line with guidelines from the World Health Organization. End of story.

So why did Russia quarantine all contacts? One explanation is that health officials knew Shipilova was exposed to something more dangerous than a natural strain of Y. pestis.

“Physical lockdown indicates it cannot be controlled with prophylactic antibiotics, implying engineered pan-resistance or that it isn’t plague at all,” biologist Kevin Esvelt at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology posted on social media. The response “clearly indicates that Russia believes an epidemic is possible – and that the responsible agent is likely a pandemic weapon or otherwise embarrassing for the government”.

Free newsletter

Esvelt created the first artificial gene drive capable of wiping out an entire species, and has since pivoted to preventing bioterrorism. He may well be right. There are certainly good reasons to suspect a cover-up.

We know that the Soviet Union had a massive bioweapons programme that included trying to make Y. pestis resistant to antibiotics (the “engineered pan-resistance” Esvelt mentioned), and it had a long history of denying related accidents. For instance, in 1979, at least 68 people died after the accidental release of anthrax from a bioweapons facility in the city of Sverdlovsk. The Soviet Union claimed the deaths were caused by food poisoning.

What’s more, a 2006 paper by Raymond Zilinskas at the Center for Nonproliferation Studies in California says the Irkutsk institute was involved in bioweapon research, though this was only “a small portion” of its activities. Bioweapons research has continued in Russia and probably expanded recently, though there is no evidence the Irkutsk institute is still involved.

Plague, leprosy, smallpox and other diseases didn’t jump from animals to humans when we thought. Ancient DNA is revealing where they come from and how they changed history

The other explanation is a secondary screw-up: that the officials who imposed the quarantine measures didn’t know what killed Shipilova and leapt to the conclusion it was something nasty. It can take three days to test for Y. pestis, after all, so the results might not have been available on 2 October. Even if the results were known, officials might not have believed them, given Russia’s history of lying about such things.

Alternatively, maybe Shipilova had a strain of plague that could have been treated with antibiotics if they had been given early enough (all the strains that were tested in the abstract linked to her were susceptible to these drugs), but officials overreacted because they weren’t aware of the appropriate procedures.

What really happened may never be clear. After all, Russia doesn’t have a reputation for being trustworthy – so even if it tells the truth, we won’t know it.

AI or ‘super intelligence’? Trump isn’t the only one who is confused

New Scientist October 08, 2026

In the decades since the field began, most of the debate surrounding artificial intelligence has been about the intelligence part: can machines really think like we do? But in recent weeks, US President Donald Trump has kicked off an argument about the other part – and joined a long tradition of shifting the goal posts when it comes to AI.

“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing,” said Trump during a speech at the UN General Assembly on 22 September. He is calling for artificial intelligence to be rebranded as “super intelligence”, backing this move with an executive order signed on 29 September and the launch this week of a body called the Super Intelligence Force for coordinating US AI policy.

The most interesting mathematical discoveries in OpenAI’s 722 new papers

Putting aside the fact that “Super Intelligence Force” sounds like a Saturday morning cartoon, what are we to make of this attempted rebrand? Trump isn’t actually alone in seeking to distance modern AI systems from the original conception of AI in the 1940s and 50s. Last year, Meta CEO Mark Zuckberg published a note declaring that “superintelligence” (one word) is now in sight. Reaching further back, the word was originally popularised by philosopher Nick Bostrom as the title of his 2014 book.

Advertisement

For me, Trump’s super intelligence and Bostrom’s superintelligence have distinct meanings that are worth preserving. Trump’s rebrand is an effort to cement US dominance in the field of AI – his executive order states that “the term ‘Super Intelligence’ more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies”. But superintelligence as envisioned by Bostrom goes far beyond the capabilities of our current AI systems. To understand why, we need to dig into history a bit more.

Long before the birth of ChatGPT, AI researchers distinguished between weak AI and strong AI, terms first defined by philosopher John Searle in a 1980 paper titled “Minds, brains, and programs”. Loosely speaking, he considered weak AI to be a computer simulation of a human mind, but not an actual mind itself, whereas he felt strong AI describes actual cognition emerging from software. Searle dismissed this latter idea as ridiculous: “No one supposes… that a computer simulation of a rainstorm will leave us all drenched. Why on earth would anyone suppose that a computer simulation of understanding actually understood anything?” Decades on, I find it hard to disagree.

In the wake of Searle’s influential paper, weak and strong AI underwent their own Trump-style rebranding, as people began to discuss differences in AI capabilities rather than AI consciousness – perhaps because the former is much easier to measure and moves the arena of debate from the philosophy department to the computer science lab. Weak AI merged with another term, narrow AI, to mean a system capable of human-level performance at a specific task. We have been living with narrow AI for decades, depending on how you want to define it, encompassing everything from spam filters to chess playing to driverless cars. In some sense, once something becomes achievable by narrow AI, it is just software – a phenomenon known as the AI effect.

Strong AI, meanwhile, gave way to general AI – a system capable of human-level performance at any task. A general AI is a highly desirable goal because it means that, rather than having to build a new system for every possible task, the AI would be able to transfer learning from one domain to another, just as a human can. In 2002, general AI morphed into “artificial general intelligence”, or AGI, largely due to Shane Legg (who would go on to co-found the firm DeepMind) popularising the term.

Most of the big AI companies, including DeepMind and OpenAI, were founded with the stated goal of achieving AGI. In the 2010s, this was seen as a slightly wacky and sci-fi research goal. Today, it is a business model, with trillions of dollars of investment riding on building an AGI in the near-future.

Despite this, definitions of AGI are woolly. OpenAI’s charter defines it as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. An agreement between OpenAI and Microsoft that was leaked in 2024 defines it as a system capable of generating $100 billion in profit. OpenAI isn’t yet profitable, with expenditure far exceeding revenue, but that didn’t prevent its president, Greg Brockman, from saying “welcome to the AGI era” with the release of its Astra model in September.

However you define AGI, it isn’t the same thing as superintelligence. Bostrom defines this plainly in his book as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest”. In other words, a superintelligence must be more cognitively capable than any human scientist, artist, philosopher or other cognitive performer that ever lived. It isn’t enough to be better than Albert Einstein or Marie Curie – you must also beat William Shakespeare, Leonardo da Vinci, Steve Jobs, Jane Austen and many, many others. Clearly, we haven’t achieved superintelligence. A real superintelligence would probably transform the world in ways we can’t imagine.

There is one problem running though all of these definitions, though, and it lies in the second part of AI: what actually is intelligence, and how do we measure different levels of it?

The standard answer is intelligence quotient, or IQ. Attempts to measure the IQ of various high-end AI models (by having them produce answers to IQ test questions) give ranges of 130 to 150 IQ, although this is complicated by the fact that the tests themselves may have formed part of the models’ training data. Human IQ scores have reached over 200, often in young children because the scores depend on age, but higher scores are increasingly difficult to measure reliably. More pressingly, IQ is now widely considered to be a flawed measure of intelligence, rooted in eugenics, that ignores many aspects of human capability. Attempting to apply it to AI feels fairly fruitless, then.

As an alternative, some computer scientists have tried to come up with AI-specific intelligence tests. One of these is ARC-AGI, which looks not only at the capabilities of a model, but also at the cost of running it, meaning that less computationally intensive models can score higher. The test is now in its third iteration, and one of OpenAI’s latest models, GPT-6.1 Sol, scores 96.2 per cent, completing the test at a reasonably cheap $3800. Does that make it AGI? I don’t think so, and I would expect a fourth version of the ARC-AGI test to come along soon, resetting the bar that models must exceed.

Does this mean we will never achieve AGI, and then superintelligence? Despite the certainty of the AI firms that we will – which is probably half real belief and half marketing – I think at this point, it is impossible to say. The meanings of these terms and our methods for evaluating them are constantly shifting. What seemed liked magic in 2022 – a computer that could answer you back – is now an annoyance in 2026, with Google’s AI Overviews often producing confidently incorrect information at the top of your search results.

Today, the most impressive achievements in AI seem to come from mathematics, but perhaps that will soon become passé. My feeling is that, if AGI ever comes, there won’t be one moment in which we declare it has arrived, but rather a gradual realisation that it is already here and we’ve just started calling it something else.

When OpenAI announced its surprise solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, it produced one proof for humans and one for computers – however, they don’t match

Read original article

OpenAI mistranslated mathematics into code for its Navier-Stokes proof

New Scientist October 08, 2026

OpenAI appears to have made a subtle error when publishing its proofs of the Navier-Stokes problem, a team of mathematicians has claimed. The error doesn’t mean that the proofs are incorrect or that OpenAI hasn’t correctly solved the problem, but it does call into question whether mathematical results generated by AI models can always be relied on.

“What has to be done with all of these large language model-generated proofs is that they will have to be read by humans, and this creates an enormous extra burden on mathematicians,” says Anders Hansen at the University of Cambridge.

On 8 September, OpenAI announced that it had found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the most famous open problems in mathematics. It published the proof in two versions – one written in “natural language”, meaning a combination of English and mathematical symbols, as a human mathematician would write, and another written in the computer code Lean. The Lean proof is meant to be a formalisation of the natural-language version, allowing a computer to mechanically verify that all of its logical statements are true. The problem is, say Hansen and his team, that they don’t match.

Advertisement

“This formalisation process is trying to replace peer review,” says team member Fabian Circelli, also at the University of Cambridge. “Peer review would mean that human eyes look at the proofs. But what we’ve shown in this paper is that using this type of AI auto-formalisation can’t serve the same purpose.”

The most interesting mathematical discoveries in OpenAI’s 722 new papers

To be clear, the researchers aren’t saying that OpenAI has failed to solve the Navier-Stokes problem. It is entirely possible that both the natural-language proof and the Lean one provide a solution, just as there are hundreds of valid proofs of Pythagoras’s theorem. Instead, their point is a more subtle one: that OpenAI’s model has “mistranslated” when converting into Lean.

“We are not saying that the natural-language proof is wrong,” says Hansen. “Nor do we say that it is correct.” The issue is that OpenAI presents the two proofs as identical, stating on Github that “This repository contains Lean 4 formalizations of the results presented in [the paper] ‘Finite time blowup for Navier–Stokes’”.

This mistranslation occurs because the AI has to produce a Lean proof that “compiles”, meaning that the computer code is fully self-consistent and doesn’t produce an error, says Hansen. If, in the process of auto-formalisation, the AI finds a section of the proof that doesn’t compile, it will attempt to find a workaround even if it means diverging from the proof as written in natural language.

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

The team’s specific claim hinges on part of the proofs called Lemma 8.6. In the natural-language proof, an equation in this part requires that a certain value be below m + 4, where m is a whole number. In the Lean proof, the equivalent value is required to be below m + 5, which is mathematically weaker.

To understand why, imagine being asked to solve the equation x + 3 = 6, to which the answer is x = 3. It is possible to write a proof that x must be less than 4, and also that x must be less than 5. Both of these are perfectly true mathematical statements, but they say different things. The latter proof allows more possible answers for x, making it mathematically weaker.

OpenAI told New Scientist that it is aware of the mismatch between the natural-language proof and the Lean code, and that this doesn’t mean that either proof is invalid. It says it will rectify any errors in the natural-language proof as they are found, and will also continue the process of formalising the 722 maths papers the firm released this week, only some of which are accompanied by Lean proofs, which themselves haven’t been checked by hand.

Finding the divergence involved a slightly surreal process of asking ChatGPT to look for potential discrepancies between the natural-language and Lean proofs, then checking them by hand. Many of the discrepancies suggested by ChatGPT turned out, on inspection, to be consistent after all. “Going through all of these things manually was a nightmare,” says Hansen.

In all, it took the team about two weeks to identify a true discrepancy, compared with the 88 hours OpenAI said its agents spent generating the proofs. “OpenAI boast about how quickly they were able to generate this result, but that’s only part of the process,” says team member Alexander Bastounis at King’s College London.

Answering the question of whether AI models can accurately auto-formalise mathematics is essential if mathematicians are to trust these results. Anders and his team have demonstrated that it is possible for ChatGPT to produce a Lean version of a proof that doesn’t match the original natural language one, with the AI silently altering the logical argument in the process to cover up any errors. “It is trying to help me, but by doing that, it is not helping,” says Hansen.

Subscriber-only newsletter

If this were to happen for a long and complicated proof, it would be very difficult for anyone to notice without inspecting both versions in detail. This issue is only more pressing because of the batch of 722 papers OpenAI just released. If we think ‘all of this is now true, the only thing we need to do now is read the paper’, then that is dangerous, says Hansen. “The purpose of doing science is that mankind should have an understanding of how the world works so we can make educated decisions. If we lose that understanding, what are doing?”

Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London notes that in discussions like these, it is important to distinguish between the statement of a theorem and its proof. For example, the statement of the famous Fermat’s last theorem is that for positive whole number a, b, c and n, aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ only if n is 1 or 2. This is easy to convert into Lean and can easily be checked. Once you are happy that a statement in Lean is correct, if the proof of that statement compiles, you can be confident the proof is true.

The issue, as Hansen and his team have pointed out, is that this tells you nothing about the natural-language version of a proof published as a PDF document. “I am confident that the Navier-Stokes problem has been correctly resolved,” says Buzzard. “I am far less confident that the proof described in the PDF is correct.”

Hansen says he hopes OpenAI will take the team’s work “very seriously” and that more work must be done on developing robust auto-formalisation techniques. “Do we have the solution? Not yet. Is it possible to do this in a controlled way? Yes, it will be, but the optimal and the ultimate way of doing this is completely unknown.”

Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began a 10-year survey of the sky in June 2026. Advertisement

Two space rocks in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter were even more unusual ultra-fast rotators. Each was larger than 2 kilometres wide, but completed a full spin once every 5 minutes, something never seen before for such big asteroids.

The high rotation speed suggests that these asteroids aren’t rubble piles, but instead monolithic objects at least 30 times stronger than clay, says Vavilov.

This probably means our models of how asteroids have smashed together over the 4.6-billion-year history of the solar system aren’t correct, he says. That might mean these are pristine objects from the early solar system.

See Catherine Heymans at New Scientist Live 2026

Other fast-spinning asteroids have been spotted before, but nothing as large as these two. Standing on their surface, a person would travel at more than 100 kilometres per hour (over 60 miles per hour), much slower than Earth’s equatorial rotation of 1670 km/h (1040 mph). But because of the smaller size of the asteroids, it would feel “like a rollercoaster”, says Vavilov, and clinging to the surface would be difficult.

The asteroids might have been spun up by the sun heating their surfaces and giving them torque, known as the YORP effect, but that in itself is uncertain because of their large distance from the sun. “That’s another mystery,” says Vavilov, who hopes to study the asteroids in more detail in future.

A seasonal rise in covid-19 cases in Europe and North America has focused attention on a group of variants called XFG, which has dominated worldwide over the past year. Advertisement

AI predicted that a forgotten breast cancer drug could be repurposed to treat many respiratory and gastrointestinal viruses, and subsequent animal tests suggests it may be right

Aris Katzourakis at the University of Oxford points out, however, that real-time assessment of the impacts of a virus can be very difficult. “It takes time for something that sweeps through to turn into hospitalisations and for those to be recorded.”

This doesn’t mean a more dangerous strain couldn’t emerge in the future, for example, if many mutations accumulate in a single, immunosuppressed individual, which is how Omicron originated. “There is a risk that a new strain could emerge that causes a wave of infections again,” says Mellis.

There is also now far less monitoring that could provide early warning of such an event, he says. In particular, the amount of sequencing data has “fallen dramatically” over the last year.

Governments around the world also have worryingly “lackadaisical” attitudes to vaccine boosters, says Altmann. He points out that most children who are starting school have never been vaccinated, and it’s unclear what the consequences of that may be.
