Tattoos could be radically reimagined following the development of inks that can be turned on and off by exposing them to light. This could be used medically – or to hide the butterfly on your ankle from a judgemental relative.

Bruns has had a tattoo of fish scales using this method for the past two years, and says he has experienced no known side effects. “I get a lot of compliments on the fish scale tattoo,” he says. “After over two years in my skin, I haven’t seen any obvious fading yet.”

Advertisement

Instead of traditional inks, which people have used for thousands of years to decorate their bodies, Bruns and his colleagues employ photochromic dyes, which change from a transparent state to a coloured one when exposed to certain wavelengths of light. They call the new technology, which has been tested on silicon, “PhotoTat”.

There is little mechanical difference between a traditional tattoo and the new inks, says Bruns. Both are pigment particles implanted in the dermis with a needle, he says. They also both stay there permanently and are applied with the same machines and methods.

The difference is the pigment, says Bruns. With PhotoTat, “ultraviolet light writes the colour in, bright visible light erases it, and the cycle can be repeated”, he says. “The tattoo is permanent, but its appearance is not.”

Free newsletter

This could be useful in medical applications, such as for the tattoos used by doctors to guide radiation beams, which leave many patients permanently marked, says Bruns.

The light-sensitive tattoos can currently be made from 16 colours, which are clearly distinguishable from each other. From these colours, there are at least 300 different shades. White is unavailable because it reflects light, rather than absorbing it, so can’t be switched on and off like other colours. The researchers have also been unable to develop a true cyan.

Another issue is that the blue ink gradually develops a permanent, purplish colour as the dye slowly photo-degrades over many on/off cycles. Someone with one of these tattoos would also need to apply sunscreen to prevent the colour activating when they are exposed to sunlight.

In terms of safety, Bruns says the polymer that encapsulates the dyes is non-toxic and has a long history of use in permanent biomedical implants. “The colour-changing [dye] toxicity is unknown, but the toxicity of most tattoo pigments is equally unknown,” he says.

A temporary graphene tattoo that monitors blood pressure has been awarded the highest possible accuracy grading for such a monitoring device

Still, extensive safety studies need to be carried out before the tattoos will be available to the public.

Signe Bedsted Clemmensen at the University of Southern Denmark says tattoo ink in the body is a foreign substance, which has been linked to cancer, regardless of whether it is visible or invisible. “Therefore, many of the same health considerations and concerns that apply to traditional tattoo ink are also likely to apply to invisible tattoo ink,” she says.

Earlier this year, it emerged that red tattoo ink caused one man to lose all his hair and stop sweating. Tattooing has also recently been linked to localised damage to the immune system.

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Nearly 1 in 10 younger adults have plaque in their arteries, according to a study of almost 17,000 people. Known as atherosclerosis, the build-up of fatty plaque can cause narrowing that reduces blood flow, leading to heart attacks and strokes. Atherosclerosis is more common in people aged over 50, so younger individuals may be assumed to be at low risk.

“The most important message is that atherosclerosis is already present in a meaningful fraction of people in their 20s and 30s,” says Olli Raitakari at the University of Turku in Finland, who wasn’t involved in the study. “Atherosclerosis is a lifelong process, not a disease of old age.”

The profound effect the heart-brain connection has on your health

Previous studies have already suggested that atherosclerosis can occur surprisingly early. In 2025, Raitakari and his team found plaque in the carotid arteries – which supply blood to the head, face and neck – of about 5 per cent of Finnish adults aged under 30. But there hadn’t been large-scale investigations spanning multiple adult age categories that examined several artery locations.

Advertisement

To fill this gap, Borja Ibáñez at the Spanish National Centre for Cardiovascular Research in Madrid and his colleagues recruited almost 17,000 adults, aged 18 to 70, in Denmark and Spain. They divided the participants, who had no known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, into five age groups, starting at 18 to 29. The study was made up of around the same number of men and women.

Free newsletter

The researchers looked for plaque using CT angiography, which creates detailed 3D images of blood vessels, for arteries supplying the heart. They also used ultrasound for arteries in the neck and legs. Overall, they found “silent” atherosclerosis in 57 per cent of the participants, including 63 per cent of men and 51 per cent of women. This is defined as plaque that isn’t causing any symptoms, but may lead to cardiovascular issues down the line.

In the youngest group, 9 per cent of the men and 7 per cent of the women had some degree of atherosclerosis.

Among those in their 30s, 35 per cent of the men and 21 per cent of the women had atherosclerosis. The numbers continued to rise with each decade, with women beginning to catch up with men around the age of menopause.

A newly discovered collection of neurons suggests the brain and heart communicate to trigger a neuroimmune response after a heart attack, which may pave the way for new therapies

Atherosclerosis was generally more common among the participants with known risk factors, such as higher LDL cholesterol and blood pressure or a family history of the condition. But these factors didn’t reliably predict the presence of plaque, particularly among the younger adults.

The findings suggest that measures to detect plaque could identify people who seem to be at low risk of atherosclerosis, but might benefit from earlier preventive measures, such as medication or dietary changes.

But the presence of plaque doesn’t necessarily predict a future heart attack or stroke, says Raitakari, and there is no evidence that screening people without known health problems would prevent such events. The researchers also state that it is unclear if the results apply outside of Denmark and Spain.

Rising water is creating inland ghost forests in the US

New Scientist October 09, 2026

Millions of trees seem to be dying in the US, both near the coasts and inland near lakes, thanks to rising water levels. The finding may force a re-evaluation of how much carbon is stored in forests, which are important carbon sinks for mitigating the more severe effects of climate change.

Rising sea levels and intense storms linked to climate change have driven widespread tree die-offs along the US Atlantic coast, creating armies of skeletal dead trees known as ghost forests. North Carolina, for example, is thought to have lost 21 per cent of its coastal forest between 1985 and 2021 because of waterlogged soil and higher salt levels resulting from rising seawater.

To see how widely this is happening, Henry Yeung at the University of Virginia and his colleagues used aerial imagery from the US National Agricultural Imagery Program. They analysed images captured between 2012 and 2023 to map dead trees within 10 kilometres of the Pacific, Gulf and Atlantic coasts of the US, as well as along the US shorelines of the Great Lakes, down to a resolution of about 1 square metre.

Advertisement

Lake levels are rising across the world and climate change is to blame

They have identified more than 260 million dead trees and found that more than half of the mortality was concentrated in just 10 per cent of the mapped forests. These hotspots weren’t only in low-lying coastal forests prone to flooding, but also in high-elevation inland wetlands, far from salty water.

Over the decade they studied, tree mortality tripled in low-lying coastal forests, where water inundation was combined with increased levels of salt.

But mortality rates also doubled around expanding freshwater lakes, including the Great Lakes, and in inland wetlands, which have experienced more precipitation.

“This is the first map of ghost forests that covers the entire US. It’s also perhaps the first comprehensive study that takes the concept of sea level rise killing trees and applies it to more inland locations,” says Matthew Kirwan at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. “As a coastal scientist, I immediately think of salt as the culprit. These authors have extended it to water in general.”

Hear from three of the world’s leading climate scientists at New Scientist Live 2026

Arya Iwantoro at the University of Plymouth, UK, says it is striking how widespread the pattern is. “Prolonged inundation and salinity are already known to stress and kill trees, but the study suggests that water-related forest mortality may be more widespread than is usually recognised,” he says. “That broadens the issue beyond sea-level rise alone.”

Yeung and his colleagues found that between 2013 and 2020, high levels of precipitation and water runoff drove record-high levels in the Great Lakes, and they suggest that this led to sustained waterlogging, increasing the chances of nearby trees dying.

“The study provides convincing evidence that changing hydrological conditions are an important contributor to the mortality patterns, but I would be cautious about attributing every tree death directly to inundation or salinity,” says Iwantoro, adding that tree mortality is often influenced by other interacting factors, including storms, drought, pests, local drainage and soil conditions.

Deforestation could trigger Amazon tipping point in the 2030s

He says the work adds to evidence that the water-related effects of climate change could accelerate ecosystem shifts.

As the climate warms, the melting of ice means global mean sea levels are rising at about 4.1 millimetres per year, and saltwater intrusion is expected to affect nearly 77 per cent of the world’s coastlines by 2100. What’s more, climate warming also fuels heavier rain and snow, because for every 1°C that atmospheric temperature rises, the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere can increase by about 7 per cent.

This means that in coastal and lakeside areas, forests may retreat as conditions become more suitable for wetland vegetation, with knock-on effects on carbon storage, says Iwantoro.

In cities such as London, trees are already struggling with hot and dry summers. Botanists warn that we need to start replacing them with drought-adapted species

“Tree mortality and decomposition releases carbon into the atmosphere, and if the forest does not recover, then these areas may not regain their capacity to sequester carbon, and it could represent a more long-term carbon stock loss,” says Michelle Sims at the World Resources Institute, a global non-profit.

However, the ecosystem that replaces the forest may also accumulate carbon, says Iwantoro. “The important question is how carbon storage changes as the landscape transitions, rather than simply how much carbon is lost when trees die.”

Grief and tech collide in uneasily brilliant sci-fi film The Remotes

New Scientist October 09, 2026

The promise of much modern technology is that it will make our lives easier and take some burdens off our shoulders. An AI chatbot can tweak your emails; a delivery service can spare you the walk to a restaurant. But when does wanting to let go of something burdensome cross into giving up control? In John Torres’s The Remotes, grief, control and technology ominously intertwine on dark roads near Manila in the Philippines. A fast favourite of this year’s film festivals, it is a stunning and transfixing film that disorients and enthralls in equal parts.

Told in four parts, each of which feels as intimate as if some of its footage were documentary, The Remotes follows detective Mijares, who is trying to solve a series of car crashes where drivers’ bodies seem to have been controlled by a mysterious app. “You saw a ghost again,” a colleague tells him early on, except that the ghost once lived on the app store. “Were you fully in control of your body?” Mijares asks an older woman as she sits in her car after an accident. Something has clearly gone wrong here, and Torres builds a sense of a supernatural unease and visceral dread from the film’s first frame.

Notably, Mijares is not only haunted by this nearly unbelievable case, but he is also grieving his late wife. He narrates this grief as much as he narrates the case, through an often-poetic voiceover, until the film shifts focus to two sisters. Eva and Gill Cantero run seminars for delinquent and unsafe drivers. The ghost in the sisters’ lives is their dead mother, but they are also spectres in Mijares’s investigation; in their seminars drivers use an app that tells them how to drive, sometimes in a kind voice, sometimes sternly. In one emotionally resonant scene, after the seminar the students gather over drinks and recount how nice it is to drive with the app and listen to the voice, how good to temporarily relinquish control. The narrative threads start to intertwine, and Torres hints at something like resolution. A few scenes show motorcyclists explicitly losing control of their limbs once they punch into the app; Mijares seems to be vindicated and the sisters indicted.

Advertisement

But Torres isn’t interested in quick or easy conclusions and most of The Remotes isn’t told in order. Even though the film is over 2.5 hours long, parts of the story seem to be deliberately left out. This moodiness and nonlinear quality make the film both impactful and, at times, also deeply frustrating. As the connections come together, some of the emotional punches of that convergence are dulled by the sheer difficulty of following the story. I found the cinematography incredibly beautiful and pleasurable, but I also really wanted to pull out a notebook and try to sketch out a timeline. In a room full of critics and journalists at the New York Film Festival, I got a sense that I was meant to understand the story by feeling it more than by understanding each beat of its plot.

Though challenging, Torres’s commitment to lingering in this uncertainty and discomfort is also what recommends The Remotes the most. This is the feeling of grieving, and it is also the feeling of living in an uncertain world, one where we are constantly inundated by information and choices with inscrutable consequences. The increasing number of documented cases of people turning to AI chatbots for advice or tragically ending up in a state of psychosis after spending too much time talking to one speaks to how – much like in The Remotes – the temptation to offload some responsibility and control on a technology that talks back is very real.

In all its knottiness, this film is a good reminder to think about it twice, maybe even to say no to ghosts in the app store more often.

The Ukrainian president has expressed outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November’s midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue.

The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.

He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.

That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 20 people, including three children.

“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.

“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.

There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.

Andy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks.

“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” ​Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.

The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.

“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.

Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.

Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The moment I knew: We were babysitting my younger siblings and he wore a tutu to make them laugh

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:00:08 GMT

When Sarah Maloney’s primary school crush danced back into her life, she braced for a ‘teenage whirlwind romance’. Then one night, she realised they were both all in

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

In 2017 I was 16, went to an all-girls Catholic school in Melbourne and had zero tolerance for teenage boys and their nonsense. Instead, I spent a lot of gossip time lamenting Jake, who broke my tiny heart in primary school and then moved hours away.

A local debutante ball was coming up. It was an expensive tradition that was fundamentally at odds with my values, but I couldn’t say no to a pretty dress and dancing – I was still a teenage girl after all. Some friends asked cousins or co-workers from our part-time jobs to be partners. I got knocked back by everyone. When I complained to my mother, she let me know Jake had moved back to town, and did she want me to ask his mum if he would be willing?

Jake accepted, and we spent weeks rehearsing. My mum would pick him up on the way to the dance hall and we would sit in the back seat catching up on the last five years and laughing at our juvenile romance. It felt as if we just clicked again, and our giggly behaviour during dance rehearsals earned us more than one disapproving look from the teacher.

I was done for. I frantically asked my friends: did they think he might like me too? Should I ask him to my year 11 formal? Should I kiss him on deb night?

The ball was wonderful. While everyone else hit the dancefloor, Jake and I hit the couch in the foyer and stayed there all night talking. We missed dessert and I couldn’t find the courage to kiss him, but he asked me to see a movie with him the next day.

On our first date – where we were dropped off at the local cinema with a curfew – I had my first kiss. I almost chipped my tooth.

The first months of our relationship were full of nonstop texting during the day and after-school visits with my bedroom door wide open.

I was surprised at how earnest he was; I felt as if I didn’t have to pretend to be a cooler version of myself. I wrote in my diary about how excited I was to finally have my “ill-fated teenage whirlwind romance”. I figured if I held on to the idea that we’d break up, then I wouldn’t get hurt.

About two months into our relationship, my mother tasked Jake and I with babysitting my younger siblings. We weren’t technically allowed to spend the evening in my room with the door closed, but that didn’t stop us. After a few hours of laughing at YouTube videos, I went to have a shower and heard a crash down the hallway. My little sister had dropped a plate and it had shattered all over the tiles. I rushed out to help before she started crying. But when I got there, she and Jake were already cleaning up together and giggling. I snuck back to the bathroom with relief. Jake was good with my siblings, and that was important to me.

Later that night, I wandered into our lounge room to find Jake elbow-deep in our dress-up box and wearing a bright-orange tutu. My sister was beside him wearing a white wig. They ran around the room, Jake spinning like a ballerina to make her laugh. Neither of them noticed me. I stood and watched as I came to terms with the sudden feeling of certainty in my chest.

Lying in the dark that night, I told Jake I loved him. It flew out of my mouth before I could stop myself. I remember my heart playing jazz while I waited for his response. He whispered, “I love you too”, and hearing him sound so sure made me cry.

Nine years on, my “ill-fated teenage whirlwind romance” has turned into a loving, long-term relationship.

Jake and I make each other laugh more than anything else. Life might throw a curveball, but one of us is sure to make a joke about it. We often fall into comedic improv bits when we’re together, and I’m sure our neighbours think we are completely nuts when they hear us bicker like old people for the fun of it. But it’s safe. And it’s home.

Being with the same person since age 16 might seem crazy, but I always say that kids are dumb, not stupid. I knew back then what I know now – that the right person will show up even if it seems too early. You just grow together. Jake may have broken my little heart once, but I’m willing to have him hold it now for good.

Juliet Stevenson: ‘Do I have a nemesis? Where do we start? Putin, Musk, Trump, Erdoğan, Modi, Netanyahu’

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:00:07 GMT

The British actor on the genius of Bend It Like Beckham, the role she lost to Emma Thompson and why some actors get worse with age

What was the most Australian thing that you experienced while you were in the country filming Dustfall?

Working with a python? We don’t tend to work with snakes in the UK. I’m absolutely snake phobic but the python was very professional. Behaved better than I did.

Also, the phenomenal openness which I associate with Australian people – the lack of class pretension, the glass half-full approach. That seems to me a very Australian quality. It’s like the landscape: big, open and generous.

In Dustfall you play the mother of Anna Torv’s character. I understand you seek roles specifically that pull you out of your comfort zone – was Olivia one of them?

I do, because it’s very boring playing characters who are close to myself. I didn’t become an actor because I wanted to play me! On the contrary – as a kid I was always dreaming of being a very different person. Unfortunately our industry is pushing back on that. You’re supposed to be playing nearer and nearer your own lived experience and you’re not allowed to play other people’s lived experience. Well – what’s the word “act” mean, then?

As you get older, if you’re not careful, you get worse as an actor. Because you get too comfortable, too safe. You know how to do things, you’ve got a lot of technique. So you need to be pushed out of your comfort zone.

I’m certainly not like Olivia. There are overlaps. She’s a feminist and she’s my age, so we were brought up in the same culture in terms of attitudes to sexuality. But I’m a very hands-on mum, and Olivia handed over a lot of parenting to her own mother. She comes breezing back in, flirts a lot, gets drunk and stoned. She’s pretty insensitive. But it’s fun to play all that. I hope my kids would say that wasn’t like me.

Drunk and stoned acting is quite hard to do convincingly, isn’t it?

Yes. I think I’ve only ever been stoned once in my life. It just didn’t appeal to me. That was probably 40 years ago.

How often do millennial women want to talk to you about Bend It Like Beckham?

A lot, and it thrills me! I was filming a big film in Australia when that script arrived, and I thought, “Oh my god, I have not got time to read this, and what a rubbish title!” Then I opened it late one night and by page three I was roaring with laughter.

It was brilliant not just because it’s very funny but because it was touching on two really important things: women’s football, obviously, but also what it means to be a British Asian girl. There’s one reality inside your family home, shaped by your mum and dad’s values and codes of conduct and so on. And then they step out the front door and they’re in the street or they’re at school and they have to cope with a completely different set of values and a completely different culture. These young kids are negotiating all that and I hadn’t ever given that enough thought. It was a really beautiful film. Lots of young Asian girls still come up to me to talk about it. Which is great, because most of our work dies away.

Which role has been most personally fulfilling for you and why?

I’ve never felt so free as I do on stage. Nobody can stop you. Nobody can edit you. There’s a freedom in that which, on a good night, is incomparable. It’s intoxicating. There’s also nights when you’re out there and you think, “Shit, I’m so bad.” But when it’s good, it’s so intoxicating. You have this power over 1,000 people and you’re just holding them. It is hard to pin just one down, but perhaps The Doctor, the Robert Icke play we brought to the Adelaide festival in 2020, just before Covid lockdowns.

Film-wise, I would say Truly Madly Deeply. That’s had such a legacy. As I said, most of the work we do is ephemeral and that’s OK. But Truly Madly Deeply goes on having a life and I’m so thrilled by that. I think it speaks to people’s need for their grief to be recognised. Grief is so often glamorised in film but there’s nothing glamorous when you’re in grief. You feel like shit, you feel ugly and angry, you hate the rest of the world, you hate happy people. The elegant single tear rolling down the perfect cheek, which is so often what you see in cinema – we had all the snot! I think people were grateful for that. That was a blissful collaboration – [director] Anthony Minghella wrote that part for me and we knew each other very well by that time, so it felt very liberating on set in a way you don’t often feel.

What are you secretly really good at?

I’m a good driver! What else … I’m a rubbish cook. I love to draw and paint – I’m not really good at it, but I really love it. I think I’m quite a good parent. I hope that’s not too secret! And I’m a really good cleaner. If you want a cleaner, call me! I have that skill if the career goes wrong.

Is there a role that you really wanted that you didn’t end up getting?

When Merchant Ivory made Howards End, I desperately wanted to play Emma Thompson’s role [Margaret] because I just felt I was her. I loved that book so, so much. When I heard they were making a film of it, I thought, I can’t bear this. I did go up for it but it was just after my dad died and I was sort of in pieces. He died quite suddenly and I’d been nursing him, so that was my first job interview in that sort of state of skinlessness. I had an interview with James Ivory in London and I messed up so badly.

I think I’ve never got a job that I desperately wanted from an audition. Because you go into the room slightly desperate, which in my case probably looks a bit mad. Luckily most things get sent to me now. I didn’t watch the film, not out of pique I don’t think. I hope not. I know Emma and she’s wonderful.

Do you have a nemesis?

So many. Most of the men running most of the world. Where do we start? Putin, Musk, Trump, Erdoğan, Modi, Netanyahu … I’m quite politically active and I’m very preoccupied at the moment with the fact that most of the world is run by authoritarian men who are terrifyingly rolling back women’s rights, human rights, progress, civil rights, generating racism and homophobia. It’s just terrifying.

I’ve been politically engaged since I was about 16. I’m in my late 60s now, and to see everything that we have marched for and fought for being rolled back by these horrendous men is inconceivable. That we have someone like Trump in a position of power like that – a man so uneducated, so corrupt, so evidently, blatantly stupid … yes, I have plenty of those kinds of nemeses.

What has been your most memorable interaction with a fan?

Until I made Truly Madly Deeply, I hadn’t got that sort of recognition. Suddenly I had people coming up to me on the street. I was in a flower shop in London and I was in a hurry buying some flowers for a friend when this woman came in. I became aware that she was staring at me. I never imagined that she was staring at me because I was an actor; I was even getting a little angry about it, thinking, what the hell? Then she came up and said, “Please, can I talk to you?”

Her daughter had died, in her late teens, maybe her early adulthood. I think it hadn’t been very long ago. She’d seen Truly Madly Deeply and she just desperately wanted to talk about her loss. For her, the film had been an incredible catharsis. I think it was the first time she felt anybody understood what she was going through.

I really had to get somewhere, I had an appointment or an interview or something. But I could not leave her. I think our conversation went for about 45 minutes. We ended up on the pavement outside and I found it impossible to pull away. I didn’t really want to. It was memorable because I’d been doing a lot of theatre until then and you don’t really get to talk to the audience after. The impact of Truly Madly Deeply had been so huge for her and she was trusting me with so much. It was the most extraordinarily huge conversation between two complete strangers on a street in London. I still think about her.

What is the strangest thing you have done for love?

I’m married to an anthropologist – the love of my life is Hugh Brody, who has worked largely in the field with the Inuit and First Nations people in the high Arctic. We once found ourselves staying in a chief’s ranch in a remote part of Canada. I was incredibly excited about it – I mean how glamorous, how did my life bring me to this thrilling point? The chief and his wife were very keen on horse riding. I’ve always been terrified of riding, I had a bad experience when I was a kid. But there was this big expedition planned to go bareback riding and I couldn’t really say no. So there we were, galloping bareback across the Canadian landscape! I was completely terrified.

Hugh’s work is so interesting and it has taken me to thrilling places. But there have been occasions where I thought, “I like to be out of my comfort zone, but this is a little too far out!”

Dustfall airs 8.20pm on ABC TV on Sundays, with all episodes available to stream on ABC iview. It will air in the UK on the BBC at a later date

Parents fear YouTubers are bringing ‘brain rot’ to Netflix. But are kids wising up to ‘slop’?

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:00:06 GMT

As streamers poach viral creators to appeal to children, digital whack-a-mole has become a new kind of family challenge

Exasperated dad Simon Hooper shakes his fist at the camera in a recent viral video. “We managed to get rid of YouTube in our household six months ago and the kids are finally OK with it,” he says, but Netflix is “now commissioning YouTubers to make their brain rot and putting it back in front of my kids’ faces”.

The precise “brain rot” he’s referring to is the arrival of a polarising show that’s lighting up parent chats around the globe. And while Salish and Jordan Matter might be new to Netflix Kids users, the father-daughter content creators are familiar to anyone who’s spent any time on the internet. Jordan Matter, who started his YouTube career in 2017 as a photography vlogger, pivoted to family content after his energetic preteen daughter, Salish – a competitive gymnast – brought viral traction to the channel in 2019 and 2020. (Famously, his YouTube bio reads, “My daughter has taken over my channel!”)

After amassing more than 42 million YouTube subscribers, the duo signed a landmark deal with Netflix in February, constituting remixed content from the Matters’ YouTube archives. Soon an exclusive, original series starring the now 16-year-old Salish and her dad will be out as part of a broad trend of Netflix poaching YouTube creators to attract younger audiences. (YouTube is trying to stem the flow with exclusivity contracts.)

Think gamified family life challenges such as “I Went On a Fake Date To Prank My Dad” and “I Can’t Sleep Until I Find a Rare Glitter Dumpling” in the style popularised by the world’s most famous YouTuber, Mr Beast. It’s the kind of frantic, shouty, hyper-stimulating unscripted kids’ content shaped in part by an obsessive, second-by-second eye on YouTube Studio’s audience retention graphs. There are a lot of pop-up graphics and fast cuts – a style known as retention editing that has developed specifically around YouTube’s algorithm. Like Mr Beast, Jordan Matter optimises for views with aggressively A/B/C-tested, aggressively colour-saturated thumbnails.

“It’s our responsibility to ensure that we save our kids from this grey matter-destroying nonsense as they won’t do it themselves,” Hooper says. “The strength of the addiction is too strong.”

More than 3,900 comments underneath the post heartily agree, with a few exceptions. “This is super easy. You parent. That’s it. You own the house, the TV etc. Enough said.”

Michelle Yates has a long-running “no YouTube” policy in her home, but a few months ago she started to notice Netflix Kids was “suddenly more shouty, more gamified and more focused on dares”. Her eight-year-old son had discovered Salish and Jordan Matter. Around the same time, she says, people on her parents’ group chat started exchanging tips on how to block YouTube creators on Netflix. Plus, she started noticing promotion for YouTuber Mark Rober’s Roblox game on his Netflix CrunchLabs show, on top of the usual promo for his educational CrunchLab science boxes.

“The advertising thing is such a grey area,” Yates says. “I don’t mind the CrunchLab kits so much but I don’t want my kid anywhere near Roblox … and the Salish Matter show is awful. I’m thinking of cancelling the subscription because I don’t want to have to monitor every show … it’s exhausting.”

It started with Cocomelon – the mesmerising smooth-brain channel for toddlers – which moved over to Netflix in 2020, but in a concerted push Netflix have now scooped up favourites including Ms Rachel, Blippi, Danny Go!, the Stokes Twins and now Stem educator Mark Rober of CrunchLabs.

This is entertainment of varying style, educational ambition and target age group – but crucially for Netflix, these creators have all brought prebuilt audiences and pre-honed retention knowhow to the streaming service. (Cocomelon’s parent company has notoriously tested retention of focus-group children with a sinister Distractatron.)

The content boon for Netflix is part of a larger pattern of changing content presentation and consumption for kids that’s also reflected on Amazon Prime and Disney+. Digital whack-a-mole has become the ultimate gamified family life challenge. But unlike the Matter family, it doesn’t take place inside theme parks or between the candy-coloured aisles of Sephora. It’s a repetitive quest that happens inside the settings menus of digital interfaces.

“We’re going to see more of this sort of thing where … all of the streamers are going to start feeling like each other,” says Prof Tama Leaver, an internet studies researcher at Curtin University. In addition, “we’re going to see a lot of entry-level tiers where advertising comes back through streaming platforms”.

Many parents don’t see a problem or a distinction between traditional programs and those with their genesis on YouTube, but for those that do, and want to limit the content, Leaver says the challenges for parents are immense. “Defaults are very, very powerful and streaming companies could make it much easier for parents. Your experience as a parent of your child’s life should not be sitting in a command and control centre trying to read the thousand dashboards and apply them to their digital experiences.”

Sasha Giocondo’s two kids, aged 8 and 13, stream videos on both Netflix and YouTube, but she has always kept a much closer eye on YouTube. “I have noticed something like a ‘dopamine-crash effect’ after they watch this kind of thing on YouTube … Before, I could rely on Netflix not to produce that effect. Now I can’t.”

Parents often talk about this “crash effect”, but given the limited research, it’s not possible to draw firm conclusions on the impacts of specific media types – including on-demand streaming. A large-scale umbrella study published last week, examining data across 64 countries, linked higher childhood screen use to lower academic achievement and language development issues. But there is a growing body of correlational research about the negative impacts of fast-paced media on kids.

Earlier this year, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) updated its guidelines in line with research. The new guidelines step back from recommended daily limits on broadly defined “screen time”. Instead, the AAP is now mapping some of its recommendations to specific content design types, including caution around media platforms with “engagement-prolonging design” that displaces other off-screen activity.

Giocondo is among those who are troubled by the blurring of social media and long-form entertainment. “I can’t fully separate it from a broader unease about the kidfluencer industry, the pressure on young creators, and the open question of who’s really benefiting from all of it.”

Parents have solid reasons for discomfort around the treatment of kids on YouTube family channels. In a recent interview, Jordan Matter acknowledged the dark history and stressed that his daughter’s wellbeing was top of mind when striking the Netflix deal.

When it comes to YouTube, the medium is truly the message. The YouTube star is an avatar, compressed, commodified and optimised to compete in a ruthless attention economy. There are endless feedback loops, demanding and rewarding attention, for both the star and the viewer. For some parents watching their six-year-old daughters mimic Salish’s multi-step skincare routine, there’s something more at play.

Last year, the Matters co-founded a skincare brand for teens, Sincerely Yours, available exclusively at Sephora, after claiming that a generation of teens were feeling “equally unseen” by the skincare industry. Jordan Matter has seemed very open to Sincerely Yours brand tie-ins on Netflix. And why wouldn’t he be? Mark Rober enjoyed a massive CrunchLabs sales boost when he moved to the streaming platform last year and Ted Sarandos, the Netflix co-CEO, has been happy to publicise the fact.

Hooper’s video ultimately shows viewers how to block Salish and Jordan using Netflix parental controls. It has racked up over 60,000 likes, presumably because parental controls are far from user friendly. In the comments section parents rail that they are constantly blocking apps and channels across their devices, only to see blocked features pop up elsewhere, with YouTube and Netflix pre-installed into most smart TVs without the option to delete them. If parents do manage to restrict YouTube on their smart TV, their kid might stream it on the PlayStation instead, or watch videos made by YouTube creators through the Spotify app.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Netflix declined to comment for this story but provided links to their parental-control instructions, with cute tips such as “Lock your profile (and other profiles on your account) with a PIN, which helps prevent your kid from disabling or overriding your parental controls. (They’re so smart these days!)” But, as Leaver points out, you can’t block Netflix shows using the app on your TV. “You’ll need to go to another device and go to the settings in the web browser.” (Streaming companies are smart too!)

Ultimately, Leaver suggests that parents talking to their “kids about their media experiences is perhaps more valuable than trying to block everything that might be a little bit iffy”.

Jessica Balanzategui, an associate professor in media at RMIT University, tracks children’s streaming habits as part of an Australian Research Council project entitled Children’s Content in the Streaming Era. She says the data suggests kids are wising up.

“Our current research with tween children aged seven to 13 is demonstrating that children are developing more self-awareness and critical literacies with how algorithms and platforms feed content to them than we saw in our research in 2023. For instance, children … often tell us that YouTube is to be treated with care as it is full of ‘dodgy’ or ‘slop’ content, or even that it is ‘full of lies’.

“This indicates that families are developing some effective strategies and having robust conversations around YouTube at home.”

Good luck to any families attempting to embark on this ultimate gamified challenge. And don’t forget to like and subscribe to see if parents turn the mole-whacking mallets on their own heads as the great streaming convergence charges ahead.

Wallabies mugged at their own game to leave coach Kiss mulling hard lessons

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:00:06 GMT

Old habits resurface as Australia fritter away advantage and allow All Blacks to mount aerial assault at Eden Park

Les Kiss stood forlornly in the middle of Eden Park wearing a thousand-yard stare. The past 10 Wallabies coaches had all been where he was now, shaking their heads and cursing after a failed attempt to storm the fortress of New Zealand rugby. This was Kiss’s first loss as Australia coach and the little bloke was nursing a big hurt.

His side had arrived on a six-game unbeaten streak, fresh from stomping the world champions South Africa a fortnight before. Conversely, their old enemy were facing a fourth consecutive defeat after falling three times to that same Springboks side. After 25 years of Trans-Tasman pain, the Bledisloe Cup finally looked within reach.

Even the Kiwi supporters sensed it. All over town, Wallabies fans were being treated with respect rather than pity. They had seen what Australia had done against the Boks – the aerial majesty of Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Max Jorgensen, the courage to hang on with 11 men at the death. This time the threat was genuine.

After the anthems, in the calm before the kick-off, a large bloke in a faded gold jersey and three sheets to the wind, stood up and did his very best Gladiator impersonation. “Today is the day!” he bellowed. “Today we finally give it back to these Kiwi bastards.” The tiny fires of Australian support in an otherwise roiling sea of more than 48,000 black jerseys at the 105-year stronghold roared in unity.

The dream was alive when Ben Donaldson’s deft tap-on pass sent Tom Wright slicing into space after seven minutes to ignite the Kiss Army’s march into history. The All Blacks knew it too and botched the kick-off, surrendering to another attack. But then a traditional failure reared its ugly head: the Wallabies’ ability to self-immolate.

Donaldson had delivered a diamond, now he coughed up a rock, wasting the halfway scrum not by feeding his weapons out wide to get them deeper into the enemy lines but instead reefing a mindless, maddening kick for touch. The ball duly plonked out on the full and the reprieved All Blacks suddenly remembered who they were playing.

Peter Lakai scored in a sizzling piece of counterattack for seven-all, then Tupou Vaa’i crossed shortly after for 14-7 and then, with a penalty kick, Australia were down by 10. They cut the margin when Donaldson’s cut-and-run sent Wilson over before half-time, but the usually reliable Ryan Lonergan shanked an easy conversion.

Behind 17-14, Kiss must have launched a piece of half-time oratory to rival that of dusty Rusty in the crowd because he kept the home side waiting long minutes after the break. When the Wallabies finally emerged, they exploded, jagging a daring kick to the corner which Jorgensen hared after and almost collected to take the lead.

But again Australia frittered their enterprise by botching the killing stroke, giving away an idiotic obstruction penalty in their haste to maul the final metres. Spared, the All Blacks went berserk, scoring twice in six minutes before icing a 54th straight Eden Park win. The big mug was paraded around the old ground, touched by fans across the fence but out of reach for Kiss’s players, who could only watch it roll by.

after newsletter promotion

Australia had been beaten at their own game, the aerial assault they used to defeat South Africa. Jordie Barrett and Will Jordan outjumped the Wallabies flyers, and Dave Rennie outcoached Kiss. “The lessons are there,” said Kiss. “If you can’t get your strengths going and their strengths grow, it becomes a difficult game.”

Cam Roigard’s kicking game scrambled Australia’s attacking shape, a move that paid extra dividends after Australia’s midfield spearhead Len Ikitau left early for an HIA. “[It] allowed us to put a lot of pressure on,” said Rennie. “Receiving those kicks is difficult and our guys did an excellent job winning it in the air or picking up scraps.”

Len Ikitau’s likely absence for next week’s rematch in Sydney compounds the cruelty of partner Hunter Paisami’s suspension after an innocuous head clash tackle against South Africa. His replacement, Isaac Henry, made 15 tackles on Saturday, but offered little in attack. Kiss will have to shuffle his backline again or inject yet more rookies.

The Wallabies have returned to earth with a thud. They have a week to lick wounds and reset. The Bledisloe Cup is gone for another year but there’s still the chance to beat the All Blacks for the first time since 2020 and snap the Kiwis’ 12-Test dominance. “When you get a knockback, you find out more about yourself,” a defiant Kiss said.

His heroic captain, Wilson, called this Test defeat “a step back” but Kiss sees glimmers of gold even in a 41st year of mud, blood and tears at Eden Park. “Belief is created and sustained not by just wins and losses,” he said. “These boys have a strong culture, a strong belief in themselves and a confidence about what they can do. We’ll go back to work and turn the dial in the right areas so we can go to Sydney and return fire.”

Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:00:05 GMT

There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms

Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.

What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it’s perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.

Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride.

The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this.

How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air.

The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made.

But nobody should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anybody who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then.

The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their club, which in part underlies the present crisis.

That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess.

At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly.

Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Perhaps it’s not fair to be too harsh on the Premier League. This is not just modern football; it is modern Britain. As Miguel Delaney and Jack Pitt-Brooke argued on the Libero podcast this week, the Premier League is a direct outcome of Blairite economic policy, a point made clear in Oliver Bullough’s Butler to the World In the book he described the classic New Labour approach as “allowing something, making money from it and attempting to solve the problems it causes after they’ve occurred”.

But how do you solve those problems in football? How can football extricate itself from the clutches of the mega-rich? Regulation, up to a point, helps – and there may at least now be a sense that there can be enforcement. Whatever the flaws of the profitability and sustainability rules, or the squad cost ratio that has replaced them, it may be useful if football could accept the basic premise that the game shouldn’t just be about how rich your owner happens to be. But that can only go so far; a door open to the world has admitted a world of problems.

Short of some sort of financial crash in football, the sort of apocalyptic event that would make the sport unappealing to big finance and require the game to be built anew, with a fresh spirit that might recategorise football clubs as community assets rather than simple businesses, we’re probably stuck with it.

How, after all, could football ever escape the society that produced it?

Solanke strikes late as 10-man Spurs salvage point at Manchester United

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 18:50:45 GMT

Manchester United are on six points – their poorest start since 1986 – and Tottenham have three less and remain stuck in the relegation zone: testing times for Michael Carrick and Roberto De Zerbi, who must somehow revive their teams following a contest that was lit up by a moment of quality in the 73rd minute.

Matheus Cunha was fed by Luke Shaw down the left and the Brazilian crossed to Bryan Mbeumo, who spun and finished for United. It drew delirious chants of “You’re going down with the City”: Spurs, at this stage, were rock-bottom, and Manchester City’s long-term future in the division is in the balance.

Darker scenes followed when Shaw chased Bruno Fernandes’s ball and Rodrigo Bentancur launched a scissor challenge that, if it had connected with the left-back, might have caused serious injury.

An incensed Shaw, surely reminded of his horrific double-leg break sustained 11 years ago at PSV Eindhoven, hared after Bentancur and shoved him over. Up came the midfielder to push his head into Shaw’s, who went down as a melee involving both benches ensued.

Stuart Attwell sent Bentancur off and issued yellow cards to Shaw – lucky to escape a red, too, for the push – and Jan Paul van Hecke.

All of this followed a near snoozefest in which Spurs could not finish and United were disjointed: the tale, in microcosm, of their seasons.

There was more, though, as Tottenham scored an added-time equaliser, only their third league goal. Senne Lammens and Lisandro Martínez were United’s culprits as Sandro Tonali’s floated cross from the left should have been cleared by the Argentinian, but instead Dominic Solanke outfought him and headed past United’s goalkeeper, who watched the ball go in.

While averting a fourth defeat, Spurs still remain winless after their opening six league games, for only the fourth time in their history. The draw, too, means there is no clear answer to the pre-game question of which manager is under more pressure, as both De Zerbi and Carrick remain in need of a victory – or three.

When the Italian scans the table, he sees his beleaguered side third bottom, while United remain in 12th and with a solitary victory claimed all season, against Ipswich.

De Zerbi now takes his squad to Marbella for warm-weather training, while Carrick’s men are at Atlético Madrid on Tuesday in the Champions League.

After volleys of “You cheating bastards – you know what you are” rang out from both sets of fans (directed at City, again) Lammens went close to a nightmare start. A loose pass out was nabbed by Lucas Bergvall and the ball rolled to Solanke. Yet, as is Spurs’ prevailing problem, the centre-forward failed to finish, the shot saved by a relieved Lammens.

United’s goalkeeper was jittery again, when Martínez tapped the ball to him on his goalline and he dawdled before hoofing clear.

The reports said De Zerbi’s men had performed well, at times, but could not finish: a certifiable hindrance in this sport.

No boon, too, for any team is hesitation, as when Youri Tielemans waited for the ball to bounce, Tottenham pounced, and suddenly Sávio was heading forward. A sliding challenge from Leny Yoro, picked at right-back, saved a scattered rearguard.

This pointed to a Spurs ascendancy that was a headscratcher for Carrick and yet more profligacy from their visitors saved United when Mohammed Kudus’s cross found Archie Gray and the young right-back beat Lammens but not his right post.

Carrick wants his team to have control of contests but there was close to zero throughout, though on the hour Carlos Baleba came on for his debut and immediately spun and flicked the ball deftly into Fernandes’ path, and you were reminded what skill can do.

Now came the breathless denouement – a point, at the close, feeling fair, though unsatisfactory for both sides, who need to kickstart their campaign.

De Zerbi will aim to do so in Spain. “We are a great group of players but we are not a team yet and to be a team is to play for the teammates – suffer together, attack together,” he said.

Derek McInnes praised his Rangers players as they moved to the top of the league and blamed the extended international break for some disjointed play in a 3-1 win over Kilmarnock.

Christa Pike out of hospital and back in prison after botched execution attempt

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 17:10:29 GMT

Pike’s lawyers said she is back in same prison she’s lived in for last 30 years and will continue to receive medical care

Christa Pike has been discharged from the hospital after surviving Tennessee’s botched 30 September attempt to execute her by lethal injection and is back in prison, her lawyers said on Saturday.

Pike, 50, returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she has been imprisoned for the last three decades, her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement.

“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” Pike’s lawyers added. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”

Saturday’s update about Pike came 10 days after the death row prisoner was given two doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug, in what proved to be a failed execution attempt. She was hospitalized after surviving the botched execution and was declared brain dead on Monday.

But in a shocking turnaround, on Thursday her lawyer said that she was “up and walking” – though she remained “somewhat foggy” and wasn’t able to use her arms very much.

Pike said that her arms were burning during the failed execution and asked if it was supposed to feel that way. Witnesses present in the chamber said that “nothing was normal” while officials have maintained that they followed every step of Tennessee’s approved execution protocol.

There has been no official explanation about why Pike survived the execution. Medical experts speculate that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of such factors.

Her lawyers months earlier had flagged that Pike’s veins were problematic.

Pike was convicted in 1995 for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, then 18 and her classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. According to court filings, Pike, who was also 19 at the time, was worried Slemmer was trying to take her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then 17.

Shipp and Pike were convicted of taking Slemmer into a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus and murdering her. She was given the death penalty, and Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was younger than 18.

After Slemmer’s murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.

“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”

Pike’s survival of the botched execution has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty.

Tennessee’s top prison official has announced his resignation.

Meanwhile, the state’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. And Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, on Friday canceled a planned lethal injection execution in the state.

But they continue elsewhere.

For instance, the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that it planned to livestream the execution by firing squad in December of former army psychiatrist Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people at Texas’s Fort Hood, prompting condemnation from the United Nations.

Donald Trump on Saturday said Hassan “was vicious – he was violent” and that he would “make a decision” about the plans to livestream his execution.

“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show,” the president remarked. “Because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 16:52:15 GMT

Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful

Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel.

The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.

The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after demonstrators climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial, having Palestine Action placards, making a Nazi salute and assaulting police as officers made arrests.

Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.

Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organisers said 250,000 people were at the march.

The Met have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”.

The Met posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.

“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.

“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”

The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.

At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.”

Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”

Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”.

“We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued.

The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.

A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.

The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.

Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held.

The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.

The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.

Sleightholme hat-trick fires up Northampton in 11-try blast of Bath

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 16:22:09 GMT

Prem Rugby: Northampton 71-48 Bath

Second-highest scoring match in league’s history

Chalk this up as a victory for the Northampton Knicks. In a remarkable match with 18 tries, 119 points were racked up and defence relegated to the merest of afterthoughts, the defending Prem champions romped home.

Ollie Sleightholme helped himself to a hat-trick and Tommy Freeman two of Northampton’s 11, in the second-highest scoring match in the league’s history, behind Saints’ 94-33 win over Bristol in May.

Bath, for their part, scored seven tries but ended up comfortably beaten. For it was a contest that left us questioning much of what we thought we knew about the sport. Tries are supposed to come at a premium, not as an inevitability.

Some wonderful ones were scored, the fly-halves Fin Smith and Finn Russell showcased their array of tricks, but when 69 defenders are beaten in 80 minutes, you are left wondering quite what you have witnessed.

A penny for the thoughts of the England head coach, Steve Borthwick. If England try to play with this sort of abandon at next year’s World Cup they are in for a rude awakening. Knockout international rugby does not give out tries for free.

Noah Caluori [pictured] made a try-scoring return for Saracens as Bristol saw their bright start to the Gallagher Prem hit the buffers in a comprehensive 30-7 away defeat. Making his first appearance of the season after undergoing wrist surgery, the England wing produced the opening touch down to continue the blistering form that catapulted him to fame inn 2025-26.

Alex O’Driscoll and Jack Bracken also crossed on top of a penalty try as Saracens reacted to their disappointing loss to Sale by taking Bristol apart in the second half with Ben Earl and Maro Itoje particularly influential. Two penalties and a conversion from Owen Farrell helped ensure the Bears are still searching for a first win at StoneX Stadium in eight visits.

The Saracens head coach, Joe Shaw, said Itoje’s summer break has given him a 'new lease of life' after watching the England captain star at blindside flanker, rather than his customary position of second-row.

'Maro was unbelievable,' Shaw said. 'England and the club have given him a new lease of life by giving him the summer off. It’s the first one he’s had since he was 19. He had a full pre-season with us. He’s as fresh as a daisy. He’s training so well.

'His body’s in good nick,' Shaw added. It’ll benefit not just us, but it’ll benefit England in the long run going into next year’s World Cup.' Press Association

It was, however, entertaining. The comparison with basketball is often held up as a criticism by purists who love nothing more than an arm-wrestle, but not for nothing are the Harlem Globetrotters one of the hottest tickets in town. It is just that we are having to recalibrate what we thought we knew about the domestic game. A number of directors of rugby are convinced that while we are witnessing an attacking boom, defence will soon be back in vogue. On this evidence we are still waiting.

Maybe it is too curmudgeonly to complain. The skills showcased by both sides in their ability to capitalise on turnover ball took the breath away at times. Most neutrals would agree that it beats a 9-6 dogfight in the mud. But you are still left with a feeling that you have watched an 80-minute highlights reel rather than a match that ebbs and flows. It is a dream for marketing departments, but it feels like sport for the instant gratification generation.

“I know people will say it is too easy to score, but you’re not going to please everybody,” said Northampton’s director of rugby Phil Dowson. “I think there’s a balance. We don’t want it to be 99-88. It’s not basketball, but we also don’t want a 9-3.

“I used to have a coach called Mike Friday and one of his sayings was that ‘you can’t defend good rugby’ and there’s lots of good rugby being played.

“I have no doubt there will be some games this season that will be tough, ugly, horrible and nasty. But we want to be able to enjoy and reward great rugby. And, by the way, basketball is selling loads of tickets to sold out arenas.”

Northampton drew first blood with Smith cruising through a gap after a lovely show and go, but not to be outdone Russell replied with a moment of magic of his own, offloading to Arthur Green, who fed Tom Carr-Smith to score. Bath’s ascendancy was soon rewarded again with Charlie Griffin squeezing over on the left.

Saints responded with Sleightholme finishing a glorious move – showcasing the kind of dexterity the All Blacks had shown a few hours earlier – before James Pater put his winger clear.

Henderson and João Pedro lead Chelsea charge against Bournemouth

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 16:18:07 GMT

Watch and learn, kids. The day began with one for the youth audience, Cole Palmer appearing on a live stream to explain the thinking behind his latest contract extension. It finished with the oldest player to join Chelsea during the BlueCo era stealing the show with an all-action midfield display.

Even Palmer was happy to step aside as Jordan Henderson used his right foot to curl home a free-kick that drew comparisons with one of David Beckham’s specials. It was Henderson’s second spectacular strike – he marked his home debut by opening the scoring with a bending effort from 20 yards and also laid on an assist for Morgan Rogers to make it 2-0 – although it is fair to assume that Xabi Alonso did not bring the veteran to Stamford Bridge for his goalscoring prowess.

The idea was more to lift standards in the dressing room. Chelsea needed experience and are surely better off now a 36-year-old starting for them in midfield is no longer a laughable notion.

“We signed him for everything,” Alonso said of Henderson. “If he’s able to score two beauties as today, we are more than happy for him. But apart from the goals he’s done many good things. He’s always involved in the action, always giving solutions to teammates.”

Henderson set the tone for Chelsea, driving into tackles and raising the tempo with the urgency of his passing. He joined from Brentford in the summer and is keen to do more than make up the numbers. Chelsea, up to fifth after their first win in four league games, were more stable with Henderson alongside Moisés Caicedo, who lasted 72 minutes on his long-awaited return from a calf injury.

Alonso, who was without Reece James after the captain picked up a knee injury in training on Friday, was still disappointed his side have now gone 22 league games without a clean sheet. They were 3-0 up when Evanilson pulled a goal back for Bournemouth, who are finding the transition from Andoni Iraola to Marco Rose trickier than anticipated and must manage games better.

Even so, Alonso was pleased with Chelsea’s level. They have scored in the first 10 minutes in five of their six league games this season and are a match for anyone when the front three of Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro take full flight.

Palmer had a point to prove after having his desire to play for England questioned by Thomas Tuchel last month. His impact was immediate, although it owed much to Bournemouth’s naivety. The visitors lined up in a flat 4-4-2 formation and gave Palmer far too much space when he sauntered down the right in the first minute.

It was encouraging to see Palmer moving freely, especially after Alonso’s admission that the playmaker’s decision to sit out the international break was related to last season’s groin pain, but Bournemouth were a soft touch. There was no challenge on the 24-year-old, who has displayed his commitment to Chelsea by signing on until 2034.

Palmer floated into the area, turned and rolled the ball to Henderson, who hit it first time with the inside of his right foot and saw his bending effort go in off the inside of the right post.

There were 68 seconds on the clock when Henderson became Chelsea’s oldest scorer in the Premier League since John Terry in May 2017. “We knew Chelsea are a team that starts well,” Rose said. “It was our responsibility that we didn’t react the right way with this information.”

Bournemouth were overwhelmed. Chelsea pushed again in the third minute, Palmer’s flick freeing Pedro Neto to test Djordje Petrovic. The ball broke loose and Henderson swept a pass to Rogers, who cut in from the left and his shot flew in via a deflection off Antonio Silva.

He was a great midfielder in his day and will have appreciated the technique when Henderson’s free-kick flew beyond the reach of Petrovic.
