‘There is no secret agenda’: Nara Smith on home-making absolutely everything, raising four kids at 25 – and why she’s definitely not a tradwife

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 11:00:56 GMT

The model, actor and influencer is known for making her own frozen yoghurt, bubblegum or even toothpaste while dressed in immaculate haute couture. But she insists she is not who the internet thinks she is

Nara Smith is not a tradwife, she wants you to know that. Nor is she an ex-tradwife – pace the New York Times who included her in a feature on how ex-tradwives are as popular a movement now as the tradwives were in the first place. Nor was she peddling a tradwife-adjacent lifestyle choice by marrying at 18, having four children by 24, and devoting hours to cooking and documenting it online. Nor is she Mormon, by the way. Although, yes, her husband, the model and former teen heart‑throb Lucky Blue Smith, was raised Mormon, but we’ll get to that. Nor was she telegraphing subliminal religious messages in her content: “There is no secret agenda.” Nor was she abandoning her biracial heritage by wearing her hair in a sleek little bob. Nor was she leaning into a 1950s housewife archetype – even when dressed in a pink and red polka-dot minidress to batch-cook sourdough.

Smith wants you to scrap everything you think you know about her and start again. She also doesn’t care if you don’t. As with her content: “Those that get it, get it. Those that don’t, don’t. And that’s totally fine. I tell people: ‘If you don’t like my content, I won’t see you scroll past me.’ ‘If you need to block me for your own sanity, please do. I promise I won’t know.’ And if you want to stick around, that is beautiful, I’m grateful, welcome.”

For those new to Nara Smith, she is a model and influencer with 12.5m TikTok followers (plus 879m likes) and 4.8m on Instagram, who makes eccentric, seductive cooking videos in which she narrates each step in a passive hushed voice while making dupes of everyday supermarket products from scratch. Her videos start with the same shtick: her husband or children have a request – eg “Lucky leaned over, asking me whether I wanted to go grab some frozen yoghurt after the kids go to bed. I turned to him and told him it wouldn’t be as good as if I just made it. And, even though he was reluctant at first, he just went with it.” In a custom-made $900 white-satin corset dress – no apron – she’s straining the yoghurt starter, combining it with kefir, vanilla, sugar, cork gum; juicing apples and cherries to make gummy bears for the topping, whisking in gelatine and honey. Throughout, Smith stays expressionless. Throughout, her movements are mannequin smooth. Nothing splatters on her front, ever (luck, she insists, not because she exceeds all standards of perfection).

These clips blow people’s minds. Her grilled cheese video has been viewed 49.6m times. Elsewhere she’s made Nutella, ketchup, Cheez-Its, Pop-Tarts, Skittles and Snickers. She’s even made bubblegum. There’s the novelty of the recipes – she now has a cookbook of scratch-made ones, Homemade, coming out. Then there’s the outfits. She wore a $5,000 cashmere Prada suit to make chicken drumsticks, a $10,000 Schiaparelli to grate tomatoes for a gnocchi sauce. Nigella, Gwyneth, your domestic goddessing has been out-luxed.

All of which brings me to Deborah Ann’s Sweet Shoppe in the white clapboard town of Ridgefield, Connecticut, where Smith is sitting opposite me in the narrow red booth, tapping her phone with acrylic nails. Around us is the loud hum of ice-cream refrigeration units, the smell of hot fudge and candy floss. There are sugar pourers and napkin dispensers and Jay & the Americans sing Come a Little Bit Closer on the radio. Smith surely had a sense of humour when she chose this as the backdrop to talk about not being a 1950s homemaker? “They have the best soft serve,” she says, a hint of smile. “And Lucky comes for the cotton-candy ice-cream.”

Today, a fortnight shy of her 25th birthday, Smith, is in jeans, a white vest, Chanel flats and a lot of flashing jewellery (“I love a diamond ring”). For the record, she drove here in her own car. And, while it is true that Lucky once said that he drove “no matter what”, that he was “bothered” by the sight of a woman driving a man, she loves driving. She listens to her favourite podcasts while doing so – Aspire With Emma Grede, founder of Skims, and for fun, The Girls Bathroom – “so entertaining. And I do love an audiobook also. I love fantasy. Are you into fantasy?” I ask if she made the gum she’s chewing. She laughs. “Not today.”

Smith’s content attracts millions from advertising (among others, she works with Marc Jacobs, Miu Miu and YSL). As well as her cookbook, she acts, and has two films in post-production. One is an indie film she can’t talk about. The other is Tyrant, “a culinary thriller” starring Charlize Theron, Demi Moore and Paapa Essiedu. Then there’s a “consumer goods brand”. I ask what. “We’ll talk about that later. We’re still figuring it all out.”

Does she make more money than her husband? “That’s a loaded question. How do I even answer that?” She can answer it with a broad smile? “Yes, I will do that.” She has excellent teeth.

What is staggering about Smith is that as well as devising and researching the recipes themselves, she does all her own styling, makeup, art direction, video editing, voiceover and mixing, spending upwards of eight hours a day on one 90-second clip. Her agents and managers beg her to take on help. “I always say no. I am very type A.” Type A? “Very rigid, very scheduled.” Her assiduous attention to detail and devotion to her “art” mean “I’m still figuring out where to relinquish control”, she says.

I ask if she’s like The Princess and the Pea when something is not quite right. “That’s literally me. That should be the title. I can’t sleep. I’ll be tossing and turning, bruised.” The cookbook is a sumptuous, high-production volume, but the recipes are down-to-earth in a homely way. They include some from her German childhood: milchreis, schnitzel, rouladen. She doesn’t shy away from refined sugar. There’s meat, there’s chicken in cream, there’s roast potatoes in duck fat. “Do I have sugar and duck fat all day every day? Absolutely not. But roast potatoes occasionally? Absolutely. A little dessert once in a while? Absolutely.”

What I try to keep in mind while she’s telling me all this is that Smith has four children: Rumble Honey, Slim Easy, Whimsy Lou and Fawnie Golden. (“Unusual names build character; Lucky had an unusual name and it helped him in ways.”) The book photoshoot took place three weeks after the youngest was born. So, as well as organising and slipping into, for instance, the Rodarte custom-made gingham dress on the cover, she was breastfeeding a newborn and overseeing renovations to the family home they had just moved into here in Connecticut.

Then not long after, while the cookbook was still being edited, her daughter Whimsy Lou was diagnosed with cancer. It was Lucky’s mother who first noticed “this thing on her body” (for her daughter’s privacy, Smith doesn’t want to go into specifics) while they were all together on a family photoshoot for the holiday season late last year. “My mother-in-law was, like, ‘I don’t want to alarm you, but maybe you should go to the ER.’ Long story short, the doctors did a bunch of tests, from biopsies to ultrasounds, and then called us back and said: ‘She has cancer. She needs to start treatment immediately.’”

Smith’s world “flipped”. Until that point, the couple didn’t even have childcare. Suddenly they were juggling work, kids, chemotherapy appointments, “while also making sure that we weren’t falling apart for her”. Five days out of every fortnight or so, depending on her blood count, Lucky stayed with Whimsy in hospital when she went through treatment while Smith was at home breastfeeding. They couldn’t explain to Whimsy what was happening to her. “She was under two years, so there wasn’t a lot she’d understand.” But they explained it to the older two, “and we got children’s books about cancer that would explain the hair loss and different parts of this journey through stories”.

They found “a community” of mutually supportive parents – the reason Smith publicly disclosed Whimsy’s condition once she was in remission. “You don’t realise how many parents or children go through similar experiences until you’re in that situation in the hospital,” she says. “People speaking about it makes you feel less alone.”

The shellshock is palpable. She sounds dazed as she runs through the litany of family upheaval that preceded diagnosis – new house, new book, new baby, big dose of postpartum anxiety. “I was still in the thick of dealing with all of it mentally, being pulled multiple different directions [when it happened]. Then all I wanted was to be present for Whimsy. It was hard.” Smith’s mother, Joyce, a nurse, not long free of her own treatment for breast cancer, flew in from Germany to help. “Everyone rallied in my family, and it was beautiful to see.”

Without doubt she’s been changed by the experience. “When you come that close to a life-changing thing, you view the world a little differently.” On the one hand, she appreciates the beauty of “mundane moments”; on the other, she’s tougher. A lot of thought now goes into what her job means in terms of exposure of her children online. “But I’ve always had a boundary around my kids. I show as little of them as possible while acknowledging that they are part of my life.” When people come up to ask for her photograph, her children automatically turn their backs, or stand behind her, or move to a corner of whatever store they are in. “I try to avoid certain places if I can during peak hours.”

Will she keep them off screens? “Like phone screens?” Her face is a picture of horror. “Oh, I’m not going to get them phones! No, I’m going to get them a little – I don’t know what they’re called, a Firefly? A Brick? I want them to be able to communicate with me and get a hold of me. I’ll get them a camera because my kids love taking pictures. But I don’t see the need in having them be on social media, or playing video games, or any of that. I deliberately moved to an area where there’s nature, stuff they can do and explore outside; not be on screens.” Until what age? “I don’t know, 18? I mean, if I could have my time again, I would have done it so different.” Does she ever wonder what her life would look like if she hadn’t done all these videos?

“All the time. All. The. Time.” Later, she says: “The landscape on social media has changed so much. I had to learn the hard way and reconsider what I put on the internet.”

Most nights, Smith takes her computer to bed. Her bedtime routine is specific. “I need clean sheets, that’s non-negotiable. I love freshly washed sheets.” Every night? She stalls. “Twice a week, probably. Linen sheets. I need a shower every night, take my makeup off, do my skincare, brush my teeth, have water on my bedside table, and then I just work in bed until my eyes are rolling.” Often, she’ll look over and Lucky is already asleep. “Sometimes, he’s, like, ‘You can go to bed, and I promise the email is still going to be there in the morning.’” She gets up around six after one night‑time interruption (she insists on doing nights with Fawnie: a, because of the guilt of travelling a lot, and, b, because this baby is her “last”). First thing, she takes their dog Archie out back. He’s a pyrenees-pitbull cross (He’s adopted. Lucky wanted a puppy, but she said no). It something of a relief to learn she doesn’t exercise. “I wish I could. That just feels … too much.”

A common theme in her stories is meticulousness in being willing to start from scratch. Three months after her kitchen had been done here in Connecticut, it flooded because of an ice dam on the roof. Ripping the whole thing out was not the headache you imagine because, she says, “I hated every decision that the designers made. I trusted them instead of my gut. So, we redid it the way I wanted and now it’s beautiful and totally different.

“I feel like an adult now, having bought a home and furnishing it for the first time.” The vibe: “I want people to feel like a grandma lives here, not a 24-year-old. Grandma chic with an English twist” – because Ridgefield reminds her of the Cotswolds, she says, where she would have moved “in a heartbeat”.

I ask what makes her lose her shit. “Mess,” she shoots back. “I get very stressed out by mess. I don’t like a messy house. I don’t like a messy kitchen. I don’t like a messy closet. Messes are overstimulating. On top of everything else that’s going on in the home, four kids running around, screaming and everything, messes then set me over the edge. So, I don’t necessarily lose my shit. I’m, like, ‘Let’s just tidy it up, OK? Everyone, start picking up your stuff.’”

The children tidy? “I make the kids do their stuff. Anything they may need help with, like, putting socks together, sometimes they can’t do that, I’ll help. But usually the kids do their messes, I do our messes, and we’ll get it whipped super quick.”

Twice a month she has a cleaner who comes to “deep clean”. Everything else, she and Lucky do themselves. Laundry? “I do it.” Ironing? “I steam.” If I opened her cupboards, would they be neat and ordered? “They would. Because it just makes everything more efficient. I love a system when it comes to getting dressed or doing laundry or schedules or routines or the kitchen. It makes life so much easier if you don’t have to think about all these small things.”

While she talks, Smith is miming tidying on the laminate-top table between us. She is funny on the potential hazards of her daughter choosing her own outfits. “My eldest is very opinionated. She’s got good taste, so usually I don’t have an issue with it.” If she had bad taste, would she? “I would.” She laughs. “Sometimes it’s the craziest combinations. I have to intervene and kind of bargain a little bit. I’m, like, ‘Tights and socks over pants? That’s crazy.’”

Elsewhere, the need for this level of control can be “stressful”. “A lot has changed over the last six years. Being very type A makes it hard when things happen that I can’t control,” she says. Any “wildcard” causes excessive anxiety. “When it came on, I didn’t know what it was.” She read self-help books, had individual therapy, she and Lucky went to couples counselling.

She’s laughing when she says she’d been convinced she was a “brilliant” communicator until she got to couples therapy. They go in person, when they need it. “We married so young and have so much life ahead, so it’s more a prevention than cure, if that makes sense.

“I grew up in Germany. He’s American. Sometimes, we kind of miss each other a little bit. One time I said ‘I don’t care’ about something, and he was, like, ‘You don’t care?’ It was just, like, ‘I don’t care about talking about it any more.’ Because I speak German, and the language is different, when I translate it into English, it comes across harshly, blunt, to an American. He was, like, ‘Whoa, that’s a little crazy, honey.’ But it’s small things.”

Nara Aziza Smith was born in South Africa to a German father, a teacher of history and biology, and Mosotho mother, who grew up under apartheid (“She saw things no person should ever see or go through or have to deal with”). After Smith was born, the family moved to Frankfurt and two younger siblings followed. As a child, Smith had a host of allergies including to eggs and was hospitalised twice at young age for eczema (she also remembers a later operation on her “janky” toes). She describes herself as a child who wanted to hang out with adults, who saw the kids’ table as a punishment: “Like what am I going to do with these kids my age? Play tag?” She was fascinated by figures from history and mythology: Marie Antoinette, Medusa, Athena. She could recite Maya Angelou’s Still I Rise.

Banned from Facebook by her parents, she signed up to Instagram, which they’d never heard of, and used it as a way into modelling. She was scouted at 14 by IMG Models through an online programme and her parents took her to castings. In many ways it was a great experience. “But it was also taxing on my 14-year-old mind: the pressure to look a certain way; the focus being only on how you look.” Back then, measurements were very particular, she says. “Getting older, your body changes. So, it was hard on me at times to maintain the standard [weight].” She wouldn’t “necessarily” want her children to go into the business, but if they did she would support them. “But would I recommend it over other interests that they may have? No.”

“Obviously” she knew who Lucky Blue Smith was before she met him. “He was a crush of mine aged 15. I watched his Ellen interview and I remember thinking, ‘That guy is really fit.’ Then when he DM’d me on Instagram years later, I was, like” – dramatic intake of breath – “it’s him!” In that first message, Lucky asked her where she was from. He didn’t text back to her reply. Sometime later he messaged: “I’m going camping with a friend so I’ll be off grid for a little bit. But when I’m back, I would love to hop on a phone call.” He was in Los Angeles; night-time in Frankfurt. They spoke all night and she watched the sun come up. Over seven hours, they covered family, hobbies, interests, teen stuff. “After that there wasn’t a day that we didn’t spend time on the phone, whether it was two hours or seven hours. We would fall asleep on the phone.”

She was attracted by his calmness. How mature he seemed. “Also he’s beautiful, which was a bonus.” They decided to marry not long after their first meeting. Posted it all online, photos of them in bath towels, the ring. It was cute, until you looked at the comments. How did she deal with the racism? “Race has been something that I’ve always talked about with my parents. I’ve always been aware of it growing up in Germany and not looking like the other blond girls. I remember this specific time: I left the school bathroom with my hair out of a ponytail for the first time, and as I walked out one of my friends burst out laughing. I was mortified. I never wore my hair out in school again.

“When Lucky and I got together … I don’t know, I kind of just brushed it off because it said more about the other person and how they choose to treat people. Did I talk to Lucky about it? Sure. Did I sometimes get sad about it? Yes. But I just tried to ignore it.”

When she relocated to the US to be with Lucky, old health issues started to flare up. She started checking the labels on the food she was eating. “I wasn’t aware how many ingredients were involved. Bread had 20‑plus ingredients, some of which didn’t necessarily belong. I realised it would be easier and healthier if I started making things myself.” In this way, cooking from scratch became “a necessity … I wasn’t just coming up with crazy recipes.”

Like other gen Zs, Smith’s early content was “fit checks” and get-ready-with-me videos. And she wasn’t wildly different from other “mommy” influencers when she began propping her phone on a tripod to film herself cooking dupes of, say, Oreo ice‑cream or ranch dressing. But something about the package – the exquisite face, the heart-throb husband who goosed her at the stove, the fashion, the breathy monotone used because she was recording at nap time and didn’t want to wake the children, but which everyone compared to ASMR – elevated her above the rest.

Then there was her willingness to keep taking it to the next level. She made cough drops. She made sun cream. She made Coca-Cola. She coordinated outfits and recipes so that she made Capri-Sun in a yellow gown with balloon sleeves. Fellow chef Ruby Tandoh wrote of Smith’s content: “It’s addictive. The low-stakes suspense of seeing just how much Too Much she’s going to do this time.” In less than a year, Smith went from under 1 million to 9 million followers. Among them, Bella Hadid, Ariana Grande, Selena Gomez, SZA and Doja Cat.

All this coincided with a new and toxic movement online: tradwives. They were a domestic expression of the rightward swerve in American politics. Religion often played a part in their commitment to maintaining patriarchal structures. Women claiming their sole ambition was to serve men were suddenly all over the internet packing their husband’s lunchboxes. What Smith did seemed of a piece. Internet sleuths spied The Book of Mormon behind her in one clip. It’s a backstage prop, they argued, an attempt at mass conversion.

It didn’t help that Smith was friendly with Hannah Neeleman, the 36-year-old Juilliard graduate and mother of nine who makes home-cooking videos dressed in vintage prairie dresses at Ballerina Farm in Mormon Utah. The internet ecosystem encourages influencers to cross-fertilise. Smith and Neeleman milked cows together. They posed on the farm porch, babies dandled on hips, husbands looking cocky in jeans and cowboy boots. Smith was accused of promoting regressive gender roles, of promoting teenage pregnancy, as well as “culturally appropriating” Mormon life, and distancing herself from her black heritage. Thinkpieces followed. Memes. Reams of Reddit discussion.

Smith sighs when I put all this to her. “To begin with, I didn’t think too deeply about what I was doing. Cooking was something I did for health and because I enjoy it, and I also enjoy fashion. I had fun. I put it on the internet. People started reading into things, deciphering outfits, deciding I was saying things that would never even cross my mind.”

Now she thinks that making your living in the kitchen is always going to be political. “It just is,” she says. “I feel people always want to put women in boxes, to try to explain them, to read into things they do. This is an expression of myself through food and fashion. People tune in for the voice, or the fashion, or the recipes, or all of it.”

Does she see herself as a feminist? “Yes, absolutely. A woman should have the right to do it all, to do whatever she needs to do.”

Does she vote? “I would vote in the United States, but I’m not an American citizen so I’m not allowed.” But she worries about politics. “It’s scary everywhere right now.” She talks to family, to friends, to Lucky, about the rise of the AfD in Germany, deliberately keeps it offline. “People who see me know what I stand for. I have four kids. I’m a mum. I’m a woman. I would hope that people can put the pieces together. I don’t feel the need to speak about it on my socials because that’s for my artistic expression.”

The Mormon thing? Well, she was curious, she admits. It was her husband’s background, she was open to hearing about it, to seeing if she identified with any of it. “If you marry someone that grew up that way, and you’re building a family, you’re figuring things out. That was happening when my social following exploded.” Are her children Mormon? “No. Our family isn’t. It’s a perception that people hold, but I’m not a Mormon, I was never a Mormon. I never got baptised. I never did anything that would make me Mormon. We figured out what we’re doing for our family, and it’s not being part of the [Mormon] church.”

Every Wednesday and Thursday, Smith does three hours of acting class over Zoom with a teacher in Los Angeles, which she tops up with individual in-person sessions when she is in the city. She caught the acting “bug” on the set of Tyrant. She watched the big Hollywood names make mistakes, try it again, interpret lines in different ways, and realised you didn’t have to be perfect first time. Somehow, that blew her mind. She realised acting was an extension of what she was doing anyway. “I called my team after. Like, ‘We need an acting manager.’” She signed with a big agent and has started auditioning.

Can she envisage a time where she’s not doing her cooking videos any more, or at least there’s less emphasis on that? “Yeah. I could see a time where my content evolves. I’ll never not be on social media because it’s such a pillar of my work, my business and the way I connect with people.”

Is she competitive? She hmms and tilts her head to the side. “I wouldn’t say competitive. I’d say, what’s the word?” She snaps her fingers in the air. “Ambitious. That’s the word I was looking for. I’m very ambitious. But it’s one-upping myself. I couldn’t care less about one-upping other people. I’m in my own lane, and I have a goal I want to get to.”

We’re ready to leave. As we rise from our chairs, a sea of teenage girls I hadn’t noticed converge. They look tiny next to Smith’s towering 6ft frame. They’ve been waiting, phone cameras at the ready. “You’ve, like, inspired me. I’ve been making stuff from scratch,” one says, grinning in train-track braces. “I love that,” says Smith. “What have you been making?” “I’m trying to make bread. It hasn’t gone well … ” “You know what? That takes a hot minute. It took me a hot minute. But you’re going get there.” She gives them a little hug.

Homemade by Nara Aziza Smith is published by 4th Estate on 13 October. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 11:00:55 GMT

In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan

Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales.

Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely.

When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere.

Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople.

Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans. Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16.

“I’ve done a full loop, because this is where I started,” she says, from her seat behind a sewing machine on the factory floor. Deftly handling the indigo fabric, she moves individual pieces through the machine and a pair of jeans begins to take shape.

In its heyday, the Dewhirst factory in Cardigan where Evans once worked employed about 400 people, representing about 10% of the town’s population, and cranked out 35,000 pairs of jeans each week for Marks & Spencer.

When Dewhirst decided to outsource production to Morocco, Evans was given the opportunity to move to Tangier. But the founding of Hiut led to her returning home to Wales and to a sewing machine. “I hoped it was like riding a bike,” she says, “but you never forget and the rest is history”.

As Hiut took off, the company moved into what was once part of the Dewhirst factory, taking Evans back to the place she began her career. A slogan painted on the factory wall proclaims “Our town is making jeans again” and Welsh flag bunting flutters above the sewing machines, in celebration of the annual cultural festival, held this year in early August just a miles south of Cardigan.

Evans and the other grand masters who joined Hiut have spent decades cutting pieces of fabric, creating pockets and stitching denim.

The brand’s production levels are far removed from the mass manufacturing which previously took place in Cardigan – Hiut employs 20 people, who make 120 pairs a week.

The company insists its product is no ordinary wardrobe staple. Each pair is made by hand from 17 pieces of fabric, with a “made in Wales” label inside the waistband and another label signed by the member of staff who stitched the jeans. Hiut also offers lifetime repairs.

“The majority of the time, you know the name of the person that’s bought your jeans. You know your customer and the customer gets to know us as well,” says Evans. “We’re very proud of what we’re doing and the quality is top notch.”

Indeed, online fashion reviews praise Hiut’s attention to detail, such as neat seams and how all of the rivets featuring the brand’s name or owl logo are added by hand to ensure they face the same way.

Such premium jeans come with a suitably premium price tag – about 10 times higher than the cost of a high-street pair – starting at £245 for men’s and women’s slim-fit styles, made from organic cotton from Turkey, and rising to £350 for pairs made from premium Japanese selvedge.

Hiut customers includes TV personalities Ant and Dec and the brand got a big boost when the Duchess of Sussex wore a pair during her first official visit to Wales in 2018, resulting in a three-month backlog of orders.

Despite such endorsements, the company hit financial difficulties in the wake of the Covid pandemic, when the founders approached some of their top customers to ask if they wanted to invest in the company.

One of these was the German von Loeper family. They initially became minority shareholders in late 2024, before taking over the company in September 2025. Johann von Loeper, 26, became the company’s chief executive, leaving a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan.

He says his father, Philipp, was a loyal customer first, which prompted the family-owned investment group to take a stake in a firm beyond its usual investments in life sciences or agricultural companies.

“We don’t do anything in retail or fashion really, this is more of a passion project,” von Loeper says. “My father sort of became obsessed with the product … I think he bought more than 30 pairs.”

The family has committed to keeping the manufacturing in Cardigan, although von Loeper adds that the factory’s west Wales location creates logistical challenges when moving finished garments or bringing in photographers and models for photoshoots.

He adds: “The thing that attracted all of us to Hiut was the purpose of making jeans again, and not just for the sake of making jeans, but to have the jobs, to have to craft, to have skills remain here.”

Some high-profile visitors have tried out the craft. A framed photo and letter from Kensington palace hangs on the factory wall, commemorating the March visit of Catherine, the Princess of Wales, where she had a go on a sewing machine.

Walking past huge rolls of fabric from some of the most prestigious denim mills in the world – in Japan, Italy and Turkey – von Loeper says he faced a big decision shortly after taking over running the company. A key Japanese denim supplier warned Hiut and other long-term customers that operational pressures meant it was about to close its order books until 2027.

“We bought £100,000 worth of selvedge in my first few weeks here because I said ‘let’s get it now before we run out’ and that was one of the better things I did,” he says.

When the von Loeper family took over, they said Hiut was “losing a lot of money every month”, but they believed that with investment and a new strategy, the brand could become profitable again.

The new owners soon got to work updating the entire jeans collection, and are hoping to take on more staff so they can increase production. Von Loeper is aware that Evans and other grand masters are fast approaching retirement age and believes the company has a “five-year window” to hire and adequately train new employees. He also wants to broaden Hiut’s appeal, and as part of that has secured new stockists, including Liberty department store in London.

“Our customer age group has always been 35-55,” says von Loeper. “Our jeans were worn to the office even before Covid, but we can definitely see that customers and what they are buying for has changed and we are trying to adapt to that.”

At the shop located just metres away from where jeans are being made, customers come to try on different denims. One customer, Paul Tomlin, has made a purpose journey to Hiut during a visit to Wales to buy more of his favourite jeans.

“I came to make sure I got the right fit. I tried on three pairs and found a style that suits me,” says Tomlin, holding a branded bag containing two new pairs. He says he likes the firm’s ethos as well as its clothing: “It’s a good story and has a good feel as a company”

The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 11:00:55 GMT

Moscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrong

Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.

In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.

Schulze Wessel makes another simple but very pertinent point: Russia’s expansion was always facilitated by cooperation with other great powers and arrested when it faced equal and opposing powers. Since Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year, the United States has ceased to be the latter and has at times looked like the former. So now it’s Europe that is shouldering the burden of being the equal and opposing power. Europe (including the UK) has now given more aid to Ukraine than the US. Its combined economies are 10 times larger than Russia’s; Germany’s economy alone is twice the size.

And it’s Germany that’s now central to this European effort. Cumulatively, since the beginning of the full-scale war in 2022, Germany has been the biggest individual country donor apart from the US. According to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine support tracker, it has given twice as much as Britain or France. As people in Kyiv and Odesa are daily pounded by Putin’s ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, it’s worth looking at the Kiel tracker’s figures for air defence systems. Germany has so far donated 19 of them, including five of the vital US-built Patriot air defence batteries – two more than the US itself has given.

In the first year of this war, I argued that Germany “has a unique historical responsibility to help defend a free and sovereign Ukraine”. At that time, I felt strongly that Germany was not yet doing what it should. Now, in the fifth year of a conflict that has already lasted longer than the first world war and shows no sign of ending, I can say without hesitation that it is. This is not just a matter of the numerical scale of its support for Ukraine and its own increased defence spending, which, on the latest projections from the German finance ministry, will reach €154bn (£130bn) in 2028 (Roughly the same as Russia’s total estimated military expenditure for this year).

It’s also a matter of political will. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shown that will, and courage, by taking the train from Germany to Ukraine on the evening of 3 October, the 36th anniversary of German unification, with a strong delegation including defence industry leaders. The Russian bombardment of civilian targets in central Kyiv, including Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences and bridges across the Dnipro River, did not stop even though – or perhaps exactly because – Moscow knew the German leader would be there.

For a historian, there’s something very familiar here. Oh no, it’s Germany and Russia again! Yet each time is different. Historically, Germany is one of the powers that has done most to facilitate Russian expansion (just think of the 1939 Hitler-Stalin pact) but also most to threaten it. In the first world war, and even at the margins in the second, some Ukrainian nationalists saw in a conflict between Germany and Russia a chance for their independence. Instead, they got imperial Germany’s colonialism (and then German defeat) in the first case and Hitler’s genocidal fascism (and then German defeat) in the second.

Now, at last, Germany is genuinely engaged, at some cost and risk to itself, for the sovereignty of Ukraine. To anyone who knows this tangled history, there is something not just redemptive, but frankly inspiring in this sight: a democratic Germany playing a leading role in supporting an independent Ukraine’s bid to assume its proper place in a wider European community of free countries.

But for how long? And with how much support elsewhere in Europe? Precisely because Putin sees Germany’s centrality, it’s one of the main targets of his hybrid war, from explosive-laden drones at Leipzig airport that the German government has firmly attributed to Russia and assassination threats against defence industry bosses, all the way to covert political interference and disinformation. While Ukraine faces its most difficult winter yet, three closely connected things will be put to the test: Germany’s will to stay committed on the right side of history; the capacity of democracies to sustain the fight against a dictatorship (a perennial concern); and Europe’s ability to remain united in this cause.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

A sceptic can point to many grounds for pessimism. Merz is unpopular at home. Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the party currently making the running in German politics, would abandon Ukraine to Russia. In France, the National Rally’s presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, says her country can’t afford to go on giving so much to Ukraine. Solidarity with Ukraine is also crumbling on the right in Poland, with two smaller parties sounding frankly anti-Ukrainian. In one Italian opinion poll last month, more than half those asked were opposed to continued weapons deliveries to Kyiv.

In Brussels recently, I found a large audience seemingly stalwart in support of Ukraine – until, right at the end, our discussion turned to the issue of using the Russian frozen assets held in Belgium. Ah now, that’s a different matter … Yet with the terrible damage being inflicted on the Ukrainian economy, including its grain exports via the Black Sea, experts estimate that as much as €100bn of additional support for Kyiv may be needed in 2027 alone – and hard-pressed European taxpayers are in no mood to cough that up.

Putin believes decadent European democracies will crumble before the iron determination of an imperialist strongman. Our job is to prove him wrong.

Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book, Europe in 7½ Chapters, is published next week

Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 09:45:40 GMT

I grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and what the state owes its citizens. The lessons leave their mark

Young British people have plenty to be angry about. Crushing student debt, private-school privilege, a housing market they can’t enter. Yet unlike their French counterparts, they have little tradition of turning that frustration into collective action. I grew up in France as a Briton, and for years I have watched my French friends do something my British ones never seem to: take to the streets.

“To arms, citizens! Form your battalions! Let’s march, let’s march!” It shouldn’t be too surprising, given the rousing lyrics of La Marseillaise, that France’s revolutionary spirit is not a relic of the past.

The lycée protests in the past week have displayed the organisation and bravery of the French students. In Lens, a 15-year-old lost his hand to a police grenade during a blockade. More than 6,000 people have been arrested, many of them under 18. Hundreds of schools across France are either blockaded or closed. These teenagers know the risks and commit to turning up anyway, day after day. I can’t imagine that happening in Britain, so what makes the French so different?

First, there’s the history. France’s republic was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it. French pupils learn that protest, uprising and rioting are the origin story of their freedoms, so these methods are championed in promoting change. We grew up in school with the idea that if you don’t like something, you have the power to change it. The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education. The French Revolution appears in the curriculum twice, for pupils aged 12 and then again at 16; the student protests of 1968 are taught at age 14 and again at 17. Debating is encouraged in schools from as early as collège, or at about 11 years old. Young people are expected to have an opinion and not be afraid to defend it.

Even I, at 11, started to feel patriotic during our moral and civic education classes, despite not having a French passport. Protesting is taught as a legally framed fundamental right and a civic responsibility. Of course, with lycéens not yet being old enough to vote, protest is the next best thing.

In the final year of lycée, pupils study Rousseau’s Du Contrat Social (The Social Contract), which argues that citizens should only surrender their unrestricted natural liberty in exchange for civil and moral freedoms. You give up your individual interests for the volonté générale (general will) – put simply, you pay heavy taxes and in return you expect the country to work. That bargain is how the French understand their relationship with the state. When the government raises the retirement age, lets electricity bills soar or cuts school budgets, that is seen as a breach of the social contract. Protest is the automatic response.

Britons, on the other hand, are subjects of the UK and are characterised more by an American-style individualism and a desire to live and let live. There is less collective spirit. Britain has an extraordinary history of protest, spanning Peterloo, the Chartists, the suffragettes and the poll tax riots, but there is arguably a different cultural relationship to these events. They can be remembered as stand-alone episodes and interruptions to the national story rather than as the story itself. The Thatcher era also did permanent damage to unions, contributing to the British public being a grumbling but compliant one, lacking in organising power.

Because these values are ingrained across French society, and in every generation, the student protesters are emboldened by the firefighters, nurses, lawyers and teachers who have joined them in solidarity. Across social media, you can see these moments of support and unity. A viral video of the mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, protecting students from the police is a striking example of this. It’s difficult to imagine British teenagers taking to the streets, because they would be alone.

Parents have joined their children in protesting, and have called on other parents to do the same for the planned general strike on 17 October. (This is also a response to the police brutality witnessed in the past week.) Many parents were themselves lycée students and marched against education reforms and cuts. The anti-Macroniste parents (of whom there are many) don’t treat their children as delinquents, but as citizens exercising their rights.

That does not mean every French parent supports every protest, or that French society is wholly united behind its students. While the French state technically encourages protest through the curriculum, the force and violence with which it has met its students says otherwise. And there is resentment of the protests among some students, particularly those who come from conservative households and believe that the blockades are a leftwing plot.

Students in France are not necessarily more political than their British counterparts – young British people are active, but tend to take part in established and larger movements such as Extinction Rebellion or the Gaza protests rather than initiate protests themselves. The biggest difference lies in the French willingness to take to the streets, suddenly and en-masse. Unlike in the UK, the state is something the French are taught to engage with as citizens, and to challenge when necessary. If anything, the lycéens are just being good students.

Kitty Sayers is a master’s student in journalism

Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 07:00:50 GMT

Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase

The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.

Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.

The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.

The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.

Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’s Restore Britain party and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.

Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact.

They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account.

She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism.

“The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.”

A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms.

“This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential.

“Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK. Social media companies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.”

A number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff.

A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”.

“Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added.

Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”.

Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it.

That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles.

The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel.

Watson was approached for comment.

How to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fences

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 06:00:50 GMT

With an extremely wet and windy winter forecast, take steps to keep you and your home safe and dry

With the Met Office warning that this year’s supersized El Niño could mean a wet and stormy winter lies ahead, it’s never been more important to maintain your home.

Payouts for storm damage to UK homes surged 32% to £244m in 2025 amid the destruction caused by the heavy rain and strong winds that accompanied the likes of Storm Éowyn and Storm Floris.

But that is just part of the picture, with total claims for weather damage to homes and possessions hitting £758m last year, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). It says this figure points to “the toll that increasingly severe weather is taking on homes”.

However, experts say regular maintenance can help prevent damage to your property. With that in mind, here are practical steps you can take to make sure your home is best-placed to ride out the storms.

Alex Peters, a cost guide expert at Checkatrade, says: “The primary line of defence begins at roof level, where high winds will dislodge weak structures and create hazardous flying debris that could damage your home.”

Tiles often become broken or loose, or slip. Ideally you would get up there to have a look, but only do so if you have the proper safety equipment – otherwise, call a professional.

Peters says: “It is important to undertake regular roof and chimney inspections to make sure they’re structurally sound. A standard professional roof inspection averages about £250 per visit to check for loose tiles or mortar decay.”

Most roof repairs cost between £110 and £160 a sq metre, depending on roof type and materials, according to Checkatrade.

A buildup of moss can cause moisture damage to tiles and the wood underneath them, so remove it if you can. The best time is after a dry spell, when you can brush it off with a stiff broom (but don’t attempt this without the proper safety equipment).

Roof “furniture” such as chimneys, skylights and vents is sealed with metal strips called flashing, which should sit flush, with no gaps where water can seep in. If yours does not, you can buy flashing strips, roof sealant and caulk in most DIY stores but, again, this repair job might be better-suited to a professional.

Peters says: “Gutters channel heavy rain safely away from your roofline down to external drains, but if they’re blocked, water can pool and lead to a range of issues.”

These include water seeping into brickwork and causing internal damp, or uncontrolled drainage which erodes the soil around your home’s foundations and, over time, can destabilise them.

Now is a good time to clean them out and make any repairs. The cost depends on the size of your home but sits at about £20-30 an hour for a skilled tradesperson, according to Checkatrade.

Andy Simms, of home service marketplace MyBuilder, says that any trees near your house should be checked now, adding: “Overhanging or unhealthy trees can cause all sorts of property damage, alongside clogging drains.”

Pruning can usually be completed for about £100, but for bigger jobs, a tree surgeon typically costs £240-£400 a day depending on where you live.

Inspect walls for obvious weak spots, including cracked render, staining or places where rainwater collects.

Michael Davie, from specialist home improvement firm PureBuilt, says one of the biggest issues homeowners underestimate is damp caused by small external defects. “A cracked or damaged section of render might not look serious at first, but if water is able to get behind it, the problem can spread quickly,” he says.

“We regularly see cases where what could have been a relatively straightforward repair becomes a much bigger job because the source of the moisture has been left untreated. A repair of about £500 can turn into thousands of pounds once damp has affected plaster, internal finishes or larger areas of the property.”

Repair any cracks or seals around your doors and windows. Peters says: “If there are any gaps or cracks, apply draught excluder tape or caulk to help prevent drafts and water from getting in.”

Window sealant costs about £10 for a 300ml tube, while draught-proofing tape works out at £5-£15 a roll. Another low-cost fix is a door seal – typically a piece of rubber, vinyl or silicone fitted around the frame or on the door edge. You can use basic self-adhesive foam strips or spend more on brush seals and compression strips (and don’t forget letterbox and keyhole covers).

Hiring a professional to weatherstrip drafty openings runs at about £50 a window or £100 for each external door, according to Checkatrade.

Plant pots, garden furniture and trampolines should be stored inside or secured before a storm. Gates and fences are particularly susceptible to wind damage and for this reason most standard buildings insurance policies will not let you claim for the cost of repairing them.

after newsletter promotion

You could reinforce your fence with concrete posts and look at replacing the panels with ones that are 50% wind-permeable (these have gaps that let the wind through without toppling over). For repairs, the price varies depending on the material, but for fence panels it typically costs £45 while fence posts cost about £25. The big cost is labour, and this varies depending on where you live and the amount of work involved, but £950 is a ballpark figure.

Damage caused by frozen and burst pipes can be significant. Household insurers settled roughly 8,000 claims for weather-related pipe damage in 2024, paying out £250m in total, according to the ABI. The average claim was almost £33,000.

Insulating exposed hot water pipes is an easy DIY job. Inexpensive pipe insulation (often called pipe lagging) is available from most DIY stores, and fitting it could also shave about £6 off your annual energy bill, according to the Energy Saving Trust.

Most modern hot water tanks have plenty of insulation, but an older tank might only have a small amount. Adding an 80mm jacket to a tank with 25mm foam built in can save homeowners in Great Britain £45 a year, says the Trust. The jackets cost about £20 and are widely available from DIY retailers.

Also locate your stopcock – it is usually under the kitchen sink. This valve allows you to turn off the incoming water supply. That’s vital if a pipe bursts, and you might also want to use it if you are leaving your property unoccupied. It is a good idea to clear remaining water from the pipes after turning the supply off.

The government is urging people to “get prepared” for emergencies by stocking up on essentials such as bottled water and tinned food. Your emergency kit should include a portable mobile phone charger, torches and batteries, blankets and warm clothing. Also keep a list of emergency numbers to hand. These should include 105 for a power cut or 0800 111999 for a gas leak.

Think about getting your boiler serviced. “Freezing storm conditions can cause indoor temperatures to drop rapidly, forcing boilers to work harder,” Peters says. “Servicing catches pressure drops, sediment buildup or worn components that could trigger a system lockout under heavy load.” A service typically costs about £100, but prices vary depending on the type of boiler.

Flood resilience champion Mary Long-Dhonau, who is behind the Flood Mary campaign, has a directory of builders who specialise in flood-related work on her website.

Long-Dhonau warns that an “awful lot of water can enter your home via the airbricks – in fact, it is often the first place flood water can enter into a home”. She recommends replacing them with Kitemarked self-closing airbricks. Alternatively, you can buy temporary covers. In an emergency she suggests creating a temporary seal using wide aluminium tape – one large roll can cover multiple airbricks and can be bought online or in DIY shops. (Once the danger of flooding has passed, you should remove any temporary coverings to allow for proper air circulation and temperature regulation.)

People often assume that flood protection means spending many thousands of pounds – and it can, says FPS Group founder Simon Crowther, who is also known as “The Flood Guy”. But some individual measures are more accessible.

“A basic domestic flood pump setup can be in the low hundreds of pounds, and a door barrier may be a few hundred pounds,” he says. “Current examples on the market put small complete pump kits at about £150 upwards, and some domestic door barriers at about £400-£600.”

If you already own flood-protection equipment, now is the time to test it.

“Check flood barrier seals and fixings, make sure all the parts are actually there, and practise fitting it,” he says. “If you have a pump, run it and check the hose, connections, float switch or sensor.”

Buildings and contents insurance typically provides some cover for weather or storm damage, says Amy Rootham, an insurance expert at price comparison website Compare the Market. It may also fund alternative accommodation if your home is uninhabitable.

But insurers have specific criteria for what constitutes a storm, which may include wind speed or rainfall intensity. Also, this sort of insurance is designed to cover sudden and unforeseen damage, so they will assess whether the storm was the direct cause of the problem, or if it exposed an issue already in need of repair.

Rootham says home insurance premiums have been falling over the past two years but warns not to “focus on price alone” when comparing policies. “Check the cover limits, excesses and exclusions carefully,”she says.

Time: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran are stellar in this horrifying and exceptional TV drama

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 06:00:49 GMT

Jimmy McGovern’s grab-you-by-the-throat prison show is back and it could hardly be more urgent, prescient or excellent. Brace yourself though … Bake Off it is not

It takes a lot to drag me away from comfort TV in the autumn. Blame the shrinking hours of light or the apocalyptic news cycle but the closest thing I like to get to televisual trauma in October is watching comedians get into their own graves in The Celebrity Traitors. I doubt I’m alone. I don’t want to psychoanalyse the British public but I’d take a punt that collectively we are just about capable right now of looking at Josh Widdicombe trying to find a purpose next to Emma Willis on the Strictly dancefloor (and reportedly, even that’s a struggle).

Enter legendary Jimmy McGovern with a new series of the Bafta-winning prison drama Time (Sunday, 9pm, BBC One) to drag the nation out of its Bake Off-related coma. Having already covered the devastation of men’s and women’s prisons in the first two series, the good news is that McGovern and co-writer Samuel Bailey’s trilogy surely can’t get any more distressing. The new episodes will be set in *checks notes* a youth offending institution for boys. OK great. It’s about children in prison. Thank you, Jimmy! I hope you’re happy! No one else is going to be.

Of course, McGovern – long known for tackling social realism and institutional injustice in iconic shows such as Cracker, The Lakes and Hillsborough – is not going to put the viewer through the wringer without proper reason. As prison overcrowding dominates the headlines, alongside the multifaceted crisis among young men, Time series three is so urgent and prescient that you wonder if the BBC were tempted to change the title to Time(ly).

Still, best brace yourself before going in. Within 90 seconds, a teenage boy is being dragged horizontally by five adult guards to his cell; a hand half-covering his jaw as he screams obscenities. That hand belongs to David Tennant, playing veteran prison officer Bobby Bailey. Tennant is an impressively blank slate as Bailey: a figure who is almost always on screen but has such sparse dialogue and emotion that at times he is – in classic McGovern fashion – defined by his ordinariness and hard to box as “goody” or “baddy.”

He’s joined by Happy Valley’s Siobhan Finneran who returns as prison chaplain Marie-Louise – the only common thread through all three series and a rare merciful sign of, dare I say it, hope. Tennant and Finneran both give stellar performances but it’s the three young actors playing new offenders who will surely be stars of the future. There’s Peter (Ollie McNulty), caught between the death of an innocent man and loyalty to his community, and James (Louis McCartney), struggling to face his broken parents after a life-changing act of violence. Then there’s Christopher (a heartbreaking Chukwubuikem Molokwu) battling a stammer and reconnecting with his birth mother.

One of Time’s strengths is its exceptional writing, but it is not afraid to say plenty without a word. The white vans that transport the boys to jail with tiny square black windows for pockets of light. The gates in D-wing that are rarely opened and keep its violent not-yet-men apart (“Gates are dangerous,” Tennant tells Finneran ominously). Cells named “Room 29”, as if the boys are on a hostel break for the week – an illusion that’s only broken when you realise there’s not a scene that takes place in the wing that’s not accompanied by the sound of screaming.

The whole thing is a lesson in tension, each minute in the prison dragging the viewer further into the claustrophobia of dread and despair.

I won’t give any spoilers but I will say you will be thinking about a moment in the first episode for days. This is not easy viewing but nor should it be. McGovern is not delivering content that plays in the background while you’re scrolling Instagram. It grabs you by the throat, asking you to question whether it’s possible to change or if the horrors of the human-made system dooms certain people – certain children – before they ever really get a chance. All of us should watch it, not least politicians across the political spectrum. Just maybe stick Bake Off on afterwards to decompress.

From The Social Reckoning to Harriet Kemsley: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:49 GMT

Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s sequel to The Social Network, and the Last One Laughing star reckons with divorce in her new standup tour

The Social ReckoningOut nowThe David Fincher-directed The Social Network has only come to seem more canny over time, with the site co-founded by Mark Zuckerberg being held responsible for all manner of social ills. In this sequel from Aaron Sorkin (this time directing and writing) based on the incidents around the 2021 leak of internal Facebook memos, Zuck is embodied not by Jesse Eisenberg but Jeremy Strong.

The UprisingOut nowPaul Greengrass (United 93) tackles the 1381 peasants’ revolt, a fracas caused partly by the decision to introduce a new tax of four pence per person, regardless of whether you were in the greedy elite or a worker who might make about £2 in a whole year. Heading up the rebels with a cause are Andrew Garfield and Cosmo Jarvis.

The Lost Children of TuamOut nowIn 2017, the New York Times chronicled the efforts of amateur local historian Catherine Corless’s campaign to expose the abuse by Irish nuns that led to almost 800 child and infant deaths in Ireland. This dramatisation of the scandal stars Monica Dolan as Corless and is produced by Liam Neeson.

Other MommyOut nowJessica Chastain stars as both regular mom Ursula and her supernatural doppelganger, creeping around the house interacting with eight-year-old Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark) in this Blumhouse horror directed by Rob Savage (Dashcam). An adaptation of Josh Malerman’s creepy 2024 novel, Incidents Around the House. Catherine Bray

Arab Strap12 to 17 October, tour starts EdinburghThe Scottish duo returned last month with their ninth album Half-Told Tales. A 14-song collection of strangely danceable odes to ageing (You You You), angry warnings about masturbation (I Get Noise), and an overarching sense of black humour, it should make for a fun night out. Michael Cragg

ManifestWembley Arena, London, 16 OctoberLike their girl group contemporaries Katseye, this Turkish sextet were created via a TV singing competition. They also share some of their musical DNA, with Manifest’s brightly hued songs bubbling like a sugary soft drink. Support on this debut arena show comes from UK girl band newcomers XO. MC

606 Club 50th anniversary festival606 Club, London, 12 to 25 OctoberWest London’s much-loved 606 Club celebrates its 50th anniversary over a fortnight, with star guests including Jamie Cullum (13 Oct), Gwilym Simcock (15 Oct), and many trailblazers of UK jazz. Founded and run by saxophonist Steve Rubie, “The Six” is as devoted to good music as it’s ever been. John Fordham

Oxford international song festivalVarious venues, 10 to 24 OctoberAn ambitious local event turned major international fixture, this festival celebrates 25 seasons with big-name performances on the theme of love. Highlights include baritone Matthias Goerne and pianist Tamara Stefanovich in Schubert’s Winterreise (10 Oct), and songs by György Kurtág from baritone Benjamin Appl and pianist James Baillieu (Mon). Flora Willson

Light and Magic: The Birth of Art PhotographyTate Modern, London, 14 October to 21 FebruaryThe Tate’s big autumn show takes a global look at the more conceptual, artier side of photography, with 200 prints by 80 artists from across the world, including Madame Yevonde, who saw the camera as more than a documentary tool.

Prem Sahib, Gordon Matta-ClarkDe La Warr Pavilion, Bexhill-on-Sea, 10 October to 4 January Prem Sahib has been making some of the most interesting art in the UK over the past few years, all about queer intimacy and clubbing, and he is getting some well-deserved institutional attention here alongside the brilliant late American conceptualist Gordon Matta-Clark.

Julia IsídrezNottingham Contemporary, to 10 JanuaryUK museums’ fascination with indigenous art continues unabated with this show of ceramics by Paraguayan Guaraní artist Julia Isídrez, filled with mythical creatures and multi-headed amphibians.

Frieze art fairRegent’s Park, London, 14 to 19 OctoberEvery autumn, Frieze shows up in a massive tent in Regent’s Park and plays host to the best art galleries in the world. It is a cultural phenomenon, and well worth visiting if you can stomach the price of entry. Eddy Frankel

Harriet KemsleyBrighton, 11 October; Hull, 14 October; Leeds, 15 October; touring to 26 FebruaryOn stage, the Last One Laughing star comes across as a giggly, chaotic oversharer – but you don’t become a successful standup without serious finesse and focus. Kemsley’s current show Floozy sees the 39-year-old relate her experiences of post-divorce dating in deceptively daffy style. Rachel Aroesti

The Cherry OrchardHarold Pinter theatre, London, to 9 JanuaryAutumn is the season when all the stage stars come to play in the West End – and there are none bigger than Kristin Scott Thomas, who stars alongside Stephen Mangan in Chekhov’s richly rewarding final play. Miriam Gillinson

Middlemarch Parts 1 & 2Swan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, to 16 JanuaryNina Raine has adapted George Eliot’s exquisite novel into a play in two parts, directed by Jeremy Herrin – who is so good at injecting ambitious shows with shape and purpose. Nia Towle plays Dorothea Brooke alongside Amanda Root, playing both George Eliot and matchmaker Mrs Cadwallader. MG

English National BalletLiverpool Empire, 15 to 17 October; touring to 25 OctoberThere are two ways to watch the ENB this week: see them live in Rudolf Nureyev’s staging of Romeo & Juliet, with one of the best ballet scores ever written. Or settle down with some popcorn for their sumptuous production of Sleeping Beauty, recorded at the Royal Albert Hall in cinemas (13 to 18 October). Lyndsey Winship

after newsletter promotion

Treasure IslandParamount+, 12 OctoberRobert Louis Stevenson’s 1883 novel – responsible for creating the pirate caricature of the popular imagination – was first adapted for television 75 years ago. This new version stars David Oyelowo, Jack Huston, and Hayley Atwell as Bess Hawkins, who helps her son Jim in his hunt for fabled riches.

TimeiPlayer & BBC One, 11 October, 9pmThe bracing, brutal prison drama returns for series three, this time shifting focus to disturbed teens locked up in a young offenders institute. Killing AnnaChannel 4, 12 October, 11pmAn expat Syrian academic sees a video of a civilian massacre in Damascus and uses social media to track down the chief perpetrator; she then poses as Anna, a regime sympathiser, to encourage him to reveal details about his work in this remarkable documentary about vigilantism in the digital age. Planet Zoo 2PC, PS5, Xbox; out 14 OctoberThe popular zoo management sim returns, letting players build their animal kingdoms from a vast toolset of detailed habitats. The addition of aquariums and bird sanctuaries bring in new animals to observe and care for.

Valor Mortis PC, PS5, Xbox; out 14 OctoberA dead soldier of Napoleon’s army finds himself reanimated in an alternate 19th century filled with plague-ridden monsters. An epic fantasy adventure crammed with gutsy combat and supernatural peril are his certain fate. Keith Stuart

Jamie T – Ghosts (100 Days of Morning)Out nowFour years after scoring his first No 1 album, south Londoner Jamie T is back with this sixth record featuring a collaboration with Damon Albarn. 13 MinutesPodcastThe BBC’s space podcast returns with a new series on the Hubble telescope touching on its delayed and over-budget launch and the discovery of a fatal flaw in the build. We hear how scientists salvaged the operation.

@DictionarycomInstagramManaging to make the mundane functionality of the dictionary more interesting, dictionary. com’s Insta account posts unusual “word of the day” picks, as well as analysis on the linguistic choices of artists such as Taylor Swift.

Blind date: ‘Most awkward moment? When she squished an insect that was on my forehead’

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:48 GMT

Holly, 42, a horticulturist, meets Graeme, 47, a forest manager

What were you hoping for?Really, just a fun night with minimal awkwardness was my fairly low expectation before the meeting. First impressions? A very positive, engaging lady with a beautiful smile. What did you talk about? Growing food, the joys of seeds, birdwatching, the failings of young people when it comes to proper raving, epigenetics and breaking generational cycles.

Most awkward moment? Holly destroying an aphid, which had landed on my forehead, with a firm thumb squish. I should make clear that the poor aphid wasn’t in the lovely restaurant; it was outside an entirely different place, which had hanging baskets. Good table manners? Impeccable. Best thing about Holly? Holly was incredibly easy to converse with. Her assured nature and wide range of interests meant she was a joy to be with. Would you introduce Holly to your friends? In a heartbeat.

Blind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the UK) and online at theguardian. com every Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you can read all about how we put it together here. What questions will I be asked?We ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.

Can I choose who I match with?No, it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely to be.

Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.

What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.

How should I answer?Honestly but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.

Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.

Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!

Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.

How to applyEmail blind. date@theguardian. com

Describe Holly in three words Nuanced, sparkling, niche.

What do you think Holly made of you? I reckon she was hugely impressed I could name every species of bird she had tattooed on her leg.

Did you go on somewhere? Yes, a nearby pub then a little nightclub.

And … did you kiss? Yes, we did.

If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I would tone down my oversharing

Marks out of 10? 9.8.

Would you meet again? I’m hugely looking forward to doing so.

What were you hoping for? To meet someone interesting and fun.

First impressions? Warm, confident. Graeme quickly made me feel at ease.

What did you talk about?Our mutual nerves about the evening. The joys of working outside. Forestry management for biodiversity. Rural living. The importance of dancing.

Most awkward moment? I got overexcited about the menu and ordered quite a lot of food. We didn’t need the extra salad.

Good table manners? Excellent: he kept our glasses topped up and was open to sharing dishes.

Best thing about Graeme? He’s got a very curious mind and is a great listener.

Would you introduce Graeme to your friends? He’d get along well with them.

Describe Graeme in three words Warm, intelligent, open.

What do you think Graeme made of you? I hope he thought I was easy to talk to.

Did you go on somewhere? We did. We made the most of being in the city and sought out some music and dancing!

And … did you kiss? Yes.

If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? Nothing – I had a really fun evening. Graeme is a lovely guy who is very easy to talk to and up for a laugh.

Marks out of 10? A solid 8.

Would you meet again? We live quite far apart, but we’ll see …

Holly and Graeme ate at the Palmerston in Edinburgh. Fancy a blind date? Email blind. date@theguardian. com
