‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to die

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:48 GMT

Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is responsible? And has there been a cover-up?

Shortly after 1am one night in April 2019, a CIA officer on a work trip to London was jolted awake in his hotel room by the most intense head pain he had ever experienced. His body was soaked with sweat and he felt like his eyes were spinning in their sockets. He manoeuvred his way out of bed, hoping to make it to the bathroom to vomit, but found his sense of balance had deserted him. Eventually, he fell back into a fitful, shallow sleep.

The next day, arriving at the work meeting he had travelled for, the officer found he could not remember the names of colleagues in the room, people he knew well. As the meeting got under way, he could barely follow the discussion. Initially, he chalked it up to a terrible – if rather odd – case of food poisoning. But over subsequent weeks, worrying symptoms persisted: brain fog, loss of balance and increasingly harsh tinnitus.

By September, he had started to feel better and was on another work trip, this time to Poland. Asleep in his Warsaw hotel room, he was again woken by terrifying head pain, even worse than in London. He later described the sensation as “someone standing over me with a baseball bat and just repeatedly hitting me on the head”. It was a nine or 10 on the pain scale, he felt, worse than anything he could remember.

Two hours later, the same feeling returned, and he started to suspect that what was happening might not be an internal process but rather some external attack. He dragged himself off the bed and curled up on the floor, where the intense pain subsided somewhat. That was the last time he had the “attack” sensation, but he went on to suffer chronic nerve pain, fatigue and other severe health problems for years.

Sources described the man in question as a senior CIA officer who had recently been assigned an important job relating to worldwide operations against Russia. At the time, he was only vaguely aware of the stories that had emerged from Cuba two years previously, about US diplomats who believed they may have been attacked with a sonic weapon.

These incidents, in which people reported feeling a variety of unusual sounds, pressure and pain, followed by residual symptoms that could last for years, had acquired the name Havana syndrome, after the city where mass reports of the phenomenon first emerged.

Later, dozens of CIA officers around the world reported Havana syndrome episodes, which in official documents were called anomalous health incidents (AHIs). Many believed AHIs were the result of a Russian intelligence operation to wound or intimidate covert US operatives using a previously unknown weapon that delivered sonic or pulsed microwave energy.

There was sustained pushback against that theory. Some scientists insisted the idea of a portable weapon that could deliver these injuries belonged in the realm of science fiction. They said a whole range of conditions could cause pain, dizziness and cognitive issues.

Various experts suggested AHIs could be down to environmental factors, toxins or even the sound of chirping crickets. One explanation was that the symptoms were psychogenic and the result of “mass hysteria”, while some inside the CIA even accused those involved of faking their injuries in the hope of a medical payout. The disagreements over what was causing Havana syndrome led to bitter arguments and broken friendships at the spy agency.

In 2022, a panel of scientific experts convened by the US government concluded that “the signs and symptoms of AHIs are genuine and compelling” and “could be due to external stimuli”.

But the next year, a long-awaited report delivered the official assessment of the US intelligence community: “The available intelligence consistently points against the involvement of US adversaries in causing the reported incidents,” read an unclassified summary. It was “very unlikely” that a sinister Russian campaign was behind AHIs, it concluded.

Yet the mystery of Havana syndrome refuses to die. This summer, the “very unlikely” assessment from 2023 was rescinded by Donald Trump’s outgoing director of national intelligence, who claimed it was based on flawed analysis.

Now, a decade after the first reports emerged from Havana, two CBS journalists who have covered the story from the start are to release a book that sets out the case for Russia being behind at least some of the episodes. It also accuses parts of the US government and intelligence community of covering up the evidence.

This article is based on early access to their findings, as well as on the Guardian’s own interviews with intelligence sources, AHI patients and scientists.

David Relman, the Stanford professor who led the official scientific panel on Havana syndrome in 2022, told the Guardian he believed there was a subset of AHI cases that were “most plausibly explained by exposure to pulsed microwave energy”.

His panel had access to patient records and to more than 1,000 classified documents on the topic. “To any reasonable person looking at all the evidence I was able to see, it inevitably leads to the conclusion that there may have been a cover-up,” he said.

Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados are longstanding producers for the CBS programme 60 Minutes. In an interview at the programme’s studios in midtown Manhattan, the pair recounted how they first came across the story a decade ago.

They covered the Obama administration’s policy of re-establishing diplomatic relations with Cuba in 2015, so when reports emerged the next year of a mysterious new condition afflicting employees at the reopened embassy in Havana, they contacted a senior US diplomat who had been posted there. “I expected him to say: ‘This is all bullshit,’” said Zill. “But he said: ‘Oh no, this is completely true. And I can put you in touch with a bunch of people who were hit.’”

The pair spoke to more than a dozen of them, off the record, but by the time they were ready to put a story together there were new reports of similar cases occurring among US diplomats stationed in China. Then there were whispers about it happening in other locations around the world.

Once the first 60 Minutes episodes devoted to the topic aired, victims started contacting the producers, keen to tell their stories. Many of these new sources were – or had been – undercover operatives for the CIA, meaning they could not speak openly as most details of their work were classified. But people stationed around the world who had not known each other told stories that seemed remarkably similar.

A pattern linked some of the key cases: the alleged victims were working, or had previously worked, on beats where they rubbed up against Russian interests.

In some cases, the location of the supposed hits was notable in itself: allies of Moscow where some part of the elite was looking to improve relations with the west. This was the case in Cuba, where the original cluster of cases had come during the Obama-era thaw in relations with the US, which had irritated hardliners in the Cuban regime and their backers in Moscow.

It was also the case in Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Serbia and Vietnam. Several CIA officers who had been stationed in Kyiv around the time of the 2014 Maidan revolution in Ukraine, decried by the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as a US-backed coup, later suffered AHIs in different locations across the world.

“I went through years of doubts about the story, and all the crazy things we were hearing,” said Zill. But the more source meetings she and Rey had, the more they felt there really was something there. “We’re meeting these highly effective intelligence officers and they’re all telling versions of the same story,” said Rey.

The origins of Havana syndrome go back long before Cuba. A cornerstone case is that of Mike Beck, a counter-intelligence officer at the National Security Agency who got sick while on temporary assignment to an undisclosed location in the 1990s to check a US diplomatic facility for bugs.

Beck developed a rare form of Parkinson’s disease at the age of 45 and died this year. A declassified NSA statement, included in his 2014 workplace compensation claim, noted that “there is intelligence information from 2012 associating the hostile country to which Mr Beck travelled in the late 1990s with a high-powered microwave system weapon that may have the ability to weaken, intimidate or kill an enemy, over time, and without leaving evidence”. The unnamed “hostile country”, sources said, was Russia.

The first known AHIs among the contemporary batch of cases occurred in late 2014, when several US government employees at the consulate in Frankfurt, Germany, became ill. One was found unconscious in a consulate stairwell after feeling sudden, intense pressure on her chest and hearing a “high-pitched squeal”, Rey and Zill reported.

The next year, a researcher at a US defence institute – who asked the Guardian not to use her name – was on a tour of the Balkans, attending meetings with military officers from the host nations alongside US defence attaches. Her itinerary took in Montenegro, which was in the process of applying for Nato membership, and Serbia, a Russian ally that harboured resentments towards the US over the 1999 Nato bombing of Yugoslavia.

On her final evening in Belgrade, as she walked through lively pedestrianised streets to her hotel, the researcher was sure she spotted someone following her. Later, as she approached her hotel room, she felt “a sinking feeling, as though I was in a lift that was descending suddenly”, she recalled in a telephone interview.

Inside her room, she continued to feel odd sensations. “I just had this falling sensation, a feeling of gravity pulling at me, and nausea.” At one point, she turned on her government laptop and found the screen was flickering with blue static. The computer never worked again.

She said she was able to continue her trip, but in the subsequent weeks she felt weak, had difficulty speaking clearly and developed pain that felt “like a drill was going into my eye”. She was unable to focus at work. “I used up all my vacation, then my sick leave, then colleagues donated their leave. Eventually, I had to leave my job,” she said. It was only much later that she connected what had happened to her with reports about Havana syndrome.

The next cohort of AHI patients included people at the heart of a new CIA policy on Russia. In 2017, as Donald Trump took office for the first time, the agency launched a drive to push back against the increasingly brazen global reach of Moscow’s intelligence agencies.

“They wanted us to take the same kind of tactics and spirit we used in the global war on terror to the Russians,” said Marc Polymeropoulos, who was made deputy chief of operations for Europe and Eurasia in 2017. Polymeropoulos, who had spent most of his career in the Middle East, was one of several veterans of the “war on terror” who were moved to senior roles focused on Russia. Even as Trump publicly denied that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election, the agency made plans to push back hard against Russian activity.

“Obviously, we didn’t have permission to run lethal operations against the Russians, but we could do things we hadn’t done as much previously, such as enlist the help of multiple friendly services and expose the Russians for what they were doing,” said Polymeropoulos, in an interview at a restaurant just outside Washington.

In early December 2017, Polymeropoulos and another senior CIA executive made a liaison trip to Moscow, to meet their counterparts in Russia’s SVR and FSB intelligence services. The official meetings were ill-tempered and lacking in substance. Late one night, Polymeropoulos woke up suddenly in his hotel room. “I had vertigo and a splitting headache. I thought it was food poisoning at first, I thought I was going to puke and crap my brains out, and I remember being like, holy shit, the room is spinning and my ears are ringing,” he said.

On his return to Washington, Polymeropoulos struggled with a persistent migraine that would not subside, and with superiors who insisted his symptoms were unrelated to other AHIs. He saw a variety of doctors on his own time, but owing to the classified nature of his job he could not share details of where he had been when he became ill.

He left the CIA in 2019 and, frustrated at being stonewalled in his requests for medical assessment, became the first CIA officer to go public with a Havana syndrome story under their real name, telling the journalist Julia Ioffe about what happened in Moscow.

The resulting publicity prompted the CIA to send him to the Walter Reed military medical centre, where he was diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury. In 2023 he was found eligible for compensation under the Havana Act, which authorised payments to “personnel who incur brain injuries from hostilities while on assignment”. The financial payout was modest, but he saw it as a moral victory after years of fighting for recognition.

One early theory was that AHIs could be the result of data collection attempts gone wrong – a machine designed to pull classified data from operatives’ electronic devices that had unfortunate side-effects when turned up too high. That is still seen by some as a possibility, although even if intelligence collection was the initial idea, the damaging health effects would have quickly become apparent to the operators.

Some observers insisted the whole concept of “Havana syndrome” was an invention. They asked why, if Russia possessed a brain-frying weapon, it was not using it on a wider range of its enemies. Why were there not more reports of collateral victims?

The sociologist Robert Bartholomew and the neurologist Robert Baloh co-authored a book that declared the whole story a hoax – “a case study in the social construction of mass psychogenic illness” – borne of high-stress work environments and propagated by excitable journalists.

Douglas Fields, a cellular neuroscientist and author of several books about the brain, claimed in a journal article that the medical studies of patients which showed cognitive changes had used unsound methodology, and that theories of an energy weapon “defy the laws of physics”. Reports of Havana syndrome should be taken no more seriously than sightings of the Loch Ness monster, he suggested.

Other scientists, including some who had reviewed patients’ medical records, strongly disagreed. “The early scepticism was perfectly appropriate, but over time we started to see an increase in the number of individuals who have gone through clinical evaluations that cannot be faked,” said James Giordano, a professor emeritus of neurology at Georgetown University Medical Center and the forensic neuroscientist on the original cohort of cases from Havana.

“We are talking about objective signs that are presenting with a very distinct pattern,” Giordano said. Key symptoms included “a profound tumbling or falling sensation” as well as pressure in the head, chest and throat, and cognitive effects. It was true that chemical or drug exposure could cause similar symptoms, he said, but this would be visible on blood tests. Another key factor was the sudden onset and the sense of a specific location where the apparent attack felt strongest.

When the Biden administration took office in 2021, the then CIA director, Bill Burns, and the director of national intelligence, Avril Haines, vowed to get to the bottom of the issue. Burns met many of the AHI cohort, including Polymeropoulos, listening carefully to their stories and promising them a full investigation.

Burns also fired the CIA’s chief medical officer, who had infuriated some AHI patients by accusing them of faking their symptoms. The same year, more than 100 CIA operatives and other US government officials reported AHIs in locations around the world. In Vienna, there were so many hits that the work of the CIA station was essentially paralysed and the station chief recalled. A spate of government employees also reported incidents on US soil, including several who claimed to have been hit on the grounds of the White House. Was this an adversary stepping up its campaign, or was the increasing publicity about AHIs leading more people to misidentify other conditions or episodes as Havana syndrome?

Burns and Haines launched two investigations, one to re-examine intelligence on whether a foreign adversary was behind Havana syndrome, and another that convened a panel of scientists and physicians to determine whether it was even possible for a weapon to cause the symptoms.

Relman, a Stanford professor who chaired the scientific panel, said its members were given access to open source and classified scientific studies into pulsed radio frequency energy, which suggested that the science behind there being a “device” that could cause AHI symptoms was plausible. Scientists who disagreed were simply unaware of the research into such technology that had been taking place for decades in several countries, especially in the Soviet Union and then Russia, he said.

Regarding the medical results, Relman conceded that plenty – perhaps the vast majority – of AHI claims could be explained by other factors. But there were dozens of cases “that were unusual in the distinctness of their features and the near impossibility of explaining them based on known medical and environmental conditions”. In short: the publicity around AHIs may have prompted a wave of false reporting, but a core subset of cases seemed real.

Determining who may have carried out such attacks was beyond Relman’s purview. That fell to the second expert group, which in 2023 issued the assessment that it was “very unlikely” to be caused by a foreign adversary, dismaying many AHI patients who had hoped to finally receive closure on what caused their health problems.

Even people who have seen the intelligence on Havana syndrome can disagree on what it suggests. Two sources offered the Guardian radically different interpretations of what the classified data shows on possible Russian involvement.

One highlighted the lack of a “smoking gun”; a piece of human intelligence or an intercept that showed Russian operatives discussing a programme to use directed energy against Americans.

“Everyone has seen how strong our collection capabilities on Russia are,” the source said, referencing how US intelligence got hold of Putin’s war plans before his February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. “If this was really a large-scale Russian programme, we would have expected to see something in some of these channels, but we didn’t.”

Another former intelligence official disagreed: “If you’re waiting for an intercept of someone saying: ‘My name is Igor and I’m going to press the button on my secret laser’ before you have confidence, that’s probably never going to happen. But for any reasonable person who has access to the intelligence and knows how to read it, the Russian fingerprints are clear.”

If that is the case, it raises the question of why the 2023 intelligence community assessment found it “very unlikely” that a foreign actor was involved. At the end of the Biden administration, a tweaked version said that while five US intelligence agencies still found it “very unlikely”, one agency now believed there was a “roughly even chance” that a foreign actor had used “a novel weapon or prototype device” in a number of attacks.

This summer, both of those Biden-era assessments were rescinded by Trump’s director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, in a memo issued just before she left office. Gabbard said the earlier assessments were marred by “selective exclusion of evidence” and “mischaracterisation of sources”, though the statement did not release any new evidence or provide a revised assessment.

While Gabbard had a chequered reputation among the intelligence community, Mark Zaid, a lawyer who represents more than 30 AHI patients, welcomed her memo and said it was a first step to overturning a CIA cover-up. When asked why the CIA might have perpetrated such a cover-up, Zaid suggested it could be to protect its reputation after prior negligence. “This has built up to a level that the agency can’t let the truth get out because it’s going to reflect so poorly on them,” he said.

Burns, in a comment for Rey and Zill’s book, said it was “simply not true that there was a ‘cover-up’ by the CIA” and described the earlier investigation as “a rigorous effort across the entire intelligence community”.

Rey and Zill believe the purported cover-up was a result of multiple factors over many years. “There’s not a single cigar-filled backroom meeting that led to decisions getting made,” said Rey. “There was a lot of, ‘This is a pain in the ass’ or ‘The president’s not going to want to hear this’. There was bureaucratic dysfunction, careerism and things that just got in the way of proper investigation.”

One example he gave is the fact that the FBI sent criminal investigators, rather than counterintelligence investigators with access to classified information, to Havana after the attacks there. Another is a nascent investigation at CIA headquarters in late 2019 which reportedly found that, in some cases, phones linked to Russian intelligence operatives had been in the vicinity of suspected Havana syndrome incidents. These included the hits that year on the senior CIA officer in London and Warsaw.

In London, a suspicious phone had supposedly been just 10 metres (30ft) away from his hotel room. But when the then CIA director, Gina Haspel, was briefed on these findings, she allegedly complained it was not solid enough to take to the president, given how sensitive he was on Russia-related matters. “The meeting abruptly ended after Haspel shouted that if she took reports like this to President Trump, she would be fired as director,” Rey and Zill write.

Outside the CIA, some have uncovered intriguing leads about possible links between Russian operatives and AHIs. Christo Grozev, a journalist and investigator who has exposed several Russian intelligence operations, claimed leaked travel data suggested at least four potential crossovers between suspected AHIs and travel by officers from Unit 29155 of Russia’s GRU military intelligence, known for its campaign of sabotage and assassinations in western countries. He also said he had traced travel by “members of what appears to be a technical unit adjacent to 29155” to Cuba during the initial attacks.

Perhaps the most significant piece of evidence to emerge recently has been the alleged US government acquisition of a “Havana syndrome-style device” in an undercover operation. First reported by the independent journalist Sasha Ingber this year, two sources confirmed to the Guardian that a device had been acquired and brought to the US in late 2024 for testing, after a purchase from a dark-web seller.

Rey and Zill’s book recounts a meeting with a person who claimed to be part of the undercover team that acquired the device. The source told them the device was “man-portable”, shot non-thermal pulsed microwaves and was acquired from “a complex Russian illicit network”.

It was not believed to have been used in a Havana syndrome incident, but testing on animals has reportedly shown it may cause similar symptoms to AHIs, which could prove that building such a device is scientifically possible.

That would make the case for a weapon being involved in some incidents more plausible, and would also raise new and worrying questions. If such weapons have proliferated to the extent that one can be bought on the dark web, how many devices could be out there and who may have access to them? Could AHIs thus have not one perpetrator, but many? And is there a future in which such weapons become a widespread element of warfare? “We know the technology has reached a level that enables it to be used in weaponisable ways,” said Giordano. “I see that as a clear and present threat.”

For those who have had symptoms for years, the acquisition of the device and the rescinded intelligence assessments provide some hope that, one day, they will receive official confirmation that they were targeted by a foreign adversary. For many of them, the lack of recognition at home has angered them more than the attack itself.

“The Russians are our enemy, I put them in the same bucket as al-Qaida or the Taliban, or any other groups I worked against,” said Polymeropoulos. “Do I want to see them held accountable? Of course. But I’m actually more upset and feel more of a betrayal from my own government.”

The Havana Syndrome by Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados is published by Crown Publishing in the US on 13 October and by WH Allen in the UK on 15 October.

Five Great Reads: unmarked graves, Happy Mondays, and a childhood without sugar

The Guardian Sat, 10 Oct 2026 04:24:22 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

This selection of reads from across the Guardian has chronicles of evolution, investigations and interviews which ask us to think about how we remember our loved ones when they are gone, and – of course – stories that leave you with a little something sweet.

Enjoy.

Peter Giesel was buried in an unmarked communal grave. The state government laid Giesel to rest in a cemetery on the outskirts of Sydney in a single plot with three others. This week, a Guardian Australia investigation found there are more than 100 cases like his across New South Wales. The Guardian revealed Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives such as Giesel’s sister, Nicole, have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.

Persons without means: This is the designation the state gives to those who are unable to afford their own funerals. Over the course of the investigation, the Guardian discovered at least 18 individuals known to homelessness services in Sydney who have been placed in unmarked graves in the last 10 years.

Notable quote: “How could such a heartless thing happen to someone who gave so much of his heart to others,” asks Giesel’s friend Elaine Grady (pictured).

An immediate response: When asked about the revelations, NSW Health delivered an apology to the dead and their loved ones, acknowledging they had not always been treated with the dignity and respect they deserved.

How long will it take to read: Less than seven minutes.

Further reading: Shared graves and stories such as Jayne and Barbara’s, have brought this issue to national attention.

Young people around the world are lonelier than ever, and examples of this are not hard to find. In online forums, users ask: “How do you deal with touch starvation?” Another asks: “The loneliness is unbearable, is anyone else experiencing this?” The answer to the latter question is yes. From Germany to Australia to the UK, studies show teenagers and young adults are finding social connections harder to form.

Why? The list is long. In her new book, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist Dr Michelle Lim examines why young people have turned toward solitude. She cites a long list of overlapping factors, including hyper-competitive education culture, social media, shifting family dynamics, the cost-of-living crisis, the grief many are still feeling from the Covid pandemic, and the rise of automation, “which means a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human”. Young adults are simply not being offered the opportunities to form meaningful connections, Lim says.

“People are getting used to being alone”: Lim’s biggest fear is what she calls “social atrophy”. Young people, she writes, can fall into what she calls the “loneliness loop”. When you experience loneliness, it can cause you to run away from further social interaction out of fear, making connections harder to come by.

How long will it take to read: Five minutes of solitude.

Further reading: Community-maxxing, and making new friends and connections as adults.

Taking drugs, drinking heavily and dancing to the tunes of the Happy Mondays on stage made Bez famous. The story goes, as the Manchester music scene was exploding, band member Shaun Ryder urged Bez (whose real name is Mark Berry) to jump on stage with the band when they were supporting New Order. His “wild-eyed dancing” is now synonymous with the music itself, and as the band celebrate the 35th anniversary of their landmark album Pills ‘n’ Thrills and Bellyaches, Bez is back at it as the Happy Mondays go on a global tour.

A change for the good: After decades of partying, one might expect Bez to show signs of wear from his life on the road with a rock band. But when interviewer Emine Saner showed up at “his lovely cottage, down a rural track in Herefordshire”, Bez appeared unscathed by the years of drugs and drinking. Having given up cocaine and sugar, the former 24 hour party person now “juices every day, eats only organic food, drinks filtered water and works out with weights in his garden”.

Notable quote: “There’s sheep everywhere now,” Bez told Saner. At first, Saner took it as “a reference to our zombified society”, but he meant “actual sheep in the field” they just entered.

How long will it take to read: Just over five minutes, giving you enough time to Step On.

Further reading: Which is the best Happy Mondays song?

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Denise Brown’s sister Nicole was murdered by OJ Simpson. On the last night the two sisters spent together, Nicole looked out the window to see Simpson driving by. “He’s constantly following me,” she told Brown. After her sister’s murder and the evidence of long-term abuse that emerged during the trial, Brown became a campaigner against domestic violence. She sat down with the Guardian to discuss what she wishes she had known before her sister’s death, and how she hopes her new book can save lives.

It’s rarely simple to leave: Brown says she told her sister all the wrong things. “You’ve got to leave him. You’ve got to get out of this situation. What are you doing?” she told Nicole. Brown now realises she was being unsupportive at the time, and has learned it is often not easy for a victim to leave. “Batterers usually threaten to take children away, threaten family members. When you are in a cycle like Nicole – like a lot of victims of domestic violence – was in, you are the only one who realises how dangerous that situation can be.”

The car chase: The day after Nicole’s funeral, Simpson was scheduled to turn himself in to the police, but elected to go on the run. While millions watched on TV, Brown says she joined in the chase. “We were out of our minds. We got on the road, but he was so far ahead of us. I mean, come on, really?” She laughs at herself, but says: “It was a time of our lives that was insane.”

How long will it take to read: Five minutes.

Further reading: More stories of survival.

In Australia, domestic and family violence counselling is available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines may be found via www. befrienders. org

In the dark days after the second world war in Britain, many foods, including sugar, remained rationed. Adults had just 3 tbsp (40g) a day to stretch between cups of tea and desserts. Children were offered even less, with the very young expected to have no sugar at all. But then the brakes came off, and sugar consumption in the UK almost doubled. Now scientists are looking back on this era to study the impact of sugar on our health.

Notable quote: “History created an experiment that we could never deliberately run over a human lifetime,” says Dr Jiazhen Zheng at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

What have they learned? Using data from the UK Biobank to compare the health of people born shortly before and after sugar rationing ended in the UK, scientists from the University of Southern California found that the longer people had spent under rationing, the lower their risk of developing type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure in mid- to later life. Another study, this one led by Zheng in Hong Kong, found reduced sugar exposure was associated with a lower risk of a growing list of health conditions. “In our work,” Zheng says, “we have seen associations with cardiovascular disease, liver disease, respiratory health, dementia and, more recently, broader measures of ageing.”

How long will it take to read: A sweet three-and-a-half minutes.

Further reading: Everything you need to know about sugar.

Andy Burnham is lucky – Polanski, Farage and Badenoch all seem determined to help him

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 17:05:50 GMT

Everywhere the PM turns, he finds generous adversaries. They have made his early days in No 10 so much easier

I don’t know where Andy Burnham found his magic lamp, but I hope he’s taking good care of it. In the early hours of Friday morning, the genie that’s looked so kindly on him these past few months granted him yet another wish, with a byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. It was just the latest gift for a prime minister for whom things keep going right – and who is especially blessed in his choice of opponents.

Let’s start with that win in London, where Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali defeated the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. It’s easy to miss how rare such a victory is. As the veteran psephologist Peter Kellner pointed out, this was a win that “defied history”. If the past half-century were any guide, Labour should have lost, thanks to a “truly dreadful record” defending its own seats when in government and facing a byelection challenge from the left or centre-left, the likes of the Greens or the Lib Dems. The average swing against Labour in such contests had been 24%. “On those figures,” wrote Kellner, “Polanski should have won at a canter.” But he lost.

That reinforces the case Burnham made for why he should replace the previous Holborn and St Pancras MP, one Keir Starmer, as Labour leader: namely, that he was uniquely placed to defeat challenges from both left and right. This latest win over the Greens, coupled with his own success in Makerfield in June, is early vindication of that argument.

Burnham can claim much credit for the London result: it’s his leftward shift that has persuaded many progressive voters that they don’t need to vote Green to get what they want and that they should give Labour another chance. But Burnham really ought to share the credit with Polanski himself, who has proved a most generous adversary.

Yes, Polanski brought an initial surge in energy, enthusiasm and membership to the Greens. But under him the party has steadily dismantled the moral halo it once enjoyed as the UK’s foremost advocate for the planet, reshaping itself into something darker. Thanks to Sunday’s conference vote branding Zionism as racism, which Polanski ducked, the party now demands the destruction of a state founded, and still regarded by most Jews, as an essential refuge, one whose creation was approved by a UN vote. “Destruction” is not metaphorical, by the way. The motion passed says that the change it seeks – a Palestinian state replacing, rather than existing alongside, Israel – must be secured “by all available means”, a phrase clarified in an accompanying booklet produced by the motion’s proposers to include “armed struggle”. Meaning, violence.

Thus have the Greens allowed themselves to become toxified by the kind of cranks and bigots whose manias crowd out anyone who dares hold a moderate or nuanced view, including many longtime, dedicated local activists. A moment like this calls for leadership, but all the Greens have is a quack hypnotherapist who once earned a living promising to make women’s breasts larger and who, when faced with a difficult decision, ran away. (Now, after the event, Polanski says he would not have voted for the Zionism resolution.) Instead of a leader, the Greens are stuck with a charlatan and a coward.

No wonder former leader Caroline Lucas could not say yes, when asked by Newsnight, whether Polanski should stay in his post. Burnham himself would have no such hesitation: the PM might even be quietly pleased that Polanski performed just well enough in Thursday’s byelection to fend off an immediate challenge. The longer Polanski leads the Greens, the better for Labour.

Meanwhile, Burnham’s other opponents seem similarly determined to do him a favour. Of course, there will be stormier times ahead, but the party conference season now concluded was like a warm, extended summer for the prime minister.

Reform UK, for so long Labour’s strongest challenger in the polls, saw its moment in the sun clouded by eve-of-conference revelations that two senior aides to Nigel Farage had been caught on film apparently discussing how they might get around UK electoral law to take a £500,000 donation from a US benefactor. In politics, the scandals that bite hardest are those that confirm suspicions the voters already harbour. In this case, three in four Britons told YouGov back in July that they regarded Farage as sleazy, with 56% describing him as “very sleazy”.

The party’s leading lights tried to make assorted policy announcements, but the only debate that really cut through was the one started by Suella Braverman, with her eccentric and exclusivist insistence that certain minorities, even those born in England into families rooted in the country for several generations, are not truly English – a definition that would exclude Rishi Sunak and a good portion of the England football team. Farage’s army of would-be mavericks and rebels looks increasingly like a rabble of crooks and spivs and – as if to prove the Greens have no monopoly on the demographic – cranks and bigots.

All this has created an opening for the Conservatives to reclaim their place as the dominant party of the right – but here, too, the genie has smiled on Burnham. True, Kemi Badenoch continues to enjoy higher ratings than her party, but that isn’t saying much. True, too, that she has, belatedly, woken up to the fact that victory will not come solely from trying to out-Reform Reform – people will always vote for the real thing – and that she has to appeal to that vast swathe of Middle England seats lost in 2024 to the Lib Dems.

Her conference pitch – promising to abolish inheritance tax on even the most expensive homes, and to extend free childcare to those earning over £100,000 – might conceivably appeal to some of those high earners. But it draws a dividing line with Labour that Burnham could only have dreamed of. Now the Tories have made plain that, in an age of stretched resources, their priority is to help some of the richest people in the land. That is a battle Burnham will be itching to fight.

As for the Lib Dems, the PM will be only too happy to see them muddling along, an inoffensive receptacle for Tory-sceptic voters in parts of the country that would never go to Labour. Though Burnham wants to eat into their vote too, promising that he will, in the next term, deliver on two of their signature issues: Europe and electoral reform.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

He did that in a speech that was the highlight of the conference season, one that showed a politician who understands the importance of making arguments – and is comfortable making them. After Starmer, who was the opposite in both respects, listening to Burnham was like “gulping down oxygen”, one cabinet minister told me.

And yet, everyone at Labour’s top table knows that the weather will change soon enough. The government, and everyone else, is paying too much to borrow money. At some point, the welfare budget will have to be cut: Labour MPs may be applauding now, but they will be less cheerful when asked to vote for reduced benefits, especially as they face re-selection contests in their local parties, a process that gets under way as soon as January.

There’s a hole in defence spending to fill, the full sweep of public services crying out for cash, a US president apparently bent on driving up global oil prices and therefore inflation, and a civil service machine that ministers privately curse as bloated and ineffective. What’s more, the period we’re in right now – the middle of the parliament – is when governments should be focused entirely on delivery, driving through their agenda. Instead, vital time has been spent on the transition from one PM to another – time Labour will not get back.

For now, Burnham is lucky in his opponents, whose choices hurt them and help him. But the skies will eventually darken and, when they do, the prime minister will reach once again for that magic lamp – hoping against hope that it still works.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

The Guardian view on Labour and the Greens: winning trust takes more than words

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:52:10 GMT

A byelection win is a fillip for Andy Burnham and shows Zack Polanski must confront the failures damaging his party’s credibility and appeal

By holding Holborn and St Pancras, Andy Burnham’s Labour has shown it can attract liberal and left-leaning voters. The seat has substantial numbers of young adults, students, professionals and Muslims – offering fertile ground for the Greens’ ecopopulism. However, Labour prevailed. Having won leave-voting Makerfield in June, Mr Burnham can now claim an appeal that bridges Labour’s divided electorate. It’s worth noting that turnout in London was low and Labour’s vote share fell 3.7 points. But that compares with an average 19.3-point fall in four byelections under Mr Burnham’s predecessor. The new leader clearly has bought Labour breathing space and checked the Green advance.

The Greens more than tripled their vote share in the constituency to 33%. But they were beaten. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% in Sir Keir Starmer’s former seat, leaving Zack Polanski’s ambition of entering parliament unfulfilled. For a party that began the year promising to turn voters’ hunger for change into a serious challenge to Labour, this was a sobering moment. The passing of a motion declaring “Zionism is racism” at its conference probably cost the party support – though the result in central London alone cannot definitively say that. There is a separate question of leadership. Mr Polanski now says he would have voted against the motion. Why, then, did he not make his opposition clear when it mattered last weekend?

He intends to remain leader – and the expanded, radical membership has given Mr Polanski a base in the party that likely insulates him from an instant coup. But with calls for his resignation growing, he has to try to stay in the job while restoring confidence in the Greens’ electoral chances. Clouds had emerged on the horizon long before the party’s conference. Its spring polling surge has faded. In March, YouGov put the party second nationally to Reform, on 21%. Mr Burnham has since stolen much of the Greens’ rhetorical thunder by consciously evoking a more leftwing agenda. The party is now in fourth place, polling 10% nationally.

As Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents. Since the beginning of the year his net favourability rating has fallen from -6 to -29. The Greens are not to be discounted. Mr Burnham has yet to turn hope into lasting support. That will depend on what his government delivers, especially as prices rise, rather than whom it defeats.

In an interview with the BBC, Jonathan Bartley, the Greens’ former party co-leader, warned that the influx of members has changed the party and that some newcomers are unaware of its traditions of consensus and opposition to political “purity tests”. Significantly, Mr Polanski’s deputy, Rachel Millward, said that the party structures needed to become “fully democratic and strategic”. This may not be enough for the Green MP Siân Berry, who said she wanted to “fix the serious flaws” in the controversial Zionism motion.

Leadership is missing, and responsibility for that falls squarely on Mr Polanski. He has shown that he can communicate persuasively. Now, if he remains in post, he must show that he can acknowledge what went wrong and build support for changing the controversial Zionism policy. Mr Polanski claims credit for Labour’s leftward turn. But the Green leader now needs to put his own party’s house in order.

The Guardian view on the 90s revival: the end of the analogue age

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:50:48 GMT

The new exhibition at Tate Britain is part of a wider cultural resurgence from 30 years ago. This is nostalgia for a pre-digital era

Each generation imagines itself to be cooler than the one that went before it, and weirder than the one that comes after it, to update George Orwell. Gen X is no exception. “It felt like something was happening,” Pulp’s Jarvis Cocker writes in the catalogue for The 90s: Art and Fashion, which opened at Tate Britain this week. “Something good. It felt like the weirdos were taking over.”

The exhibition, curated by the former editor of British Vogue, Edward Enninful, is part of a wider 90s cultural revival. Oasis’s Wonderwall was the UK’s unofficial World Cup anthem this summer, after last year’s sellout reunion tour. Pulp have also just completed a world tour. The 1993 novel Trainspotting has become a musical; less surprisingly, so has 90s-set romance One Day, which found a new audience with 2024’s Netflix series. Love Story, which fictionalises the doomed relationship between John F Kennedy Jr and Carolyn Bessette, broke streaming records. Cult drama This Life is now on iPlayer. Vogue has described the era as “fashion’s most revisited decade”.

And there’s more in the pipeline. The National Theatre’s 2027 season will include two new plays celebrating the “optimism” of the 1990s: James Graham’s dramatisation of John Major’s rise to No 10 and Moira Buffini’s imagining of the lead-up to the 1998 Good Friday agreement.

This sense of optimism is surely behind the resurgence. Between the fall of the Berlin Wall and of the twin towers in New York, democracy, economics and creativity thrived, at least for some. The Young British Artists and Britpop put the UK on the contemporary cultural map. The common people could become pop stars, fashion designers and prize-winning artists. Magazine photoshoots were elevated to art. Kate Moss was the face of the era. Daring, youthful and “real” – this was Cool Britannia. No wonder the New Labour government was quick to get in on the act after its 1997 victory.

Nineties grunge is seen as a reaction against the excesses of the Thatcherite 80s. Yet, as last year’s exhibitions showcasing Leigh Bowery and The Face magazine showed, a youth counter-culture had emerged. In the 90s it became mainstream.

In hindsight Cool Britannia looks more than a little London-centric and elitist. And life wasn’t glossy for everyone. Racism, Aids and sexism form the backdrop to the Tate exhibition. Many of the images explore what it meant to be a young woman at a time when “girl power” was an empty slogan in the creative industries. One of the era’s greatest cultural legacies is that these female artists now command solo exhibitions, such as Tracey Emin’s blockbuster retrospective at Tate Modern this spring.

This 30-year renaissance cannot just be put down to the “nostalgia pendulum”, whereby influential figures like Enninful are able to curate their own past. The 1990s was the last decade of the analogue age. This nostalgia speaks to a longing for a time without smartphones, social media, selfies and streaming. People watched TV, listened to music and danced together. It was a period of freedom, possibility and fun for young people. It’s not hard to see why it appeals to Gen Z. Like the magazines set up to capture the zeitgeist, that world has gone for ever. We don’t look back in anger, but in sorrow.

Zionism, racism and the Green party in turmoil

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:22:50 GMT

Readers respond to articles on the Green party’s motion

As ever, Jonathan Freedland is on the money in his article (The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think, 3 October). As a non-religious Jew-ish Londoner, I am appalled at the passing of the motion to declare Zionism as a form of racism, and I am seriously considering leaving the Green party as a result.

While I condemn the Israeli government’s actions against the Palestinian people, and I am not a Zionist myself, Zionism as defined by the motion is only one political interpretation and completely ignores ancient religious and cultural definitions held by many Jews who also condemn the current Israeli government.

I have worked with Palestinians and Israelis on the West Bank and in Jerusalem in the cause of peace and reconciliation, and firmly believe in equal rights for everyone in Israel and the occupied territories. That cause will be set back by this decision, which will give fuel to antisemites who hide their racism under an anti-Zionist guise.

This decision is a shot in the foot for the Green party, risking the alienation of British Jews and others who, like me, support peace and reconciliation, believe in equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians, and strongly oppose the actions of the current Israeli government. Simon LawsonLondon

Jonathan Freedland is right that Zionism means different things to different people, and that Jewish historical attachment to Israel cannot simply be dismissed. But that complexity can also become a way of avoiding the more important question: what has Zionism produced in practice?

“Fire is destructive” does not mean every use of fire is destructive. It means fire has destructive potential, which is why we recognise boundaries around its use. The same applies to Zionism. Jewish self-determination is not inherently racist; but when a political project pursued in its name produces permanent occupation, settlement, displacement, unequal rights and Palestinian subordination, it is legitimate to ask whether the project has crossed those boundaries. Therefore, “Zionism is racist” can be a true description of the manifestation of Zionism embodied in the current Israeli state.

The issue, therefore, isn’t whether a benign definition of Zionism can be imagined. It plainly can. The issue is whether the political reality created in its name conforms to that definition. We should be able to examine Zionism as we examine any other political ideology: by its effects, its institutions, and the boundaries it recognises. Criticising a political ideology or the actions of a state is not the same thing as attacking Jews or Judaism. Raymond O’BrienLondon

Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it. Green party success in the EU elections in 1989 saw a huge increase in membership and a wave of entryism. By 1991 it was fragmented and irrelevant. Zack Polanski’s election as leader of the Green party also saw a wave of entryism.

It was never tenable to allow a gathering composed of those who can afford, or choose, to turn up to be the party’s policymaking body. But for many Greens it is an article of faith; proof of the party’s commitment to “democracy”. They were called “fundis” (fundamentalists) in my day. A group of us (“realos”) tried to change things in 1990 with a motion arguing that a “leadership” structure was necessary in a world where we were under the media microscope. The motion passed, but the party split.

It is tragic to see a party that has pulled itself up by its bootstraps since the early 1990s, that has worked hard to win representation locally, and that has won seats in Westminster under a voting system that disadvantages newcomers, being stopped in its tracks by its lack of internal democracy.

Here’s a suggestion from an oldie. Organise an internal referendum on the motion and let the whole membership decide. And put an end to the travesty of democracy that saw it adopted in the first place. Lyn DadeTwickenham, London

As a member of the Green party, I was dismayed by the profoundly counterproductive “Zionism is racism” motion passed at conference on Sunday. Since his election as leader and his success in broadening the party’s appeal, opponents of Zack Polanski and the Greens have repeatedly sought to portray the party as antisemitic. This motion hands them the ammunition they have been looking for.

Until now, the Greens have stood out among UK political parties in their willingness to describe Israel as an apartheid state and to condemn its actions in Gaza as genocidal. That argument risks being obscured by an entirely avoidable debate over accusations of antisemitism.

The motion is also historically and politically flawed. While the form of Zionism represented by the Israeli state today is exclusionary and discriminatory, it does not follow that all forms of Zionism are racist.

Zionism emerged, in large part, as a response to the persecution of Jews in Europe. To erase that history from our understanding of Zionism is to overlook the reality of anti-Jewish racism that helped give rise to the movement.

I hope the Green party leadership can find a way to distance itself from this damaging motion and refocus attention on holding the Israeli government accountable for its treatment of the Palestinians. Prof Benjamin SelwynUniversity of Sussex

Farewell, Marina Hyde. Thank you for brightening so many of our days

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 16:15:14 GMT

New Zealand’s proud record at Eden Park – a 53-match unbeaten streak against all comers – is under threat as the hosts face in-form Australia at their Auckland fortress. Still shaken by a 3-1 series loss to South Africa, the battered and bruised All Blacks will strive to rebound in the opening Bledisloe Cup Test against a Wallabies side unbeaten in six matches and brimming with energy after a spellbinding victory over the Springboks. Les Kiss has made an impression since succeeding Joe Schmidt in July, racking up four wins and a draw. A 42-38 upset of the world champions in Perth two weeks ago showcased a measured Wallabies gameplan, built on a solid set-piece, careful game management from scrum-half Ryan Lonergan and successful contesting of high kicks. Follow the action with our live blog.

After an interminable three-week international break, the Premier League returns with a tremble in its hitherto cocky stride as fallout from the Manchester City scandal continues to spread its toxicity among the elite. Enzo Maresca’s side face the music at Anfield on Sunday but before then there’s plenty of tasty clashes to keep blog host David Tindall on his toes. Manchester United and Tottenham badly need a win when they meet at Old Trafford, while Arsenal aim to bounce back at home to Leeds after a rare defeat. For updates and good vibes, join the conversation by sending your thoughts to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Australia began a daunting 12-month stretch with a three-Test series against South Africa at Kingsmead on ⁠Friday, before tours of India and England next year and the defence of their ODI World Cup title. Having not won a Test ⁠series in England since 2001, India since 2004 and South Africa since 2014, the ​Baggy Greens face one of their toughest ‌assignments in recent years. Join us for our live blog, with Geoff Lemon reporting on the second day in Durban.

George Russell needs to throw everything he can at stopping – or just delaying – Kimi Antonelli’s title charge. That won’t be easy from the back of the grid. He made a good start on Friday by setting the fastest time in practice and must hope to make an impact in the final sprint race of the season as well as qualifying. Russell and his rivals will have an unusual daylight race on the streets of the city state, before the typical night race on Sunday. Philip Cornwall steers the live blog, with Giles Richards reporting.

Greg Wood is under starter’s orders to live blog the second day of Newmarket’s big autumn meeting. Top of the bill is the Darley Dewhurst Stakes (3pm), with Godolphin’s Desert Castle pitted against Coolmore’s Darkness Falls. The Charlie Appleby-trained mount made his debut at Newmarket in August when the word was clearly out as he was an odds-on winner. Aidan O’Brien’s Darkness Falls represents a stiffer rival, but his best furlong was his last over a mile-and-one at Leopardstown and Desert Castle should have too much speed. Also the Ian Williams-trained Beylerbeyi is aiming to be the first back-to-back winner of the Cesarewitch Handicap (3.40pm) over two and a quarter miles. Spurs have had a lamentable start to the season; United not much better. Tottenham sit rock bottom of the table, with just two points. After keeping clean sheets against Nottingham Forest and Everton, Aston Villa ripped their defence apart last time out. Martin O’Neill’s side are desperately looking over their shoulders with Rangers closing the gap to two points at the top of the table. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your views.

Rob Smyth and James Wallace pick up the live blog baton for day three of the first Test.

Max Verstappen’s victory from pole, with fastest lap, at last weekend’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia came 16 races into F1’s new rules era ⁠and exceeded expectations for those who doubted ⁠the British-based team could match Mercedes and Ferrari by building one of the most complex power units in motorsport history from scratch. Sepang was also the first pole of 2026 achieved by a car not powered by a Mercedes engine. Mercedes have won 11 of the 16 races, Ferrari and McLaren two each. Audi and returning Honda are still far off the pace. There is hope then for the Red Bulls that the corner has been turned after months of frustration. Daniel Harris tracks the action, lap by lap, with Giles Richards reporting.

What kind of reception awaits Oliver Glasner on his return to Sellhurst Park – hostile or huggy? The Austrian flounced out of Crystal Palace at the end of last season, only to turn up at a club with a revolving door of managers in Nottingham Forest. After winning the FA Cup, the Community Shield and the Conference League while at the helm in south London, there was bemusement among Eagles fans when his next stop turned out to be the City Ground. After Steve Cooper’s exit in December 2023, Forest churned through four managers before Glasner’s arrival. The hosts have lost both of their Premier League games at Selhurst Park this season while the visitors have only lost one of their last seven away league games. Also on John Brewin’s blog radar is Hull against Everton, an enticing clash of eighth versus seventh, with the visitors unbeaten in their past five games.

Batten down the hatches: City’s first game back after an international window dominated by the guilty verdict in the club’s long-running case with the Premier League arrives. It just had to be at Anfield. City have long considered a trip to Liverpool the most fearsome away game of the season. It just got even tougher, with Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki and the rest likely entering a cauldron of fury and indignation. Liverpool might consider themselves the team who suffered most from the slew of City’s financial misdemeanours between 2009 and 2018. Under Jürgen Klopp, Liverpool won the Premier League in 2020 but also finished second to Pep Guardiola’s City by one point in both 2019 and 2022. So expect indignant Liverpool fans to be seething inside and outside of Anfield. Rob Smyth helms the blog with David Hytner, Andy Hunter and Will Unwin our reporting team.

The teams will meet for the first time in the 2026 season when unbeaten San Francisco (4-0) visit Seattle (3-1).

A promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reaps

The Guardian Fri, 09 Oct 2026 07:58:41 GMT

There was a real chance of a Green byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. He made bad decisions and cost his party dear

As ever, among all the noise triggered by Labour holding the seat of Holborn and St Pancras, the most plain-spoken and undeniable analysis was provided by that sage and national treasure John Curtice, of Strathclyde University. The result, he said, echoed national opinion polls and reflected two undeniable facts: that the Greens are in need of a period of contrition and reflection, and Labour ought to be slightly less than ecstatic.

Andy Burnham’s party, with a majority of 3,364, he said, showed they “are in a much better position than they were six months ago, but still not as popular as they were in 2025”. The Greens, meanwhile, remain “a more significant player than historically they have ever been”, but have lost much of the ground they gained during Zack Polanski’s first year as leader, when the serial failures of the local MP – one Keir Starmer – provided him and his party with such a glorious succession of political opportunities.

Do not forget: the Greens’ success earlier this year in Gorton and Denton played a massive part in Starmer eventually leaving the political stage, and the man he barred from being the Labour candidate snatching his job. But now? Publicly, Polanski seems largely unrepentant about the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at his party conference, and confident he can resume where he left off. But his party’s claim that it tripled its previous vote share in the seat is very specious indeed: as the pollster Peter Kellner puts it, “the leftwing vote two years ago was divided between the Greens’ 10.4% and an independent, Andrew Feinstein’s, 18.9%. Together, they won 29.3%.” The true increase in the leftwing anti-Labour vote, therefore, is only 3.5 percentage points, and Polanski has thus taken such a significant blow that his experience of the next few weeks and months could be very choppy indeed.

Over the last week, I spent two days in the constituency, filming another episode of the Guardian’s Anywhere But Westminster video series, and got a deep sense that our politics remains in a state of unpredictable flux. So many people and the conversations we had come to mind. The young people of colour in the pinched neighbourhood of Somers Town – the urban village right next to Euston station – who were all voting Green, and talked of Gaza and the impossibility of living in our capital. The woman in upmarket Primrose Hill who told us she no longer told people she was Jewish for fear of instant uproar and upbraiding about Israel, a country she had last visited 15 long years ago. But most of all, a 24-year-old trainee teacher called Tom, who reluctantly still lives with his parents, and has no idea how he is going to hold down a job in his home city. He had once been an enthusiastic Green member and activist, he told me, and had every intention of voting for them, until the Zionism motion suggested a party perfectly happy to inflame the UK’s sense of division and polarisation. He decided to switch to Labour.

The searing summer should have provided the Greens with another boost, and a real chance of another byelection win. But now? Polanski – who endorsed the idea that Zionism is a form of racism eight days before his party’s conference began – looks not just morally questionable, but distinctly weak: one central bit of symbolism in this whole affair, let us not forget, was his absence from the Zionism debate and vote at his party conference.

And so to a geographical jump to a few other parts of the country. As I may have written once or twice in the past, I live in Frome, in Somerset: a 25,000-population settlement whose affinity with the Greens has been deepening for the last decade or so. They provide four of the six councillors who represent the town on our new unitary council. The rurality and climate-fear in the villages that surround us chimes with Ellie Chowns’s seemingly out-of-the-blue election two years ago as the Green MP for North Herefordshire and Adrian Ramsay’s success in the East Anglian seat of Waveney Valley. But there are also elements of the maverick, future-facing attitudes that waft down into our neck of the woods from Bristol Central, the seat held since 2024 by Carla Denyer, the former Green party co-leader. I think I know what was holding those two elements together, and partly powering the Greens’ resurgence: a mixture of radical, empathetic social democracy and urgency about the fate of the planet that also seems to have taken root in some of England’s suburbs.

With the possible exception of Bristol, if you wanted to completely wreck the Greens’ successes in all those places, you would bin that approach and accelerate exactly what Polanski has facilitated: not just a politics of no-surrender and provocation, but the entry into the party of embittered former Jeremy Corbyn supporters and assorted ultra-leftists, bringing with them a flimsy, pious gesture politics.

The party’s former leader Caroline Lucas and the longstanding Green activist Rupert Read are about to publish a mini-manifesto titled Climate Popularism: a guide to “breaking the grip of rightwing populism through a new politics of crisis resilience”, to be formally launched on 15 October. Written before the antisemitism meltdown, it rather minces its words about Polanski’s project, but makes it pretty clear why things have now gone wrong. “Some observers have wondered whether this new eco-populism has at times been a little too quiet about the ‘eco’ part,” Lucas and Read write. “On the doorstep, at least, this may be an understandable strategy … [But] as recent heatwaves have made abundantly clear, the salience of climate impacts will make adaptation concerns a doorstep issue before long.”

Lucas and Read make the case for “centrally funded, locally appropriate action to adapt neighbourhoods, infrastructure and ways of life, to prepare for the broad, cascading impacts of human-triggered climate change”. They propose a domestic retrofit programme that would entail a lot of “secure green jobs”. They also write, very perceptively, about an “exhausted majority” tired of our shrill politics, and suggest the “depolarisation” of the climate issue in the face of plain facts – which sounds like the direct opposite of how Polanski operates. There is talk of a politics of “courage, hope, love of place” – and, crucially, a decisive turn into the use of citizens’ assemblies. This is the kind of turn the Greens should undoubtedly take – but even if they do, they will now be starting in a deeply troubled and weakened state.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Burnham, meanwhile, still has no end of work to do. For what it’s worth, many of us have long believed that the substantial presence in British politics of a radical party free of Labour’s pussyfooting around the climate crisis and the harsh realities of inequality was an absolute necessity, and the Greens’ fitful growth was nothing but a good thing. Now, by contrast, as the fallout from Polanski’s sudden crash only deepens, they have a massive amount of self-questioning and reinvention to do. Whether they will even have the inclination is another question entirely.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

The Iran-backed Houthi militia attacked one of Saudi Arabia’s busiest airports again on Saturday, injuring a number of people and disrupting flights, as the Yemeni group dramatically escalates its campaign against the kingdom.

The Saudi civil aviation agency said it was still tallying the injuries and assessing damage at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital. Repeated, deadly attacks in recent days on the airport and other civilian infrastructure have struck at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitions to turn the city into a global travel and business hub.

Saudi officials did not immediately respond to questions about details of the attack, but a reporter for The New York Times saw backed-up traffic and several ambulances heading toward the airport, where the police had blocked off roads.

The U. S. Embassy in Riyadh, along with other Western embassies, urged its citizens to avoid the area and warned of travel disruption. With just a day to go before a major global energy conference, many flights heading to the airport were diverted on Saturday afternoon, according to data from Flightradar24, a flight-tracking service.

The Houthis’ attacks this week on airports in Riyadh and Abha, in the south of the kingdom, have killed and injured several people and damaged facilities, according to the Saudi authorities. Across the border in Yemen, Saudi warplanes have also been waging a deadly bombing campaign against the Houthis.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior Houthi official, said the group was responsible for the latest attack on Saturday, which he said was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen, including on civilian infrastructure there. “Our military operations will continue as long as Saudi Arabia refuses to meet the requirements for a just peace,” he said by phone.

The escalating violence has plunged the kingdom deeper into the regional fallout of the U. S.-Israeli war on Iran, the Houthis’ main backer. Prince Mohammed now faces the difficult task of stopping the Houthi attacks while avoiding another prolonged war that could derail his economic plans.

Over the coming weeks, Riyadh was expected to host visitors from around the world for major global conferences, beginning on Sunday with the W. P. C. Energy Congress, an international gathering of energy officials and executives.

In an email to participants late on Friday, organizers of the event said it would proceed as planned and offered alternative travel options, including coordinated flights with Saudia, the national carrier. The airline’s flights were among those diverted on Saturday, according to flight-tracking data.

Later this month, Riyadh is also expected to host the Future Investment Initiative, an annual meeting that typically draws world leaders, billionaires and top global executives.

Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began to rise again in July, after the Houthis accused the kingdom of bombing the airport in Sanaa, the capital of Yemen. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government claimed responsibility for that bombing, saying it was acting to prevent an unauthorized Iranian plane from landing.

The tensions escalated further as the United States and Iran struggled for control of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for oil and gas shipping, and as the Houthis declared their own blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

The Houthis seized swaths of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline last month in a lightning offensive that gave the group greater control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another important choke point for global trade. Backed by Saudi warplanes, Yemen’s internationally recognized government has mounted a counteroffensive in recent days to retake the territory, drawing the kingdom further into Yemen’s long civil war.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Euan Ward is a Times reporter covering Lebanon and Syria. He is based in Beirut.

Why Ketamine Immobilizes Some Users

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Potent powders can produce a nearly catatonic state, particularly in those who have not tried the drug before.

By Andrew Jacobs

“The dose makes the poison,” as any toxicology student knows, describes the dangerously disparate effects that therapeutic compounds can have on health depending on the amount.

With many drugs — whether fentanyl, Tylenol or over-the-counter laxatives — the line between healing and harm is sometimes measured in milligrams. This principle is especially important when it comes to ketamine, the powerful anesthetic and party drug that has become increasingly popular as a mental health treatment.

Depending on the dose, ketamine in its powdered form can make a person feel pleasantly introspective, uncomfortably immobilized — or sedated enough to undergo surgery and not remember a thing.

The drug has been implicated in the case of a former Cornell University student who claimed in a lawsuit that she was raped by seven fraternity brothers during an hourslong attack. The student, identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe, said that she was already drunk when she arrived at the fraternity house and that the men pressured her to snort ketamine.

She told the police it was her first time trying the drug.

“Whenever the ketamine went down, I would say, is when things really start becoming a problem,” she later told university investigators.

The men have denied wrongdoing, and no criminal charges have been filed against any of them.

For many health care providers, the case has drawn unflattering attention to a pharmaceutical workhorse that is valued for its efficacy, safety and predictability — when administered in a medical setting.

“Ketamine is one of those really interesting unicorns with a huge range of experiences and effects depending on the dose, the route of administration, the genetics of the patient and prior exposure,” said Dr. Brigitte Gordon, the clinical director at Journey Clinical, a chain of ketamine clinics.

A short-acting anesthetic, ketamine can have hallucinogenic effects at certain doses, and it can make users feel detached from pain and their surroundings.

Although considered safe when given in clinical settings, with chronic use it can cause serious bladder damage, cognitive impairment and a strong psychological dependency.

Mixing ketamine with alcohol or other drugs is especially dangerous, experts say. Both alcohol and ketamine depress the central nervous system. Together they can dangerously slow breathing, and cause cardiac problems and impaired cognition and coordination.

It is not clear how much ketamine Jane Doe snorted over the course of the evening, but she told investigators she did so repeatedly, in part to numb the anguish she said she was experiencing.

“I had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out, so my thought was, if I do ketamine again, maybe I will pass out,” she told investigators. “My thought was that if I passed out and these men had sex with me, then they could be charged with rape.”

The recreational use of ketamine has exploded in recent years, fueled in part by its easy availability via prescription and the therapeutic veneer associated with its use as an antidepressant.

In clinical settings, the drug is typically delivered intravenously or through injection, with doses ranging from 30 to 150 milligrams depending on a patient’s weight and previous use.

When given intravenously, the drug is released slowly, over the course of 40 or 60 minutes, and the patient’s vital signs are monitored throughout the session.

A modest, so-called psycholytic dose can prompt a dreamlike state and a shift in self-awareness, but patients are still conscious and able to speak.

Recreational users prefer the powdered form, because “giving yourself injections at a party is not very sexy,” said Dr. Steven Radowitz, the chief medical officer at Nushama, a chain of ketamine clinics.

Compared with its liquid form, powdered ketamine is far more portable. It is also highly concentrated. The amounts consumed in recreational settings can vary wildly, in part because the drug is seldom measured out with precision.

Dr. Sandhya Prashad, president of the American Society of Ketamine Physicians, Psychotherapists and Practitioners, said that recreational users sometimes snort more than a 1,000 milligrams at once — 10 times more than the dose used to treat depression.

“For someone who has never used ketamine before, a fairly small dose could send them into a K-hole,” she said, referring to the state of disassociation that leaves users nearly catatonic — awake but disconnected.

A K-hole seldom lasts for more than 45 minutes, but it leaves users highly vulnerable to abuse.

Given its numbing effects, ketamine might not seem to be a drug of choice for sexual activity. But Dr. Dave Rabin, a psychiatrist in New York who specializes in ketamine-assisted therapy, compared the drug’s dissociative effects with those of alcohol, which is often used to ease anxiety over intimacy.

Even then, he said, the dose matters. “Too much ketamine and a person’s judgment is impaired and they don’t have the agency to assert themselves,” he said.

Still, Dr. Rabin and other practitioners expressed concern that negative attention about ketamine could overshadow its therapeutic benefits. He said ketamine was unique as a fast-acting antidepressant that can interrupt suicidal thoughts and behavior with a single dose.

“Ketamine has tremendous utility when used and dosed properly,” he added. “As caregivers, the last thing we want is for powerful therapeutic tools like ketamine to to be classified as drugs of abuse.”

Andrew Jacobs is a Times reporter focused on how healthcare policy, politics and corporate interests affect people’s lives.
