‘What’s the Plan?’ Inside the Crisis Response at the Chi Phi House at Cornell

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Records reveal how fraternity members responded when a fellow student accused them of sexual assault.

By Michael Wilson

The brothers of Chi Phi were texting one another in a panic.

On the afternoon of Nov. 8, 2024, Cornell University suspended the fraternity for suspected drug use. Three hours later, the school sent an email blast with the subject line, “Crime ALERT: Sexual Assault — Edgemoor Lane, City of Ithaca.”

It read: “The victim reported being sexually assaulted by several males and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs.”

The Chi Phi house was indeed on Edgemoor Lane, and there was a night the brothers were worried about. But a simple detail in the email gave them fleeting hope.

“Dates don’t add up,” one man wrote to the other three brothers in the chat. Was the suspension notice referring maybe to a different Chi Phi party? Was that Risky Business Night? The more likely date the email was describing, they feared, was Oct. 19, 2024: Hawaiian Night, when things had gotten out of hand with a sorority sister.

“What’s the plan of action?” Matthew Ingalls, a sophomore studying math and economics, wrote. He had been in touch with the woman from Hawaiian Night several times since the party, text messages showed, and he had offered to call her again.

“I don’t think she would have reported this,” Mr. Ingalls offered to the group text.

He was wrong.

The woman, now known as Jane Doe, would go on to file a lawsuit describing a night at the Chi Phi house that began with a threesome with two of the brothers on the text chain but which was followed by sex acts with several other Chi Phi brothers. Those encounters, which Jane Doe said took place while she was incapacitated by ketamine and liquor, were, she later came to believe, a crime.

This article is based on a cache of documents collected during the university’s sexual assault investigation and obtained by The New York Times. Across more than 1,000 pages, the records paint a lurid picture of life inside the Tudor mansion of the Xi chapter of Chi Phi — one at odds with the “house on the hill,” as the fraternity’s website described it, that “still stands today as a monument to the ideals of brotherhood for which this chapter was founded.”

Judging from the lawsuit and even the accused brothers’ own statements, those ideals had warped and devolved inside that house on Hawaiian Night. And the events of that evening and the days that followed all played out over texts that were later submitted to investigators — texts seeming to invite anyone in the fraternity to join the brothers having sex with Jane Doe, and later ones urging calm as rumors spread.

In the wake of Hawaiian Night, the Chi Phi brothers seemed to have reason to believe that things might just return to normal. Various brothers reached out to Jane Doe with texts that sought to confirm everything was good.

“I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night,” one brother, Jonathan Newell, texted Jane Doe the following Monday, Oct. 21, 2024. He apologized repeatedly for being “too fucked up” to have prevented other Chi Phi brothers from entering the bedroom.

“We’ve been shutting down any stories we’ve heard,” he wrote. “But again I’m so so sorry.”

Jane Doe had gone to the party to see another brother, Mr. Ingalls, at the end of a very bad day. Someone had stolen her wallet while she was at the gym that afternoon, and she’d started drinking on an empty stomach and was already feeling a little drunk by the time she arrived at the Chi Phi house, she told investigators.

Mr. Ingalls had personally invited her to the party to “rip the Kraken,” the nickname for the fraternity’s bong, but soon after she’d arrived, he’d suggested a three-way, and in her drunken state, she’d agreed.

Now, days later, Mr. Ingalls sounded reassuring.

“It’ll blow over in a couple days I imagine,” he texted her. “Until then we just have to sit tight. How’ve you been coping with the stress? You need anything?”

But on private Chi Phi chats, the young men were worried about how the stories spreading on campus would affect them. As early as Sunday, there were rumblings among sororities and fraternities alike about a “gang bang” at Chi Phi.

“The talk of the town,” one of the seven men accused in Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Gillio Lopes, told investigators later. He said he had consensual sex with her that night.

“Most of the upperclassmen in the house mentioned it to me at one point or another that day,” Mr. Lopes said. “People just finding the situation relatively amusing.”

Over the next week and a half, Jane Doe’s own thinking about that night changed. Her sisters at Delta Delta Delta were alarmed by how she described what had happened that night, and bruises had formed on her buttocks. She was treated at the campus clinic for a urinary tract infection that she told the medical staff was contracted “in a traumatic way.”

But in her exchanges with the Chi Phi brothers, she seemed to be trying to move on.

“At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt,” she wrote to Mr. Newell, even as she fumed about what she felt was happening to her reputation. “i know im socially a massive slut rn and like can’t bare to hear it cuz im really not.”

But by the end of October, she was coming to believe that she had been a victim of sexual assault who was too incapacitated by alcohol and ketamine to be able to give consent. “I was raped,” she would flatly tell investigators.

There was a Halloween party planned at Chi Phi, and she’d said she planned to go until she got the sense that she had been uninvited.

“Yall aren’t my friends,” she texted Mr. Ingalls on Oct. 30, 2024. “Yall are covering your asses.”

Six days later, she went to the emergency room for a rape kit and then reported her sexual assault to the university.

“What’s the name of your lawyer,” Mr. Ingalls texted another brother three days after the email alert.

“I meeting him tmw,” the other man replied.

In the weeks that followed, several Chi Phi brothers named in the lawsuit were summoned before campus police officers and investigators with the university’s Title IX office, which is supposed to ensure compliance with federal civil rights laws.

Their versions of events that night, which often don’t line up with one another, matter-of-factly describe a room filling with men who, in their telling, have consensual sex in one form or another with the same woman. At least one brother gave his statement while his father listened virtually.

All the men have denied any wrongdoing and said that any sex that occurred that night was consensual. None of them have been charged with a crime.

The dozens of Chi Phi brothers living in the Chi Phi house most likely knew that they were under threat of eviction.

The Edgemoor Lane mansion, originally built in the 1800s on land owned by the family of Ezra Cornell himself, had a wood-paneled gallery with a fireplace and a bar where the parties took place. There was a large balcony where a D. J. could set up.

The upper floors, however, were a maze of rooms and hallways designed to accommodate the men who lived there. To the uninitiated, trying to get around could quickly become a confusing journey among various unconnected staircases.

Mr. Newell, a sophomore, shared a large bedroom with two brothers. But it was also a sort of common room in the house.

“It’s regularly used by brothers during events,” Mr. Newell later told investigators. “They just go in there, hang out, do whatever. We never lock the doors.”

This was where Jane Doe’s first sexual encounter happened that night, a threesome with Mr. Newell and Mr. Ingalls, which, according to her statement, she mistakenly presumed meant that they were bisexual, as she is.

Downstairs, the party was winding down. There were Chi Phi parties in the past that ended with people leaving in ambulances. This was not one of those parties.

“It was kind of like a ‘meh’ night,” one attendee recalled later in an interview with investigators.

Others would say the same thing about Chi Phi as a whole, which has been described as a “mid-tier” fraternity in the Greek landscape at Cornell.

Some friends and stragglers stuck around the house. Upstairs, a woman was vomiting in the fire staircase. The bartender — a sophomore studying information science named Winston Lee, who was assigned to remain sober that night — helped her get an Uber home.

The men’s accounts of that night have gaps within their details.

Mr. Newell recalled Mr. Ingalls noticing a bag of ketamine in his room and vaguely wondering how it got there — it was the second time that had happened lately, he told investigators. He took some and soon, he was vomiting in a trash can beside Mr. Ingalls.

Ketamine is a powerful and fast-acting anesthetic, rendering a dissociating or numbing effect on users for up to an hour or so, and unpredictable when combined with alcohol.

Mr. Newell described its effect on him to investigators: “I never really passed out. But there were pieces of my memory that I just can’t remember.” Mr. Ingalls eventually did pass out, and when Mr. Newell finished vomiting in a trash can, he looked up and saw that a third man, Mr. Lopes, a sophomore, had entered the room and was kissing Jane Doe. Soon, Mr. Lopes and Jane Doe were having sex. Mr. Ingalls woke up. “He was really confused,” Mr. Newell told investigators.

As this was happening, the door opened again, and “a couple other guys kind of poked their head in,” Mr. Newell recalled to investigators.

It is possible that these men had seen a Snapchat text sent from Mr. Newell’s account to a group of more than 50 fraternity brothers with an apparent invitation: “free pussy in alum pu,” meaning “pull up” to the alumni room upstairs, where Jane Doe was.

Mr. Ingalls followed up: “Like you can walk in and whip it out.”

Mr. Newell told investigators he didn’t remember sending or seeing any such texts.

Before the night ended, Jane Doe was led through the hallways to yet another room on an upper floor, where she eventually fell asleep. She woke up sometime around 10 a. m. in bed with Mr. Ingalls, who, according to her interview, asked for oral sex. She said no, and he drove her back to the Tri Delta house.

In the days that followed, the Chi Phi brothers appeared to make a plan.

“Just deny,” Mr. Newell recalled in his interview with investigators. “That was really it.”

After the fraternity was suspended in November, the Chi Phi house seems to have slowly cleared out as the semester wound down. All the brothers were told to find other housing.

“You know even if everything gets sorted before add/drop im withdrawing next semester,” Mr. Ingalls texted another of the seven fraternity brothers in January 2025, a little more than a week before the spring term would start.

“Yeah I figure this semester is cooked either way,” Mr. Lopes replied.

“Campus is gonna hate my ass for a while,” Mr. Ingalls responded, before turning to another upsetting development — his own brothers letting him down.

“Talking about ‘brotherhood’ and then no one except a couple real ones check in, much less acknowledge our existence,” Mr. Ingalls wrote.

“Dead ass bro,” came the reply.

Any code of silence seems to have eroded when the men were asked to voluntarily hand over screenshots of text exchanges about Hawaiian Night.

Scott Norris was a junior at Cornell at the time, and he showed up at his interview with investigators with a negative drug test for ketamine. “I’m excited to get this resolved,” he told them.

He had left the party, he said, and he was hanging out in an upper room with Scott Kretzschmar, a junior studying human biology. Then they saw the Snapchat message from Mr. Newell. Mr. Norris said he thought it might be a joke, but that he needed to see for himself.

“I was genuinely concerned and wanted to investigate what’s going on,” he said.

Mr. Norris and Mr. Kretzschmar, who was still wearing what he called “a Hawaiian necklace” from the party, entered the room where Jane Doe and four men were gathered. Satisfied that everything appeared “normal,” he told investigators, and nothing improper was happening, he and Mr. Kretzschmar left.

An investigator then showed him a screenshot from that “free pussy” text thread, in which he responded “Free…” and later, when someone asked, “Shop still open?” he responded “Yeah.”

Mr. Norris told investigators that the screenshot helped jog his memory. “I do now remember we were kind of just bantering about it in the chat, which I would never have done had I known what had actually gone on,” he said.

In the end, the men were given a range of punishments. Mr. Ingalls and Mr. Newell were expelled. Mr. Lee and Mr. Lopes received suspensions and disciplinary probation. Diego Sarabia, whom Jane Doe accused of forcibly kissing her and who had already graduated by the time of his punishment, was issued a persona non grata order, barring him from campus. Mr. Norris and Mr. Kretzschmar, who said they only stayed five minutes in the room, but who Jane Doe said had snorted ketamine off her body, were ordered to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention; they were also required to write “reflection papers.”

A Title IX investigator visited the Chi Phi house in January 2025. It was now vacant, months after the fraternity’s suspension in November.

The photographs the investigator took as she toured the house that day were included in the cache of documents obtained by The Times.

She photographed cigarette butts ground into a rug. A discarded condom in a wastebasket. Empty bags of snacks, empty beer cans, empty bottles. A bong.

A shelf with Narcan boxes. Beside them, protein powder.

In her own interview, Jane Doe thought back to the last moments before she, in effect, became Jane Doe, standing outside the Chi Phi house, excited to see Mr. Ingalls. She’d found him attractive.

She’d texted him to say she’d arrived, because she didn’t want to wait outside a frat house in the cold night to be let inside.

That, she said, “looks sad.”

Sharon Otterman, Troy Closson, Emma Goldberg, Debra Kamin, Hurubie Meko, Jonathan Baran, Amy Julia Harris, Alan Blinder, Maia Coleman, Nicole Hong, Duy Nguyen and Zach Seward contributed reporting.

Michael Wilson, who covers New York City, has been a Times reporter for more than two decades.

Rebuking Ukraine Over Oil Strikes, Trump Says It Should ‘Get a New President’

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Hours after President Trump said the United States would buy Russian diesel, the Kremlin said there would be no immediate resumption of discussions to end the war.

By Marc Santora and Andrew E. Kramer

President Trump on Saturday accused Ukraine of causing a “world problem” with Russian refinery attacks and said it should “get a new president,” further undermining Kyiv a day after saying he would open U. S. markets to Russian diesel.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Saturday, he said the United States had told Ukraine, “you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused.”

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, he said, “wants to make problems for the world.” He added, “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

Over four years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Ukraine has pursued a strategy of mid- and long-range strikes that have battered Russian supply lines and oil infrastructure. The attacks have helped Ukraine stall Russian advances and even claw back some territory, but Mr. Trump on Saturday linked them to high fuel prices, which spiked this year after the United States and Israel attacked Iran.

“He wants to make problems for the world,” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Zelensky. “He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.”

Later on Saturday, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said that Mr. Zelensky “has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide.” He added, “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well.”

Mr. Trump’s announcement on Friday came despite a Russian ban on exporting fuel and was followed by the lifting of U. S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April. The Kremlin apparently offered no concessions in return.

Hours later, Russian officials said peace talks would not resume immediately.

“We will think about when these negotiations might be resumed,” Yuri Ushakov, President Vladimir V. Putin’s foreign policy adviser, said in a statement Friday night.

The diplomatic efforts fizzled shortly after Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami to meet with Mr. Trump’s top envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. As those talks were about to begin, Mr. Trump spoke at length with Mr. Putin over the phone.

While Mr. Trump’s announcement of the diesel deal made no mention of Ukraine, it was poised to hurt Ukrainian efforts to defend itself, as any major purchase of Russian fuel would help fund Moscow’s war machine.

Ukrainian officials said on Saturday that the talks in Miami had ended without a breakthrough.

In an online chat with reporters on Friday evening, Mr. Zelensky did not hide his sense of betrayal.

“I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen, and that is certainly not fair,” Mr. Zelensky said. He has worked hard to maintain a stable relationship with the White House as Mr. Trump has steered America closer to Russia and away from traditional democratic allies.

“It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Mr. Zelensky added, calling Mr. Trump’s diesel announcement a “weak decision.”

For Kyiv and its European allies, the short-lived talks in Miami laid bare how U. S. diplomacy has drifted from pursuing a durable peace settlement to hunting for business deals with Russia. The Trump administration has placed the burden of compromise almost entirely on Ukraine and put little pressure on Moscow to stop its campaign to destroy the Ukrainian state.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump similarly did not suggest that Mr. Putin should make compromises. The U. S. president said that Mr. Zelensky, though, “could have settled this war many times, many many times, and he chooses not to.”

On Saturday, Mr. Zelensky said Russia had directed five guided bombs at a residential area of Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, killing at least 20 people, including three children. “In Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities,” he said.

Daniel Fried, a longtime senior U. S. diplomat and former ambassador to Poland, said it was “very clear that the Russians are completely uninterested in any diplomatic approach and are simply standing back waiting for the West, the U. S., the Ukrainians to come to them with some bigger and better offer.”

“When you start chasing after them, they simply smirk and wait for you to purchase bigger and better bouquets to throw at their feet,” Mr. Fried said.

He said Mr. Trump was undermining not only Ukraine’s security but also Europe’s.

“All of this is taking place at a time when Russia is escalating its shadow warfare against Europe, and we are acting as if that is not occurring,” he said.

It is unclear whether Mr. Trump’s move to import Russian diesel will have much immediate impact on prices before the U. S. midterm elections.

In a statement after his call with Mr. Trump on Friday evening, Mr. Putin said that Russia had “confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the U. S. market and global markets at large,” but he did not specify any amounts.

Mr. Trump’s end run around Ukraine continued a pattern that had been playing out since he started his second term claiming he could end the war in 24 hours.

Last year, Kyiv agreed to Mr. Trump’s call for an immediate, unconditional cease-fire, but Moscow flatly rejected it. That first round of diplomacy established a dynamic that still defines negotiations: Ukraine received no reward for saying yes, and the Kremlin paid no price for saying no.

Since then, ambitions of forging a lasting peace have largely evaporated. Instead, only a handful of hastily announced tactical pauses and holiday truces have emerged.

Still, when the Trump administration opened the latest diplomatic track on the sidelines of the U. N. General Assembly in late September, Ukrainian officials were startled by how far Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff went in their offerings to Russia.

According to officials familiar with the discussions, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential diplomatic talks, the Americans put three lucrative economic incentives on the table to coax Moscow into a limited cease-fire, either on energy infrastructure or at sea.

Washington floated releasing billions of Russian sovereign assets immobilized in the West. The money, the officials said, was viewed as an upfront incentive for partial truces, not a reward for their enactment. This revived a proposal from last year to release funds to Russia. Then, the suggestion was to release up to $100 billion.

The Americans also revisited a plan to sell off parts of the Russian oil giant Lukoil in a multibillion-dollar deal that would go to a group of Middle Eastern investors, including some with business ties to U. S. negotiators.

And Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner revived a U. S. proposal that would allow Belarus, the Kremlin’s ally and neighbor, to export potash, according to officials familiar with the talks.

Kyiv has avoided rejecting any proposal outright but has demanded guardrails. For instance, it has suggested dollar-for-dollar mirror payments of frozen assets to Ukraine or guarantees of additional military aid upon any truce breach.

But Mr. Zelensky’s frustration with Washington was clear earlier this week when he visited the site of a Russian missile strike on an apartment building in northern Ukraine, hundreds of miles from the front lines. The strike killed 22 people, including five children — among more than 100 civilians killed in Russian strikes last week alone.

Asked about Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s comments that talks to end the fighting were “proving elusive” because the war had reached a “strategic stalemate,” Mr. Zelensky bristled.

“We are not at a diplomatic dead end,” he said. The problem, he added, was that there was not enough pressure on Moscow.

“Shut down their entire economy,” he said. “Sew Russia’s mouth shut. Don’t feed them with your own sales.”

Valerie Hopkins and Ivan Nechepurenko contributed reporting.

Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.

Andrew E. Kramer is the Kyiv bureau chief for The Times, who has been covering the war in Ukraine since 2014.

Christa Pike Discharged From Hospital After Surviving Execution Attempt

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Christa Pike’s Botched Execution

Advertisement

Supported by

Ms. Pike, 50 and convicted of the 1995 murder of a classmate, survived two doses of the drug pentobarbital late last month.

By Emily Cochrane

Reporting from Nashville.

Christa Pike has been discharged from a Nashville hospital, her lawyers said on Saturday, 10 days after she survived an attempt at lethal injection.

She is back at Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville, the primary prison for women in Tennessee, her lawyers said. As of Thursday, Ms. Pike had been walking with assistance, but still struggling with concentration and memory.

“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” her lawyers said in a statement. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”

Ms. Pike has spent three decades in the prison, largely in isolation, for the 1995 torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, 19, a classmate in Knoxville. On Sept. 30, she survived two doses of the drug pentobarbital, the second time this year Tennessee has failed to carry out an execution.

Ms. Pike is the first person to have survived receiving doses of a drug during a lethal injection execution.

Her survival has gripped the nation and become a flashpoint in the debate over the death penalty at a moment when support for the capital punishment is at its lowest in decades, according to a 2025 Gallup poll. Conservative leaders, however, have continued to champion the practice, including in Tennessee.

The Tennessee Department of Correction confirmed that Ms. Pike had returned to the prison, but declined to offer additional details about her condition or treatment.

Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican in the final months of his term-limited tenure, had put a moratorium on executions for the remainder of the year while an independent investigation into Ms. Pike’s botched execution continues. Frank Strada, the head of the state’s prison system, said he would step down this month.

The course of medical treatment for Ms. Pike in prison was not immediately clear.

Her lawyers have asked Mr. Lee to grant her clemency and allow her to spend the remainder of her life in prison.

May Martinez, the mother of her victim, had traveled from her Florida home to Nashville to witness the execution and has expressed frustration that the promised capital punishment was not carried out. Before the execution, Ms. Martinez told the Times she remained angry not only over the gruesome torture of her daughter — carried out by Ms. Pike and two others — but the toll of lengthy litigation over Ms. Pike’s execution.

U. S. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the front-runner to be elected governor in November, has said she believes Ms. Pike should face execution again. The office of the attorney general, Jonathan Skrmetti, has not said whether lawyers will ask the Tennessee Supreme Court to set another date.

Ms. Pike would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

A teenager when she was sentenced to death, Ms. Pike had spent decades largely isolated in the Nashville prison as the only woman on death row. During those years, only one other woman, Gaile Owens, was ever held on death row at the same time and the two did not have physical contact.

At the prison, Ms. Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, which her lawyers have since said contributed to the violence of her 1995 crime. In response to questions from The New York Times before her execution, Ms. Pike said “the biggest punishment was taking me away from people and human contact.”

A 2024 settlement allowed her to physically interact with other women in the prison. But in the days before her Sept. 30 execution, Ms. Pike was returned to isolation under Tennessee’s new execution protocol.

Her lawyers have fought to shield Ms. Pike’s privacy in the aftermath of the bungled execution. But one, Randy Spivey, has described her expressing an overwhelming confusion over what happened, as well as worry about her loved ones and Ms. Slemmer’s family.

Emily Cochrane is a national reporter for The Times covering the American South, based in Nashville.

She’s Been to Gaza. She Met With the Iranians. Now She Has a Warning.

The New York Times October 10, 2026

War in the Middle East

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Philip Montgomery for The New York Times

Supported by

By Lulu Garcia-Navarro

Are we already in the middle of a new world war without realizing it? That’s the provocative question I wanted to explore when I sat down with someone in the rare position to know: Mirjana Spoljaric, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

The I. C. R. C. is a secretive organization that is not well known outside war zones. Unlike the American Red Cross, which deals with blood drives and American disaster relief, the I. C. R. C. is the independent and neutral guardian of the Geneva Conventions, a series of international agreements created in the wake of World War II that laid out the rules of war. In her role, Spoljaric travels to all sides of active war zones — Gaza, Ukraine, Iran — meeting with the heads of governments and armed groups alike. She rarely gives interviews because of the politically fraught and confidential nature of her work, but she sat down with me just after the most recent U. N. General Assembly because she is deeply worried about not only the growing number of conflicts in the world but also how complex they have become.

She is also speaking out because she believes that her entreaties to global leaders when it comes to the rules of war are increasingly falling on deaf ears. (We spoke before Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the government would be live-streaming a public execution — another sign that the old rules and norms are eroding.) Many world leaders “simply don’t care anymore,” she told me. “And this lack of empathy, this lack of anger, is what I find most dangerous at the moment.”

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

I covered wars for a big part of my career as a journalist, and the world feels more dangerous and volatile than I can ever remember. How do you see things? I see it the same way, because the statistics prove it. We now count twice as many conflicts as 15 years ago. We are at 130 international and noninternational armed conflicts that we classify in our system. That’s the highest number since the Second World War. So I think it’s time we stop admiring the problem and start acting against this.

In my own newspaper, there was a recent headline asking if World War III had already begun, and I want to speak more deeply about why those fears about a global conflict are taking root. But first, you rarely give interviews. Why are you sitting down with me now? Because I want more people to understand that we live in a decade of war. And because we live in a decade of war, we have to understand the significance and importance of the rules of war and why they need to be respected. These treaties were created precisely for times like the ones we live in. People need to understand the importance of this.

Why do you think they don’t? We hear more and more leaders say that the rules of war don’t apply anymore, and that there can’t be rules because of the pursuit of total victory. But that is not possible. In history, there has never been total victory; there has only been death and destruction, over and above what was necessary.

Is there such a thing as a necessary war? As far as I’m concerned, no. But philosophers and politicians have argued for thousands of years that war is necessary. The point is that war has always been considered as something in the pursuit of a political objective. It’s a means to an end. Today you get the feeling that war becomes the means to an end itself, and wars continue because people want to stay in power. They have created an environment where war becomes the condition under which they can continue ruling, and that’s very dangerous. You ask me whether we are approaching a third world war. Honestly, history will judge that. History books will tell us whether today we were already in the beginning, or maybe already in the middle of such a situation. The I. C. R. C. didn’t know that we were in the Second World War when it was happening.

You are one of the few people in the world who regularly travels to both sides of armed conflicts. Can you tell me where you’ve been since you took over as the head of the I. C. R. C. in 2022? I’ve been to Gaza more than once during military operations. My organization facilitated the release and return of the hostages from Gaza and the Palestinian detainees back to Gaza. I was in Ukraine. I was in Myanmar. I was recently in Iran, in Iraq. I travel to the Middle East often, but I also travel to Africa. I was in Sudan, I was in Mali. I have to go see for myself what it looks like. I need to understand what civilians endure in conflict because I’m speaking to the holders of power. I wouldn’t be credible if I didn’t know what it means to be subject to this level of violence.

Your organization is one of the few that has been allowed inside and continues to work in Gaza. International journalists, most other international organizations haven’t been given access by the Israeli government. Can you describe what you have seen? I never go to any place of conflict without people telling me that they want to stop, without people telling me that they don’t understand why this is happening. I see children without parents. I see children without arms and legs. How senseless does the world feel to you when you’re confronting these things? When you then go to the power holders and they tell you that there’s nothing that they can do, you just don’t understand. I often don’t understand what I see in connection to what I hear.

Millions of Palestinians in Gaza are now forced to live on only around 30 percent of the territory. Over 80 percent of buildings in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged. In a 2025 interview with the BBC, you called Gaza worse than hell on earth, and you described people stripped of their human dignity. Have the rules of war been followed there? What I said about Gaza is still valid today. What happened to Gaza and in Gaza to Palestinians and Israelis supersedes every legal, moral and humane standard. There are so many people complicit in what happened there and continues to happen. The worst now is the fact that people are deprived of human dignity. The perception created that if there’s enough food, that’s good enough — for some people it’s good enough to just barely survive in rubble, and for other people it is only good enough if they can return to normalcy and bring their children back to a normal school. It’s applying two standards. And this will backfire. We cannot assume that for certain people certain things are sufficient when that doesn’t apply to everybody else. You can see that by how we measure humanitarian needs in Europe in comparison to South Sudan or Somalia. Intuitively and because we can’t prevent it, we continue applying two standards.

That some human lives are more valuable than others? Yeah. I always fear that if you allow double standards, it can happen to you. You never know when you’ll find yourself all of a sudden on the other side of the line. It happened in the Second World War to the Jewish people, but it’s happened to a lot more people than we nowadays keep in mind.

I want to stay with Gaza for one more moment before we broaden out. Did the I. C. R. C. have access to the Israeli hostages while they were in captivity? Because there were horrific stories of their conditions, and one of your main roles is to make sure that detainees and prisoners are treated well. [Shakes head no] Visiting hostages is much more complicated than bringing them back. And in my opinion, they should have come back unconditionally as of Day 1. But that’s not the reality in which we operate, and so we have to work with the tools that we have. You know, there’s nothing more complex, and to a certain extent also more brutal, than hostage taking. We know that also because our own colleagues find themselves more often than they should in such situations, and we know how important it is to negotiate them out as quickly as possible. So the objective always has to be to bring the hostages back. And the longer it takes, the more complicated it becomes. I personally think that pressure should have come earlier in the negotiations. We could have saved more lives. And this was the subject of our conversations. I traveled twice to Qatar to meet with the leadership of Hamas, to sit with Ismail Haniyeh at the time. I sat with Prime Minister Netanyahu myself. These were tough discussions, and trust me, we are very frank in these meetings. This is why these meetings have to always remain confidential.

Israel has also not allowed you access to detainees inside of Israel. How have they explained that to you, and how do you then respond? Prior to Oct. 7, the I. C. R. C. has had access for decades to detainees held by Israel, and we’ve organized tens of thousands, if not more, family visits, and that’s important. Access to prisons in situations of war is extremely challenging and complicated to achieve. And at a certain point in the conflict, parties decide that for security reasons they don’t want to give us access. That’s the most common argument. But it doesn’t matter what the reason is. According to the Geneva Conventions, which all these states have ratified, they have a legal obligation to give us access, and in my opinion also a moral obligation, because we need to inform the families about the whereabouts of or the fate of their relatives. You capture a soldier, this person is detained, but a soldier is not, per se, a criminal. And no matter how you classify these situations, torture is never allowed. Never. That is clear, and this is what we discuss with those who don’t give us access.

But there’s a different reason for me to be able to go, irrespective of my legal mandate. Detention is the place where you lose your identity. When there’s no possibility to notify the families and to receive information about them, detention becomes the place of utmost deprivation of yourself. And we’ve seen more often than not that people detained under horrible conditions over extended periods of time forget who they are. When I recently visited a detention facility in Iraq, the detainees told me their biggest challenge is information. What is always most important for everyone is to have information about what month it is, what day it is, where their families are, where their children are, whether the children are safe. You’re talking to human beings.

This is a bit of a basic question, but why does it matter how you treat your enemy? Of course it matters! Because you’re dehumanizing yourself if you torture. If you tell your soldiers, “Go and kill women and children, go rape them, looting is allowed, it’s our strategy,” these people dehumanize themselves. They will never be able to return to a normal life. I listen to so many interviews of former soldiers. All of them say that what haunts them is this child that was left in the street because they weren’t allowed to turn around and collect it. That they saw it bleeding to death. It remains with you. You debase yourself. This is why soldiers have all these problems when they return. I refuse to believe that the core human essence is bad. We are good people, we want to live with people we love, we want to have children that thrive, we want to be able to build a house and know that our grandchildren will be better off than us. This is a very normal human motivation. Our motivation is not to live in rubble. How could it be?

I want to learn a little bit more about you. You are Swiss Croatian, you studied philosophy and you worked primarily in international development and peacemaking for most of your career. Why did you want to take on a job about war? Do you have memories of the war in Croatia? My first memory of war was everybody telling me about the Second World War and how they endured it. My father was born in the middle, and when he was 5 years old he had to work in the field for 12 hours in the sun for a glass of milk. He said his whole childhood was marked by the memory of being hungry. And my mother was equally traumatized. She said that every time a child died of a disease in her neighborhood, she thought that the parents were lucky, and probably happy, because there was one less child to feed. Can you imagine thinking as a little girl that somebody’s happy about losing a child because you don’t have enough food for everyone? These are the stories that marked me probably more profoundly than anything else. And then came the Yugoslavia wars and my direct exposure to the impact of conflict. I cannot imagine how anybody could say we need this war. I’m not naïve. I’m surrounded by harsh interlocutors in a harsh environment. But I still think that if you keep the people in mind, if you at all times remember that it could happen to you, it could happen to your children, you will think twice before you start the war.

You are the first woman to be president of the I. C. R. C. Do you think gender matters in how you’re dealing with conflict? When I came into office, everybody was asking, “How is it being the first woman president of the I. C. R. C. after 160 years of male dominance?” And it’s not only at the top; it’s across the institution, because it’s an organization that was created in war, for wars. Then I went to northern Mali, and for the first time an I. C. R. C. president could sit with the women in a tent, because social norms prevented my predecessors from doing the same. I felt so shaken throughout the night when I realized what is happening to women in conflict and how brutal it is, because you have an overlap of many things affecting women and depriving them of even the minimum protection that any human being should have. And that night I realized it is different when it’s a woman. If there would never be a woman at the head of these organizations, we wouldn’t be as conscious of what it means for 50 percent of the world’s population.

You’ve seen many horrible things as part of your job. You deal, as you said, in a very harsh environment. How do you protect yourself from the relentlessness and awfulness? I mean, I’ve seen you get a little emotional thinking about it. In German, we say, “I was built close to water.” I’m very emotional. I try to be hard, but it doesn’t work. Maybe it’s good that I’m emotional, maybe it’s good that I get angry when I see bad things or unjust things, because it keeps me going, it keeps that feeling alive that you have to do something.

I was thinking about the I. C. R. C. and the difficulty of staying neutral in this era — this idea of having to speak to both sides and not taking sides. There have been many accusations that the I. C. R. C. hides behind its neutrality to mask inaction. The Holocaust is a moment where the I. C. R. C. failed catastrophically to prevent or to even acknowledge the extermination of the Jews. I know your background is in philosophy. What does it mean to be neutral in the face of extreme suffering? Is there an inherent tension in that? When I started my studies, I had my thoughts. I could get impatient with the stubborn insistence on neutrality and confidentiality. I very, very quickly changed my mind when I became president myself. Having accepted this unique opportunity, I had to learn quickly and acknowledge that we wouldn’t be able to do what we do without this strict insistence on neutrality, not in the context of prisoners of war in Russia and in Ukraine, and definitely we wouldn’t have been able to bring back the hostages from Gaza. You’ve seen the pictures of our colleagues unarmed among thousands, if not tens of thousands, of armed men, surrounded by rubble from which there was no escape. We had to negotiate the terms with everyone. Nobody would have trusted us to be able to do this highly complex operation if we hadn’t defended our neutrality over 160 years. You tweak it once, you become political, and that’s it. I know it makes so many people angry, but that’s the essence of our mission.

In that context, I want to ask you about Iran. You’ve spoken with the Iranians about the negotiations [with the United States]. I understand that you cannot divulge the nature of those discussions, but I am wondering how much you can say about how this conflict may or may not be resolved. I followed the nuclear talks between 2013 and 2015 under President Obama. It became clear to me at the time how complex these negotiations were. It’s much more complicated today in comparison. The first challenge is to establish trust. We have created a world where war is not a means of last resort. It happens at any moment in a process, which leads to a situation where parties always keep that possibility in mind and always keep a high readiness and preparedness to return to conflict. That in itself is not helpful, because these negotiations will take a long time and will require a lot of compromise. But on top of this, we have created a situation that is much more complex because of the overlapping of conflicts. Today’s conflicts are not limited to a given situation. They are turning into systems.

Explain what you mean exactly. You have countries aligning over continents. You have shifts in military cooperation. You have shifts in interests and economic goals.

So Iran’s relationship with Russia, Russia’s relationship with China, the conflict spreading to Saudi Arabia and Yemen with the Houthis —— And then you have the nonstate armed groups that are connected with other nonstate armed groups — ideological groups, or radicalized groups, however you want to name them, they share ideologies, they share common objectives, they align, they realign, they trade their arms, they ensure the availability of technology and cheap weapons across many countries and thousands of kilometers. So if the situation escalates in Yemen, you can be sure that it won’t remain contained to that territory for long. You already have two very important sea straits affected. So you have a lack of trust. You have asymmetric warfare that allows these conflicts to continue for an extended period of time. And on top of this, there’s a total absence of economic growth and a fast loss of development gains that have been essential for the welfare of the people in many countries of the world. Take Iraq: Over the last 10 years, the country has been recovering from very large conflicts that have had a heavy impact on society and the economy. These gains are being undone. Countries don’t have the fiscal space anymore to cope with the fallout created by continued warfare. The convergence of these trends is extremely dangerous. And now, what do we need? We need political will. We need negotiations. We need powerful politicians to have the power to negotiate.

In his recent speech at the U. N. General Assembly, President Trump threatened the annihilation of Iran by U. S. forces, speaking of this idea of trust and using war as a method of negotiation. He’s used language like that quite a bit, but it was notable to me because he made that statement at a body explicitly created to stop wars, which is the United Nations. What do you think that kind of language says about America’s understanding and commitment to these very complex, in-depth negotiations that you say are needed? You know, I started my career as a diplomat about 25 years ago in New York. And ever since, I’ve been observing eroding language. Certain things said back then would have triggered points of order. People would have left the room. There would have been outrage. I remember when Hugo Chavez spoke at the General Assembly and what reactions this triggered.

When he talked about President Bush and the smell of sulfur, implying that he was the devil. Exactly. This is a gradual erosion. But there are things being said that in certain situations could even lead to war crimes, because depending on who you are and what the situation looks like, it could entice people to do things that would actually amount to war crimes. This is why hate speech and this brutal language is so dangerous. But I’m not accusing a specific person today, because this erosion has been happening for far too long, and I’ve been alert for many years now. Every politician that uses any term that points at there being no rules and no red lines sends this signal to any person in the world that bears a weapon. You have to be conscious that as a holder of power, you have far bigger reach. Many more people hear: Oh, there are no red lines. I have weapons. I can use them.

One of the things that struck me about why we’re in such a period of global conflict is that it’s relatively easy to get into wars but increasingly hard to get out of them. So they drag on and accumulate. Are we losing our capacity to resolve conflicts? Definitely. If you don’t negotiate over 10 years, you lose the practice. It’s like being a heart surgeon. You don’t stop operating and then come back and they give you the instruments and you resume. I spoke once with a senior representative of the A. N. C. [African National Congress] in South Africa who told me: “Our adversaries never had to negotiate anything. They didn’t know how to do it, so we had to train them first before we could sit at the negotiation table.”

Undergirding this whole discussion and your call for leaders to pick up the phone is the breakdown of many democracies and the institutions that hold them together. The weakness that we’re seeing in upholding liberal democracy means that international organizations are also weak. Are you worried about the complete breakdown of the post-World War II order? Of course I am. Because that order made it possible for Europe to stay out of a third world war, to stay out of the levels of destruction that we have seen. Europe is also the leader of bad wars. I feel very bad saying that, but we have to acknowledge that European or Western history is not one of peace and security. But coming out of that rubble, there were a few people who had the foresight and courage to establish an international system that is in no way perfect but for a long time prevented the worst. I mean, everything that is written in the Geneva Conventions today is still as valid. If you had to rewrite them, you would come back with the same principles because they’re so intuitive and logical. In any society, religion, culture, nobody will tell you it’s correct to torture a child.

To come back to this idea that perhaps we might already be in this third global war without us knowing: What can we do? Let’s go back to that time when we believed in peace. Why is it so wrong to start a global movement around the notion of world peace? It’s possible. When I talk to my children, peace is not something completely away and absent for them. This is how they imagine their future. I think we have to listen to them. We have to start retreating from an overfocus on weapons, weapons systems, defense technologies. But we also have to recreate a positive narrative about humanity, about peace, about coming together and working together and living together. We have to come back to recognizing that humanity is what holds us together and is something we need to protect as a priority today, because we are debasing almost everything.

I covered wars for most of my early career and so I was deeply familiar with the important work of the ICRC. It’s rare for them to speak out because of the sensitivity of their work so I was surprised that the head of the organization was willing to do a lengthy sit down interview. When you read it you’ll understand why. Her warning is simple: we are careening into a global catastrophe she worries we may not be able to pull back from.

This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Cal Christie

Lulu Garcia-Navarro is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a series focused on interviewing the world’s most fascinating people.

Exasperation and Resignation in Greece Over Allegations Against Kimberly Guilfoyle

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The U. S. ambassador to Greece is facing accusations that she asked a donor to pay off her credit card bill before she took up her post in Athens.

By Niki KitsantonisLara Jakes and Lynsey Chutel

Niki Kitsantonis reported from Athens.

As the U. S. ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle has cultivated a highly visible profile, attending late-night parties and appearing on the cover of Vogue Greece. Lately, however, she has drawn a different kind of attention from Greeks.

Revelations this week that a Republican donor said Ms. Guilfoyle asked him to pay her American Express bill in exchange for access to senior Trump administration officials were the latest allegations of hardball tactics or outright misconduct to emerge against her.

Greeks interviewed in Athens in recent days expressed exasperation and cynicism about the steady drip of reports about Ms. Guilfoyle’s dealings, and some said they saw them as signs of what smaller countries are forced to endure from larger, wealthier nations.

“Greece is not a major power,” Petros Malliaros, 35, a freelance lighting technician, said. “We have to get along with the U. S. and whatever representatives it chooses to send us.”

The accusations against Ms. Guilfoyle are “hardly a shock,” said Anna Markaki, a 38-year-old school teacher. Of President Trump, she added, “He probably thinks she’s done a good job.”

Pavlos Iliopoulos, a 47-year-old pizza store owner, shrugged it off. “Greece is a small country and pretty much has to play along with the U. S.,” he said. “One corrupt diplomat staying or going isn’t going to make much of a difference.”

Anta Rapaki, 52, a former health care worker, criticized the administration’s decision to send Ms. Guilfoyle to Greece in the first place. “They’re underestimating my country as a faithful ally — instead of honoring that friendship, they sent her here as a favor,” she said.

She added, “Because we’re a small country, we have to have friends, and we need the U. S. But we’ll dance the dance up to the point that serves us; we won’t knuckle under.”

Ms. Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Mr. Trump’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., was one of the first ambassadors to be nominated in the president’s second term. She has said that her experience with Greece before being nominated as Mr. Trump’s envoy last November came from college history classes and a honeymoon trip. She has served in Athens with a mixture of MAGA glitz and what her supporters have described as relentlessness in securing business deals involving American interests.

She has come under fire in recent weeks in reports in The Wall Street Journal, which reported last month on potential conflicts of interest in Ms. Guilfoyle’s involvement in energy deals in Greece.

This week, the Journal revealed her communications with a Republican donor, Eric Deters, who said that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked him to wire $100,000 to pay off her credit card just before her confirmation hearing, which he did not pay. The New York Times confirmed their discussions.

A lawyer for Ms. Guilfoyle declined to comment. The U. S. Embassy in Athens directed requests for comment to the State Department in Washington, which did not respond.

In a visit to Athens, Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to answer questions on Thursday about the ambassador’s conduct. Ahead of his trip, he had described her as “an incredibly effective advocate for the President’s agenda in Greece,” adding that she had “successfully advanced U. S. energy interests in Greece and across southeastern Europe.”

Mr. Trump said he knew little about the allegations against Ms. Guilfoyle. “I don’t know too much,” he told journalists on Friday. “But she was always very nice.”

For some Greeks, more troubling was a comment she was reported to have made at a dinner in Athens in March insinuating that the United States could replace the Greek government. “The fact that they would send someone like that here, with no tact or diplomacy skills, shows how low we rank in Trump’s priorities, how insignificant Greece is for them,” Maria Stefanou, a 68-year-old retiree, said.

Ms. Guilfoyle’s lawyer has disputed the characterization of the dinner, and the foreign minister, George Gerapetritis, said on Friday that the Greek energy minister who was there denied it as well.

Asked about Ms. Guilfoyle’s purported comment, Pavlos Marinakis, a government spokesman, said, “There was never any question of the Greek government being threatened, nor would anything of the sort ever be tolerated.” He added that the Greece-U. S. partnership was founded on “mutual respect.”

In Parliament on Friday, Mr. Gerapetritis said it was not necessary to summon Ms. Guilfoyle to explain herself. “Summoning an ambassador and potentially creating a diplomatic incident would serve no purpose,” he said.

Their responses were part of a Greek government effort seeking to tamp down a national debate over Ms. Guilfoyle. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has aligned himself with the Trump administration, seeking cooperation on security and other issues.

“As long as Ms. Guilfoyle enjoys the support of the U. S. president and secretary of state, the Greek government has to respect the position of the U. S. government,” said Constantinos Filis, a prominent analyst and director of the Institute of Global Affairs at the American College of Greece, said. “It’s as simple as that.”

Leftist parties have called on the government to demand clarifications from Ms. Guilfoyle.

“Favors from Trump’s America come with a price tag,” Rena Dourou, a prominent lawmaker of the leftist Syriza party, said Friday. “The question is: How much will the Greek people ultimately have to pay?”

Ms. Guilfoyle is the latest of Trump administration ambassadors accused of engaging in decidedly undiplomatic behavior. Many serve in Europe, which long has been a destination for American political appointees of both parties who have little to no experience in official diplomacy.

Bill White, the U. S. ambassador to Belgium, was asked by that country’s foreign minister to stop making derogatory statements about government officials. Charles Kushner, the chief envoy to France (and father of Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law), ignored summonses by the French Foreign Ministry after criticizing Paris for doing too little to combat antisemitism.

Sharon LaFraniere contributed reporting.

Lara Jakes, a Times reporter based in Rome, reports on conflict and diplomacy, with a focus on weapons and the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years.

Lynsey Chutel is a Times reporter based in London who covers breaking news in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.

We Had Questions About A. I. Joseph Gordon-Levitt Had Answers.

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Video

By Joseph Gordon-Levitt

Video by Jared GellerEdward GallacherAmanda Su and Mehron Abdi

Joseph Gordon-Levitt has spent much of his life telling stories about what it means to be human. Now the actor and filmmaker is grappling with a technology that could change how we communicate, cooperate and think: artificial intelligence.

Mr. Gordon-Levitt believes storytelling is humanity’s defining technology. As the United Nations’ global advocate of human-centric digital governance, he wants to help people understand what’s at stake as A. I. grows more powerful — and why its future demands human judgment and global cooperation.

In the video above, Mr. Gordon-Levitt takes Times Opinion to the U. N. General Assembly. Along the way, he answers five questions about A. I., from the risks that worry him most to whether governments can keep up with Silicon Valley.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Joseph Gordon-Levitt: This is the seal of the United Nations. They offered me this role: Official U. N. Global Advocate for Human-Centric Digital Governance. Why did they offer a global advocacy role to an actor?

Clip from the film “500 Days of Summer”: Things have been a little difficult.

My name is Joe Gordon-Levitt. I’m an actor. I make movies. It’s now my job to convince a bunch of world leaders and officials gathering at the U. N. that the way this technology —

Archival clip of “The Daily Show”: A. I.

Archival news clip: A. I.

Archival clip of Elon Musk: Or S. I., pardon me.

— is about to unfold over the next few years will be deeply, deeply impactful on all of our lives.

And The New York Times asked me to bring along a camera. Morning, fellas.

Man off-camera: How are you?

Gordon-Levitt: All right. They’ll be asking me some questions along the way. I’ll do my best to say something worth saying.

All right. I just got the first question from The New York Times: Why should the public listen to an actor on A. I. safety? Very fair question.

Why listen to an actor? Don’t listen to an actor. You should read “Human Compatible,” by Stuart Russell. Go look up Yoshua Bengio. Read posts by people who work in alignment and safety and policy. You don’t want to read all those things? Well, I did! So, you know, if you want to listen to me, that’s a shortcut.

What we don’t want is a bunch of people confused or apathetic while these very fast-moving businesses design the future by themselves, just in the interests of their own profits. A lot of what needs to happen, I think, has to do with communication, which is ultimately kind of what acting or filmmaking is.

Event host: Please help us welcome the United Nations Global Advocate for Human-Centric Digital Governance, Joseph Gordon-Levitt.

Gordon-Levitt U. N. speech: We can choose to govern this new, revolutionary technology for the benefit of people — and held accountable by people. We can set up systems to compensate people for their intellectual property and their personal data — I heard another round of applause, I’ll take it. Come on, that’s how this works. Let’s get the energy going.

I hear that The New York Times is sending me another question: What does human-centric digital governance even mean? Even mean? What does that even mean?

Human-centric digital governance — it’s sort of a mouthful. It just means that digital technology should be governed by people and for people. “A. I.” is nothing but algorithmically recombined, human-produced data. It’s humans. Calling it artificial intelligence sort of decenters humans. It offers this kind of magical fictitious character, this A. I. that we’ve seen in various sci-fi movies, but really — really all it is is us. It’s us.

This has nothing to do with A. I. or the U. N. This is just that I like walking in New York at night. When I was a kid, you couldn’t smoke blunts on the street. [Laughs.]

Archival news clip: OpenAI revealed on Friday that its systems went rogue and accessed U. S. government websites.

Archival news clip: An A. I. researcher warning the technology could “kill us all” within the next 10 years.

Archival news clip: Young workers increasingly are wary of the threat A. I. poses for their job prospects.

What’s your biggest A. I. fear right now?

At the risk of annoying The New York Times, I would object to that question just because reducing these concerns into one sound bite of fear — that’s one of the problems. To me, saying: Oh, I’m scared that A. I. could exterminate all of humanity — that doesn’t really get at the substance of the concern. There’s real validity to that concern. But that’s not the thing that really worries me.

The thing that worries me is a lot more complicated and a lot more boring to talk about, because it’s a lot more dense. The decline of democracy, the decline of human empathy. These companies are betting on the notion that they’re going to take over the entire economy. That would be totalitarianism, and that would be really bad.

Simultaneously, these models are being trained to hijack your intimacy, to make friends with you, to get you to fall in love with it. We shouldn’t be scared of an A. I. We should be concerned about the people building A. I.

Archival news clip: And the United Nations chief is urging artificial intelligence global competitors to work together.

Just got through security. Security’s quite a bit more hectic today. Today is the day that, I guess, the president will be addressing the General Assembly.

Clip of Donald Trump U. N. address: I’m not going to stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution. Whoever wins A. I. — you have to remember this — wins.

OK. Another question from The New York Times: How does a slow-moving U. N. force a fast-moving Silicon Valley to play by its rules?

To be honest, this is one of the things that I have found sort of daunting or troubling. I don’t know the answer. I think if it does take, say, seven years for the U. N. to put together an internationally agreed upon regulatory framework for A. I., then seven years from now we’ll be glad that we started now.

Yoshua Bengio in an interview with Gordon-Levitt: We need to move away from this model that all the companies are following, the same recipe that’s training A. I. s like we train animals: To seek rewards. Because that leads to these entities trying to cheat in order to obtain those rewards.

Gordon-Levitt: They have to do that, because they’re profit-driven companies.

Bengio: Yes.

Gordon-Levitt: How can an A. I. be built without the profit incentive?

Bengio: I think we should move into a world where that power is shared. Not in the hands of a few companies, or even just a few countries — because it’s too much power. Power-sharing changes the incentive structure that drives us currently into this crazy race — competition between companies, competition between countries. Once we say: OK, we share the power. And how do we do it? I mean, we need institutions for that, we need to move toward that — but if we don’t do it, someone is going to abuse that power and we’re all going to be suffering.

All right, it’s time to go. I just finished my last talk. But of course, there is one more question coming in. We’ve got the three dots right now — you want to show it? We’re waiting.

OK, here’s the question: Governments and technology companies clearly have work to do. But what about the rest of us?

Well, the midterms are coming up. We Americans have an extra responsibility because the frontier of this technology is being developed in our country. So a lot of the world — and I’m hearing from them here at the U. N. — a lot of the world is looking to see what we, as Americans, are going to do. What’s the signal that we are going to send our government in these next elections? And I hope we send a very clear one.

There are large groups of very bright people working day and night to develop these AI models so they can try to stay ahead of the other companies doing the same work. It's a sprint, not a marathon. The rewards for winning are a cash prize, prestige, a sense of accomplishment, and, perhaps, world domination. Meanwhile, those realizing these technologies need to be controlled are just now lacing up their running shoes.

Economic Pain and an Unpopular Trump Put G. O. P. on its Heels With Three Weeks to Go

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Inflation has hurt Americans at many levels: Farmers, truckers, consumers. It has also expanded the electoral map into what was safely Republican country just a few months ago.

By Patricia Mazzei and Shane Goldmacher

Patricia Mazzei and Shane Goldmacher cover national politics. She reported from Miami. He reported from Pennsylvania and New York.

Three weeks from Election Day, deep frustration over an economy that feels unworkable for Americans at most every level, from farmers to truckers to consumers, has expanded the map of competitive electoral contests into areas that seemed safely Republican just a couple of months ago.

Sustained high prices are putting at risk some of the constituencies, states and congressional districts that President Trump and Republicans won decisively in 2024. The widespread discontent has prompted candidates, parties and major G. O. P. fund-raising groups to shift their messages and ad spending in crucial races to try to move voters in the final days of the midterm campaign.

With control of the House, Senate and the vast majority of the country’s governor’s offices and legislatures at stake, Republicans are examining their own deteriorating internal polling, along with their experiences with voters, and say they are reassessing their odds and triaging the map.

On Friday, for example, the leading Senate Republican super PAC began to plunge another $30 million into advertising in Texas to try to save the state’s Senate seat for Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general.

Several races that are likely to determine the overall outcome on Election Day — the Maine and Michigan Senate elections, for example — remain tight. Control of the chamber could easily boil down to one or two of these razor-thin contests.

Still, Republican baggage is piling up, regionally and nationally. Mr. Trump is facing backlash to mass deportations in South Texas and South Florida. His party is bracing for anger at expanding data centers in states including Ohio and Michigan. In big farming states, record diesel prices have arrived just in time for harvest season. In colder northern states, spiking heating oil costs loom for families.

“When you’ve got a sitting president whose job approval rating is in the high 30s,” said Colin Reed, a veteran Republican strategist, “it makes it really difficult for any Republican candidate to compete and win.”

The White House is racing for stopgap solutions. Mr. Trump announced $90 payouts for millions of seniors on Medicare, and on Friday began sending $500 rebate checks he had promised for some Affordable Care Act customers. He has also promised a $5,000 check for every adult U. S. citizen if his party retains control of Congress. This week, in Nebraska — a typically solidly Republican state — Mr. Trump announced an executive order to loosen restrictions on the use of tax-free diesel on the roads.

On Friday, Mr. Trump said he would allow Russian diesel imports after years of sanctions, in an attempt to lower prices.

Mr. Trump’s unpopularity over his handling of the economy — one of his biggest strengths when he ran two years ago — is driving Republican troubles in a nationalized political environment.

The party still holds structural advantages over Democrats, including a Senate map with more contests in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024; redrawn congressional maps that made more seats favorable to the G. O. P.; and a wide financial lead, bolstered in part by Mr. Trump’s own powerful super PAC, MAGA Inc. In past elections, particularly when Mr. Trump has been on the ballot, some polls have underestimated his popularity.

Those advantages have provided little comfort to Republicans who see their candidates faltering in increasingly red corners of the nation.

The leading House Republican super PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund, all but ceded the first Republican-held seat of the election this week, moving money out of a district in Nebraska where Representative Don Bacon is retiring. Mr. Bacon occupies the most Democratic-leaning seat of any Republican in the House.

In an interview, Mr. Bacon said he had urged party officials not to abandon the seat just yet.

“I wish they could have shown a little more patience,” he said. “The No. 1 issue is the president is not popular in the district.”

Republicans also recently pulled money from the Senate race in North Carolina, where Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican, is retiring. They redirected cash to Kansas and South Carolina, which remain a stretch for Democrats but would have seemed out of reach earlier this year. The top super PAC backing Senate Democrats, Senate Majority PAC, is reserving $5 million in ad time in Kansas.

“There are states right now in play that I would not have imagined being in play,” former President Barack Obama said at a fund-raiser for Democratic Senate nominees in Virginia on Wednesday, rattling off states such as Texas, Kansas and Nebraska.

“We could end up losing all of them by two points,” he added, according to excerpts released by his office, warning against Democratic complacency. “But we have a chance.”

Republicans, privately and publicly, are concerned about an enthusiasm gap. Culture war issues, such as transgender athletes’ rights, are still in heavy rotation in Republican ads. But polls show voters are focused squarely on their deep unhappiness with the direction of an economy that Mr. Trump had promised to fix.

“Angry people vote and satisfied people don’t,” Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, warned a crowd at a diner this week in Nazareth, Pa. He said Republicans had successfully closed the border from unauthorized immigrants, but the achievement had pushed the issue out of mind.

Mr. Johnson, typically an optimist, later in the week mused aloud to Fox News about what he might do if his party were to lose the majority this fall. “If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor,” he said.

Mr. Trump has traveled in red states, including three times to Texas over the past month, with another visit by Vice President JD Vance planned for next week. They hope to get Trump supporters who typically vote only in presidential elections to also vote in the midterms. The president has repeatedly urged them to act as though his name were on the ballot.

The challenge with that plan, said Paul Shumaker, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, is that many of those voters vote on the economy.

“The lower-income, blue-collar voters that Donald Trump brought to his winning coalition for Republicans is the demographic group of voters who are being impacted most by the higher energy costs,” Mr. Shumaker said.

Recent New York Times/Siena University polls of red states show Democrats also doing well with younger voters, older voters, independent voters and Latino voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024.

Still, Republicans could flip the Kansas governorship, which Democrats have held for eight years. And Democrats face unexpectedly competitive statewide races in Minnesota, which has not elected a Republican in a statewide election since 2006, when Gov. Tim Pawlenty won re-election.

Mr. Pawlenty said the state has offset some of the tough national political environment for Republicans in part because voters there blame a spate of fraud scandals on Democrats.

“Democrats are trying to make the election a referendum on President Trump while the Republicans are trying to make it a referendum on fraud,” Mr. Pawlenty said in an email.

Democrats in states like North Carolina vividly remember past elections where they expected to win or win comfortably only to lose or win by razor-thin margins. Republicans remember them, too. Austin Barbour, a Republican strategist based in Mississippi, invoked a quote made famous by his uncle, Haley Barbour, a former Republican National Committee chairman, to describe the political climate: “It’s never as bad as it seems or as good as it seems.”

The younger Mr. Barbour said he believed Republicans would ultimately prevail in states that are historically Republican, in part because of “the level of far-left candidates that the Democrats are nominating.”

But cries about looming socialism are proving a tough sell when voters are unhappy now.

Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democratic state senator and Lutheran minister who is trying to flip an Iowa congressional seat, said a farmer told her it would cost $16,000 more this year to harvest his crop because of higher diesel costs. That was after dealing with tariffs in the farm market and higher costs for fertilizer, which made spring planting more expensive.

“I was at the Labor Day parade, and I had a union member say to me, ‘My parents told me if you vote for Republicans, your life will get better,’” she recounted. “And he said, ‘It isn’t getting better: We’ve got dirty water; we’ve got cancer; we’ve got higher costs. I’m voting all Democrat this year.’”

Ms. Trone Garriott said the evidence that Iowa Democrats are doing well is not merely anecdotal: Representative Zach Nunn, the two-term Republican she is trying to unseat, voted in Congress last month to end the Iran war or seek congressional authorization to continue it — after having campaigned with Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, just a month earlier.

On Friday, the Cook Political Report moved Mr. Nunn’s seat to “lean Democratic.”

Jim Runestad, a state senator and the chairman of the Michigan Republican Party, said it was smart for former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee, and other Republican candidates to distance themselves from the president. Mr. Rogers has supported a one-year moratorium on data center developments in Michigan and called for an end to the Iran war and to what he has called the “tariff war.”

“You shouldn’t walk in lock step,” Mr. Runestad said. “In an off-year election when the president of your party is in office,” he added, “there is always a headwind.”

The next three weeks will determine whether seeking that distance this late in the campaign season will be enough.

State Representative Carrie Rheingans, a progressive Michigan Democrat, has been campaigning across the state for Democrats including Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s Senate nominee. In past election years, she said, Trump voters “wanted somebody to come in and make things different because it wasn’t working.” Now, they have been let down again, she said.

That dejection created an opening for the left. “The voters are just tired of big corporations,” she said. “They’re either price-gouging us, or they’re monopolies.”

Vince Bjorling, a retired doctor from Scottsbluff, Neb., said he planned to vote for the Democratic nominee for governor and independent candidates for House and Senate.

Mr. Bjorling, a former Republican who said he left the party early in the Trump era, said he had volunteered for a independent House campaign and had encountered “a lot of people out there who are very, very angry with the policies that the president has put forward, and also our representatives basically falling in line.”

“The tariffs were a big problem, because that created affordability problems,” he said. “The war in Iran was miscalculated and misguided, and now has led to even more affordability issues.”

Republicans “can’t run on the issues,” he said, “and they can’t run on their record.”

Mitch Smith contributed reporting.

Patricia Mazzei is a national political correspondent for The Times, based in Miami.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.
