How Is Child Marriage Still Legal in the U. S.?

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Nicholas Kristof

By Nicholas Kristof

Opinion Columnist

Every three seconds, on average, a girl under the age of 18 is married somewhere in the world. In India. In Ethiopia. And, to our shame, in Illinois, Maryland, Colorado — and most of America.

Thirty-two states still allow child marriages in some circumstances, such as with the permission of a parent or a judge. Two states, New Mexico and Mississippi, have no minimum age at all.

Some of the defenders of child marriages in America are religious groups on the far right, but as a liberal myself, I find it deeply dispiriting that in a number of states they are joined by left-leaning organizations such as the local affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union and Planned Parenthood — even, in Illinois, the National Organization for Women.

That’s right: Some progressives and feminists fight to defend child marriage, usually on the basis of “child rights.” I shake my head in disbelief: If you actually talk to girls and women who have been married young, what you often hear is the opposite of empowerment. Instead, it’s oppression and rape and the loss of education and childhood.

For progressive organizations to ally themselves with right-wing extremists to defend what sometimes amounts to state-sanctioned statutory rape — this is liberal self-caricature.

Thankfully, child marriage has just been banned in California, after a nine-year battle that should never have taken so long. Ten days ago Gov. Gavin Newsom of California signed a bill banning all child marriage in the state, in the presence of Courtney Stodden, a model and singer who was married at 16 to a 50-year-old actor who she says was abusive; he has denied that.

Previously, there was no minimum age for marriage in California, so long as a parent and judge consented. Progressive groups, including the state affiliates of the A. C. L. U. and Planned Parenthood, had worked to block passage of a ban, but opposition melted when the issue drew more attention.

As a longtime foreign correspondent for The Times, I often saw girls in Africa or South Asia married to older men; like most people, I saw this as a human rights issue. But in 2017 I realized, to my astonishment, that the same was happening in the United States — and at that time every single state allowed children to be married.

That year I interviewed a Florida woman, Sherry Johnson, who was married at 11 to a 20-year-old man, a member of her church, who had raped her. Johnson had become pregnant, child welfare authorities were investigating, and her parents and church wanted to avoid a messy criminal case.

“I guess you’re just going to get married,” she recalled her mother telling her.

I’ve been writing about the issue since, and there has been progress. Delaware and New Jersey were the first states to ban all child marriages, in 2018, and a succession of others followed, mostly blue states. California is the 18th state to ban all child marriages.

Child marriage isn’t routine in the United States, but neither is it rare. Unchained at Last, a nonprofit that fights child marriage, pored over marriage records and calculated that some 315,000 children were legally married in the United States between 2000 and 2021. A great majority were 16 or 17, but some were as young as 10. Most were girls married to adult men.

At least 66,000 of those marriages involved ages or age differences that would have constituted a sex crime in that state.

“It’s a workaround for statutory rape,” said Fraidy Reiss, the executive director of Unchained at Last.

Red states have lagged in banning child marriage, and in those states it has often been religious conservatives who defend such marriages, either because they’re giddily pro-marriage or because they fear that a pregnant girl will get an abortion if she must wait to marry the baby’s father.

“Marriage is not the problem; the abusers are the problem,” Norman Woods, the director of a conservative Christian nonprofit called Family Voice Action, told South Dakota legislators last year.

Conservatives and progressives who defend child marriage emphasize that they’re against forced marriages of any kind but think that 16- or 17-year-olds should sometimes be allowed to marry when there’s no coercion. Those on the left talk about respecting the rights of children and also worry that if underage girls are barred from marrying, they could also be blocked from getting abortions.

“Young people have the right to agency over their own lives,” a group of progressive organizations wrote this year in opposing a ban on child marriage in Colorado. “Marriage is an important right that young people may willingly decide is the best option for them in building their lives.” This is earnest and well intended, but to me it sounds as if it comes from people who haven’t spoken to children who have actually endured these early marriages.

The progressive groups that in Illinois have successfully opposed a ban on child marriage include the A. C. L. U. of Illinois, the Illinois branch of the National Organization for Women and Planned Parenthood Illinois Action. In some other states and at the national level, those organizations have been either neutral or helpful in banning child marriage.

Planned Parenthood Illinois Action should listen to the International Planned Parenthood Federation’s warning that child marriage “is one of the most persistent forms of sanctioned sexual abuse of girls and young women.”

Likewise, as the Illinois chapter of NOW defends child marriages, it is at odds with the national organization. NOW as a whole is part of a coalition trying to end all child marriage, and its website calls on states to ban child marriage on the basis that it is “extremely detrimental to the health and well-being of girls.”

A married underage girl (and it’s almost always a girl rather than a boy) is vulnerable because if things go wrong, she often won’t be accepted at shelters or be able to hire a lawyer. She can be married young but may not be able to escape the marriage until she turns 18.

“It’s some surreal alternate universe where the groups that I would think would be our biggest allies standing up for girls have somehow instead taken this outrageous position in fierce support of a human rights abuse and archaic harmful practice that destroys girls’ lives,” said Reiss, of Unchained at Last. “I don’t know how to wrap my brain around this.”

These are the states that still allow child marriages in some circumstances: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

The United States has called on other countries to end child marriage. Yes! We should continue to do so. But we don’t have the moral authority to tell other countries to ban child marriages as long as we retain this abusive practice at home — defended by impractical zealots at both ends of the American political spectrum.

My views on child marriage are greatly shaped by the people I've interviewed over the years who endured rape and abuse after being married off — overwhelmingly they were girls handed off to adult men. I mentioned one, Sherry Johnson, married at 11 in Florida to her rapist, and there are many others. Child marriage often marks the end of the girl's education, and if the relationship goes sour she usually won't be accepted by a shelter until she's 18. One I spoke to ended up homeless and surviving as a nude dancer. So I have little patience when a coterie of fellow liberals proclaims that child marriage is about "child rights" — no, as I see it, too often it's state-sanctioned child abuse. Grrr. Your thoughts?

Fact-Checking Senate Ads in Iowa, New Hampshire and North Carolina

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

We assess three campaign ads in the battleground states that have focused on the cost of living.

By Linda Qiu

With less than a month to go until the November midterms, both parties have blanketed the airwaves with campaign ads in battleground states as they seek control over Congress.

In Iowa, New Hampshire and North Carolina — three of the most competitive Senate races in the country — candidates and groups supporting them have all spent millions on ads faulting their opposition with failing to curb the cost of living, a top issue for voters, among other attacks.

Here’s a fact check of some of those claims.

What Was Said

“Here are the facts. It’s Ashley Hinson who’s missed nearly 200 votes in Congress. Votes to crack down on child pornography, reduce crime and lower health care costs.”— Senate Majority PAC, a top Democratic super PAC, in an ad that began airing in September

This is misleading. Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate in Iowa, and various groups supporting her candidacy have spent millions of dollars on ads attacking Josh Turek, a state representative and the Democratic nominee, for missing 58 percent of votes in the Iowa legislature this year (the claim is accurate).

In response, Mr. Turek and groups that support him have retorted that Ms. Hinson, too, has a record of absenteeism in the House — including missing votes to lower health care costs — by making an apples-to-oranges comparison.

The Senate Majority PAC cited Ms. Hinson missing 33 roll-call votes — or recorded votes on the House floor — as well as 163 votes in various committees she sits on since January 2021, when she first entered office.

But typically, a missed vote refers to a roll-call vote on the House floor, and Ms. Hinson actually has a better attendance record than most members of Congress. According to GovTrack, a nonprofit website that tracks congressional activities, Ms. Hinson has missed 33 of 2,915 roll-call votes from January 2021 to September 2026. That’s about 1.1 percent, less than the median of 2.1 percent among current members in the House. This year, she has missed five out of 314 votes, about 1.6 percent.

“A missed vote is a missed vote, and Ashley Hinson missed nearly 200 of them during her time in Congress,” Lauren French, a spokeswoman for the Democratic group, said in a statement.

The tally in the ad included missed committee votes. Ms. Hinson missed a roll-call vote in the House Appropriations Committee on a specific proposal to increase funding for community-based violence prevention programs (the motion failed 28 to 34).

Senate Majority PAC said Ms. Hinson missed a voice vote on an amendment to increase funding for programs that combat the exploitation of children and another voice vote on extending medical education programs in rural areas. But it is not clear whether Ms. Hinson was present for those particular votes as, by definition, voice votes do not take attendance. Both amendments passed without any opposition.

Billy Fuerst, a spokesman for the Hinson campaign, argued that by the ad’s logic, there is no record of any member of Congress supporting those amendments since names and position were not logged. Morevoer, he said, Ms. Hinson voted to advance the funding bills that included the two provisions to the full House.

What Was Said

“Pappas voted to line the pockets of health insurers with billions of tax dollars. Pappas even voted against vital funding for rural and vulnerable hospitals. Bigger profits for big insurance, higher costs for you.”— No Going Back PAC, a Republican super PAC, in an ad that began airing in September

This is misleading. This ad attacking Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic nominee for Senate in New Hampshire, describes his opposition to the Republicans’ signature tax cut and domestic spending package as a vote against funding for rural hospitals.

That characterization omits the bulk of what the legislation actually does (extend tax cuts and cut social safety net programs). And it ignores that a provision creating a fund for rural hospitals was largely included to address deep funding cuts to Medicaid that threatened rural hospitals.

The domestic spending legislation created a $50 billion fund for rural hospitals but also cut Medicaid spending in rural areas by $137 billion over a decade, according to an analysis by KFF, a health policy nonprofit. So while Mr. Pappas technically voted against the $50 billion fund, he also voted against the $137 billion cut to rural Medicaid spending.

The ad also cites Mr. Pappas’s support for legislation to extend extra subsidies for Obamacare as votes to “line the pockets of health insurers,” echoing a longstanding criticism.

Extra subsidies created in 2021 during the pandemic made health insurance less expensive for most people enrolled in plans under the Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare. But despite Democratic efforts to extend them and Mr. Pappas’s support, those subsidies expired this year. As a result, millions of Americans have dropped Obamacare coverage, and premiums have increased for many more. Conservative critics have argued that the extra subsidies enriched insurers, even as premiums continued to increase.

The ad was funded by No Going Back PAC, a new super PAC with ties to MAGA Inc., President Trump’s main super PAC. The group said Mr. Pappas “should be ashamed” of his vote.

What Was Said

“I’m going to show you something. No A. I., no special effects, just Michael Whatley in his own words: ‘Grocery prices are down, gasoline prices are down, housing prices are down, inflation is down.’ Unbelievable. And so is this: ‘There is no inflation.’”— Former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for Senate in North Carolina, in an ad that began airing in September

This needs context. It’s true that the ad features remarks made by Michael Whatley, the Republican candidate, without special effects or enhancements by artificial intelligence. But the ad omits that those remarks occurred more than a year earlier, in an interview in July 2025, when overall prices were increasing at a slower pace and gas prices were stable.

At the time Mr. Whatley made those remarks, mortgage rates had dipped slightly and Mr. Trump’s war in Iran, and its accompanying surge in gas prices, was still months away. The New York Times had reported that inflation had accelerated, but remained relatively calm in the early months of the second Trump administration. Economists, though, were warning that the impact of Mr. Trump’s tariff policies would soon manifest in the form of higher prices.

The average price for gas in the country was $3.13 a gallon, not too different from the $3.10 a gallon at the end of January 2025, when Mr. Trump began his second term. Average 30-year mortgage rates had fallen to about 6.7 percent in July 2025 from about 7 percent that January.

“Prices were down considerably in 2025 from the record-setting inflation caused by Joe Biden’s reckless spending policies endorsed by Roy Cooper,” DJ Griffin, a spokesman for the Whatley campaign, said in a statement.

Still, Mr. Whatley was wrong that grocery prices, housing and inflation were “down” in the summer of 2025. The Consumer Price Index had risen by 2.7 percent in June 2025 from a year earlier, housing by 4 percent and food-at-home by 2.4 percent. Median home prices in June had also risen, albeit modestly, by 1.8 percent year-over-year, according to the National Association of Realtors.

In comparison, the C. P. I. increased by 3.4 percent this August, the latest available data, food-at-home by 2.2 percent and housing by 3.1 percent. In the first week of October, gas prices averaged $4.35, and mortgage rates were higher than when Mr. Trump took office.

The Cooper campaign said Mr. Whatley has for months engaged in a pattern of downplaying and making false statements about inflation, for example, saying in January that “there is no inflation” and in September that “we are not getting gouged” on gas prices.

Linda Qiu is a Times reporter who specializes in fact-checking statements made by politicians and public figures. She has been reporting and fact-checking public figures for nearly a decade.

At Cornell, a Sorority Finds Itself Sued by One of Its Own

The New York Times October 10, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Some Delta Delta Delta members are asking if the sorority shares blame in the bombshell case — or if the group is a scapegoat.

By Julie Bosman and Andrea Barnes

The searing lawsuit brought by a former college student known as Jane Doe lays blame at the feet of her school, Cornell University. The seven men she accused of sexual assault, the fraternity Chi Phi and an off-campus bar where she drank at a private party have also faced public backlash.

Less scrutinized in the uproar is the role of another defendant: Delta Delta Delta, Jane Doe’s sorority.

It was the 113-year-old Cornell chapter of Tri Delta, Jane Doe claimed in the lawsuit, that also bears responsibility for what she described as a violent, traumatic assault. The sorority had put on a public face promising safety for the women who joined, the lawsuit said, vowing to monitor and protect the sisters of Tri Delta who lived in the stately brick sorority house on Triphammer Road.

Yet on that night in October 2024, an underage Jane Doe drank alcohol with her sorority sisters at their house, downing what she later estimated to be about six shots of vodka. The “house mom,” an employee of the sorority who supervised the women living in the house, escorted an intoxicated Jane Doe in an Uber from the sorority house to a bar in downtown Ithaca, the lawsuit said. At that bar, where Tri Delta hosted a “date party” for women and their guests, Jane Doe was able to drink even more alcohol, ordering a cocktail from a bartender without interference, the lawsuit said.

These events, the lawsuit said, led directly to the sexual assault of Jane Doe later that night at the Chi Phi house.

Tri Delta said in a statement that it “supports women and will continue to stand beside those who have experienced sexual violence.”

But the naming of Tri Delta as a defendant has roiled the sorority’s members in Ithaca and beyond, prompting many to ask whether an organization founded on principles of sisterhood and personal character could have been culpable in the rape of one of its own members.

Others have questioned whether the lawsuit has made Tri Delta a convenient scapegoat, another instance of women shouldering blame for the actions of men.

“It makes me angry that it’s even a conversation of, ‘What didn’t we do to protect our sister?’” Lucia Montes, a Tri Delta member who graduated from Cornell in 2017, said in an interview. “But that’s the reality.”

By Jane Doe’s account, the night of Oct. 19, 2024, began with a scene of sisterly camaraderie at the Tri Delta sorority house.

In hundreds of pages of confidential investigative files obtained by The New York Times, Jane Doe said that she and her fellow Tri Deltas had gathered at their house, preparing for a party at Moonies, a bar off campus. Jane Doe, who was relieved of her “sober monitor” duties after her wallet was stolen earlier that day, took swigs of Tito’s vodka from a bottle while the young women chatted and got ready to leave, drinking quickly enough that at least one friend gently told her to slow down.

But when the group eventually loaded into a pair of Ubers for the party, Jane Doe was mistakenly left behind.

Alone and struggling to hold back tears of disappointment, she sought out the “house mom.”

“I didn’t want to tell her I was drunk because she’s a mandated reporter,” Jane Doe said, according to a transcript of her conversation with investigators.

Sororities nationwide have strict rules banning alcohol in their houses. The lawsuit claimed that Tri Delta, whose Cornell chapter counts more than 160 members, failed to “exercise reasonable care to prevent plaintiff from binge drinking at its sorority house on Cornell’s campus, when plaintiff was in its care, custody and control.”

The house mother offered to drop off Jane Doe at the party in an Uber, since she was also heading in that direction. At the door at Moonies, Jane Doe, who was then 20, was given a mark on her hand to indicate to the bar staff that she was not allowed to drink.

But, according to documents obtained by The Times, she was able to order a cocktail from the bartender anyway, socializing with friends and vaping tobacco in a back room at the bar.

“Everyone kind of knows that if you want alcohol, you will find a way to get alcohol,” Jane Doe told investigators, according to the transcript obtained by The Times.

Sometime around 10 p. m., Jane Doe walked over to another bar, Lot 10, and bumped into more friends. Most of the women, she recalled in the transcript, were accompanied by their boyfriends or friends.

“It was a pretty solid group of people there,” she told investigators of the scene at Lot 10. “They all had somebody watching out for them.”

Around 11 p. m., Jane Doe set out to meet a friend at the Chi Phi house, walking alone.

Last week, Tri Delta members across the country received an unexpected email. The subject line read: “A message from Tri Delta.”

It was a jarring interruption from the usual updates on scholarships, class reunions and efforts to raise money for childhood cancer research. In the email, Stacey Dickenson Cox, the president of the sorority, said she was “saddened, outraged and deeply concerned” by the news reports about the “incident” at Cornell in 2024.

Because the sorority was named in the lawsuit, she added, there are details that she could not share publicly.

“There will undoubtedly be difficult conversations and strong reactions as the lawsuit moves forward,” she wrote. “Some of what is said publicly may be painful for our sisters to hear.”

To some devoted Tri Delta women, the email did not go far enough.

“Sickeningly thin,” said Haisley Smith, a dues-paying Tri Delta alumna from Mountain Brook, Ala. “It was just completely inadequate to make any current members, alumni or prospective members feel like the national organization is feeling the gravity of this in any substantial way.”

Brittany Robb, a spokeswoman for Tri Delta, said in an email that the organization does not comment on pending litigation. “As an organization, we are committed to supporting women and victims of sexual violence,” she said.

The Cornell chapter of Tri Delta said in a statement that it was “inspired by women like Jane Doe.”

“We stand in solidarity with Jane Doe and every other survivor,” the statement said.

Lenore Schiller, a Tri Delta member who graduated from Cornell in 2019, saw Jane Doe’s lawsuit as something unique to the sorority: an embodiment of the Tri Delta values of strength and solidarity, the kind of philosophy reflected in its members’ standard email sign-off, “Loyally.”

“Our values were always like women’s rights, standing up for each other, not taking B. S.,” Ms. Schiller said. “She was brave enough to come out to say something because that’s what Tri Delt stood for.”

Some members questioned whether the sorority had enough safety measures in place to protect its young women from fraternity men, in a Greek system where alcohol and drug use is commonplace.

“What do we expect to happen?” said JoDee Neil, a Tri Delta alumna of Texas A&M University. “We’re not giving them any tools. And we’re sending them off, basically, into a lion’s den.”

Legal experts said that the inclusion of Tri Delta as a defendant in the lawsuit reflected a common strategy in civil legal actions like this one. Including every party who could be held liable for a plaintiff’s suffering helps make a case to a jury. And the more defendants found liable, the more financial damages a plaintiff could presumably recover, the experts added.

“You want to be able to tell a full story to the jury,” said Heidi Li Feldman, a professor emerita of law at Georgetown University Law Center.

She cautioned that simply being named as a defendant in the lawsuit does not suggest that Tri Delta would bear an equal burden of responsibility to other defendants.

“To say that the sorority might have played a causally significant role and not acted perfectly is not to say that the sorority is the big villain,” she said.

Thomas Giuffra, a lawyer for Jane Doe, said in an interview that she never should have been allowed to leave the sorority house.

“That’s the first failed guardrail,” he said. “Somebody should have said: ‘Hey, no, you’re intoxicated. You’re not, you shouldn’t be going outside. It’s not safe.’ And that failed.”

But holding Tri Delta liable could be an uphill battle for Jane Doe.

“I can’t see a world in which the sorority would be held responsible for this conduct,” said Rebecca Zipkin, a lawyer who has represented victims of sexual assault on college campuses.

She added that sorority and fraternity life should be examined more broadly.

“There’s a larger conversation around Greek life and what kind of culture fraternities and sororities are creating on campus,” Ms. Zipkin said.

Davaughnia Wilson and Hurubie Meko contributed reporting.

Julie Bosman is the Chicago bureau chief for The Times, writing and reporting stories from around the Midwest.

AI Is Getting Really Good at Messing With Cybercriminals

Wired October 10, 2026

Welcome to Kernel Panic!, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Even as AI supercharges digital scamming and cybercrime, it’s also being recruited in the fight to protect potential victims. Governments around the world have consistently struggled to address the global crisis of online crime, grappling with the limitations of attempting to crack down on criminals beyond their borders. This has inspired alternative efforts, like using automation to attempt to go after scammers en masse—perhaps by spamming the spammers to squander their resources. Now, AI platforms are turning these types of experiments into real tools in the fight against cybercrime.

For the last two years, the Australian company Apate, named after the Greek goddess of deception, has been building a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots that are trained to keep conversations going as long as possible without, of course, ever actually falling for the scam. The goal is to give scammers enough hope that they stay on the phone, while also collecting intelligence about the scams they’re running.

“What we really like to think is that we’re building the perfect victims for scammers,” Dali Kaafar, the founder and CEO of Apate, tells us. “A minute that a scammer is talking to a bot or an agent is a minute where you’re probably saving hundreds, if not thousands of possible people being reached out to by that exact same scammer,” he says, referencing the ability for scammers to use automated dialing tools.

Kaafar says Apate’s platform, which is used by banks and supported by telecom companies, has around 350,000 bots. They not only pick up calls, but also infiltrate scam chat groups online and respond to text messages with similar goals of frustrating scammers while collecting intelligence from them. He says the company has collected more than 250,000 pieces of information about fraudsters in real-time, from scam URLs to money mule accounts and bank details.

The bots have different personalities, language skills, and profiles, Kaafar says, so scammers hopefully don’t detect that they’re conversing with an AI. Like real people, “sometimes [the bots] do have WhatsApp, sometimes they don’t. Sometimes they pick up the phone, sometimes they just actually hang up on the scammer saying, ‘I'll come back to you later,’” he says.

But are they convincing? Kernel Panic tested the tool using a demo version where users play the role of the scammer and talk to one of Apate’s AI “victims.” The personas are designed to express a healthy amount of skepticism but leave enough openings for scammers to continue to try to win them over, a dynamic that we could immediately feel and found intensely frustrating.

Scammers are likely familiar with this type of skeptical interaction, and Kaafar says that Apate calls regularly go on for more than two hours. In our testing, the Apate system was engaged and responsive, and the timing of the conversation felt natural, even with both of us tag-teaming the AI as a friend, “Lucy,” and her financial adviser “Mickey.” We did not succeed at getting the Apate AI system to invest in our cryptocurrency opportunity even after six minutes of diligent effort. (The returns are truly incredible, though, we swear.)

For now, even with Apate’s massive swarm of bots on the case, it’s only a matter of time before you get your next scam call or text. Cybercriminals initiate billions of messages and calls each year, with the most sophisticated operations running physical, industrial scale scamming sites. And while professional scambaiters and initiatives to infiltrate scam operations have done critical deterrent work for years, law enforcement and research efforts haven’t been able to stop the expansion of digital scamming overall.

But AI could create a new era for anti-scam efforts, not just scammers themselves. Better intelligence sharing between cops, social media companies, banks, and other industries is desperately needed and could potentially be aided by AI-driven monitoring and data analysis. Increasingly, too, innovative efforts have been looking to disrupt cybercriminals by exploiting their “psychological vulnerabilities.” In some cases, these psyops have included directly trolling those behind ransomware attacks. As the focus on disrupting scammers and cybercriminals expands, the use of generative AI as a way to keep them preoccupied, wasting resources, and not launching other attacks appears to be increasingly effective.

Take honeypots, for instance. For years, companies and security researchers have deployed false virtual machines to attract hackers, waste their time, gather information, and understand their secret hacking techniques. Mark Vero, a doctoral researcher at the department of computer science at ETH Zurich, says open source honeypot providers have increasingly been incorporating LLMs into their systems to make them appear more realistic.

In recent research, Vero and colleagues found an LLM-powered honey pot would keep AI agents attacking their system “significantly longer” than a honey pot with more predictable behavior. “The agentic attackers are much more convinced by the LLM simulated honeypots and they also mark them as actual honeypots at a much lower rate,” he says. “If these systems are built well enough, then I think it’s quite advantageous for defenders.”

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at kernelpanic@wired. com. And stay safe out there.

I’ve Been Tracking My Weight for Years. These Are the Best Smart Scales

Wired October 10, 2026

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

Withings

After years of sleepiness, the smart scale world has finally woken up—driven almost certainly by the GLP-1 craze, as millions of consumers find themselves wondering if those weekly jabs are actually working.

What was previously a category occupied by dated gear has abruptly exploded, and for good reason. Today’s smart scales don’t just report on your weight; they do things like measure your heart rate and break down muscle composition, and some can even give you an eye on your heart health, courtesy of technology like integrated ECG systems. Through mobile apps, they can track all of this information over time.

The big shift in the category in the past year has been a flood of new full-body scanners hitting the market from all corners. Essentially bathroom scales with handlebar-based scanners, these don’t just use bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) to measure conductivity (and, thus, body fat percentage) through your feet. They can now scan through your hands, too, giving you a much more holistic (and ostensibly accurate) look at your body metrics than a floor scale will provide. I’ve personally seen body fat percentage numbers swing up to 6 percent between the two types of scales. (Spoiler: The full-body scanner data is always higher.)

Do you really need all that information? I’ve long suggested that it’s really the trend line that matters most, not the absolute numbers, and as long as your metrics are headed in the right direction, it doesn’t matter quite as much whether things are off by a small percentage. Consistent weigh-ins are the most important part of the process, along with tracking that information over time to determine whether your diet and workout regimen (or medication routine) is getting you the results you need.

Mind you, scale prices are headed up, and new full-body scanners can now top $600 for top-tier tech. That’s part of the reason why I still recommend a standard scale for most users, as these devices are considerably less expensive, and the results they offer are likely to be good enough for all but serious athletes.

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Either way, this roundup has an option for every type of user.

Updated October 2026: I've added Withings’ BodyScan 2 and new honorable mentions from Runstar, Tanita, and Withings. I've also added scales to avoid and ensured up-to-date prices throughout.

How Do Smart Scales Work?

Smart scales come in two basic flavors: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. The former connects directly to your phone to sync its readings. The latter uses your home’s wireless network to sync readings straight to the cloud, which your phone’s app can then access. Wi-Fi scales are generally more expensive but more versatile. While older scales often featured erratic wireless connections, newer models have many of their kinks worked out—and firmware updates have improved connectivity.

Virtually all smart scales use the same type of system to gauge your additional vitals: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which involves sending a minuscule electric current up one leg and measuring what happens when it comes down the other side. Some mathematical magic converts all of this into any number of derived measurements about things like your body’s percentage of fat, water, and bone; body-mass index (BMI); and, sometimes, arcana like your basal metabolic rate (BMR), which is a measure of your body’s energy consumption at rest. All the scales I tested can sync data with Apple Health and Google's Health Connect, either directly or by passing data via the app.

When Is the Best Time to Weigh Yourself?

Most experts say that the best time to weigh in is first thing in the morning, before you’ve eaten and after you’ve used the restroom. The main reason for this is consistency: Weighing yourself at the same time every day is the best way to ensure that consecutive weigh-ins are taken under conditions that are as controlled as possible. Since eating and drinking will cause your weight to fluctuate considerably, weighing yourself on an empty stomach means you’re getting an apples-to-apples comparison each morning.

As a small bonus, your weight is usually at its lowest right after you wake up, so you potentially stand to give yourself a gentle confidence boost by stepping on the scale then instead of after dinner.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Withings

Amazon

Withings

Early Withings scales weren't great, dragged down perhaps by complications related to the company changing ownership a few too many times in the past decade. Now back in the hands of its cofounder, Withings is doing things right again, starting with the Body Comp, a much more advanced version of its earlier Body Cardio scale, which suffered from a few flaws. In contrast, the experience here is quick and painless: Step on the new Wi-Fi–enabled Body Comp and it (very) quickly runs through a series of measurements, starting with your weight and moving on to a variety of biomarkers that include heart rate, various fat and muscle measurements, vascular age, and electrodermal activity—which measures “skin response via sweat gland stimulation in your feet.” Strangely, the scale’s heart rate measurement regularly skews about 10 beats per minute too fast. It also reports the day’s weather and even forecasts air quality in your area. After the crawl of personal data, I’ve come to rely on seeing the weather on the Body Comp’s bright color display first thing each morning.

The company has resolved long-standing issues around the user having to stand in the perfect spot to get readings, and its app has matured impressively over the past few years. That’s good because this scale isn’t cheap. But as an unintentional weight-watcher, I think it’s worth it. The Withings app tracks data for up to eight users seemingly forever; I now have readings on Withings devices going back to 2010 and hope to keep the streak going well into the future.

Etekcity

Amazon

Etekcity’s smart scale offers a bevy of features you’d normally pay for through the nose, including Wi-Fi connectivity, a bright color display, and long-term tracking of 14 biometrics that are quickly synced to your smartphone via the VeSync app (a kind of do-everything app that works on a broad group of home appliances). The scale, fortunately, doesn’t suffer from being part of this vast environment, offering an easy-to-understand interface that quickly syncs after each session and tracks your vitals by week, month, quarter, and year. It supports multiple users, and a baby mode adds extra flexibility.

The hardware is sleek and clean, and the display is customizable. You select up to nine metrics to showcase. They rotate across the screen after each weigh-in, so you don't need to turn to the app at all, unless you really want to drill down into specifics. It can even connect to Alexa devices if you want to announce your weight loss success to the entire house.

Wyze

Amazon

Wyze

Wyze has built its entire business by offering smart home technology at a fraction of the price of other brands, and its products always manage to be capable and well-made. Its latest scale is the Wyze Scale X, an update of its old, no-frills Wyze Scale. The Bluetooth-only device displays your weight on its LED screen; you’ll need to turn to the Wyze app to get additional metrics—13 in total, including muscle mass, visceral fat, and BMR measurements.

You can share the scale with up to eight users, and there are even modes for babies, pets, and luggage, so you don’t screw up your stats before you go on a trip. As with most Wyze products, it’s an amazing value, as sale events have brought the price to as low as $20.

Withings

Withings

If two sensors are good, then 12 must be even better, right?

Full-body scanners or body composition scales hit the market a few years ago, initially coming across a bit like a novelty by offering not just a blunt look at your weight and body fat markers but a more in-depth analysis of your health, limb by limb. Electrodes built into a retractable handle send small pulses from your feet to your hands and back in various combinations, ostensibly giving you a much deeper look at your health than a simple scale, which can’t “see” above the waist, can provide.

Early body scanners felt fairly primitive. But with the BodyScan 2, Withings fully kicks out the jams, offering one of the most advanced weigh-in experiences you can find.

The scale offers two types of scans: The daily scan measures weight—hyper-accurately, thanks to a built-in leveling system that forces you to be perfectly balanced before it records the day’s number—fat, muscle, and water percentages, visceral fat, and your heart rate. Once a week, you’re urged to upgrade to the longevity scan, a 90-second experience that totals a massive collection of 60 metrics, including blood oxygen level (courtesy of a thumb-based scanner), nervous system response, and a guesstimate of your heart health. Perhaps most impressive is the inclusion of a six-lead ECG, which can even help suss out AFib situations without a trip to the doctor.

Wi-Fi connectivity beams all results to Withings’ impressive app, usually instantaneously (aside from ECG results, which take up to two days to show up because a cardiologist reviews them first). While the Withings software is extremely busy, it’s actually easy to navigate, letting you fixate endlessly on every aspect of your health.

Also consider the Renpho MorphoScan Nova for $200, the brand's latest high-end scale. It evolves the chunky metallic-pad design of the standard MophoScan (see below) in favor of a much sleeker glass base and a new app, while keeping the original's oversized handlebar-based LCD screen. For an extra $30, it’s an excellent upgrade for the better looks alone. Additional features include voice prompts during your weigh-in (which you may very well hate) and an upgraded BIA sensor that other MorphoScan devices lack. The only legitimate problem I had with the scale was pokey Wi-Fi performance, but it's generally strong enough to get the job done. The app isn’t as intuitive as Withings’, but for a third of the price of the BodyScan 2, the Nova is worth serious consideration.

Renpho MorphoScan

Renpho MorphoScan for $170: The Renpho MorphoScan full-body scanner looks surprisingly similar to the Runstar FG2015, including a near-identical display attached to the handlebars. Well, spoiler alert: They are basically the same scale. They even use the same app to collect data (you can use both scales simultaneously with the app).

Runstar Smart Body Fat Scale (FG2015) for $140: My former pick for best full-body scanner, this admittedly garish offering tracks 20 metrics and supports 24 users, effectively breaking down information, limb-by-limb, in its Starfit mobile app. USB-C rechargeability is a nice plus, but the price tag—just $140 if you buy it directly from Runstar—is probably its best feature.

Tanita RD-953 InnerScan Pro

Tanita RD-953 InnerScan Pro for $230: One of the few new feet-only smart scales to hit the market this decade, Tanita’s RD-953 is defined by its Cylonesque looks—and its relative simplicity. The costly Bluetooth-only scale scans quickly, though the placement of its display in the center of the scale, right between your feet, can be awkward for those with even a small breadbasket between their head and the floor. I also didn’t love the very high and hopefully overstated body fat reading the scale gave me, but my harshest criticism is directed at the Healthy Edge app (a different app than is used by Tanita’s other scale), which is about as engaging and motivational as a shopping list on a Post-It Note.

Withings BodyFit

Withings BodyFit for $230: The middle child in the Withings family sits comfortably between the no-holds-barred BodyScan 2 and the feet-only Body Comp Smart Scale, offering a pleasant alternative for users who want full-body analysis but don’t need (or want to pay for) the fitness extremism of Withings’s top-tier model. It’s a sleek and demure unit with a small but informative color screen, quick Wi-Fi connectivity, and fast performance—and, of course, it works seamlessly with Withings’s excellent app.

Arboleaf Body Fat Scale CS20W

Arboleaf Body Fat Scale CS20W for $50: This affordable Bluetooth scale isn’t the most eye-catching I’ve tested in light of its big silver electrodes and an oversized display that comes across as a bit garish. While weight is easy to make out, the six additional statistics showcased are difficult to read, all displayed simultaneously. I like the Arboleaf app better than the scale, where five additional metrics are available, each featuring a helpful explanation when tapped. It’s a solid deal at this price, but the upsell to get an “intelligent interpretation report” for an extra $40 per year is probably safe to skip.

Hume Health Body Pod

Hume Health Body Pod for $229: Hume Health’s Body Pod, another full-body scanner with handles, is heavily advertised—at least to the apps on my phone—and touted (by Hume) as the Next Big Thing in the world of body management. While the app is indeed glossy and inviting, I was shocked to discover how flimsy the hardware felt, that it lacked Wi-Fi, and that some features are locked behind a $100-a-year Hume Plus subscription plan. It works fine enough, but you can get results that are just as good with a cheaper device.

Garmin Index S2 for $200: Five years after its release, the Index S2 is still Garmin’s current model, a surprise for a company otherwise obsessed with fitness. It’s still noteworthy for its lovely color display, which walks you through its six body metrics (for up to 16 users) with each weigh-in. The display also provides your weight trend over time in graphical form and can even display the weather. The scale connects directly to Wi-Fi and Garmin’s cloud-based storage system, so—unlike with Bluetooth-only scales—you don’t need a phone nearby to track your progress. A phone running the Garmin Connect app (Android, iOS) is handy, so you can keep track of everything over time. Unfortunately, as health apps go, Connect is a bit of a bear, so expect a learning curve—especially if you want to make changes to the way the scale works. You can turn its various LCD-screen widgets on or off in the app, but finding everything can be difficult due to the daunting scope of the Garmin ecosystem. The color screen is nice at first, but it ultimately adds little to the package.

Omron BCM-500 for $85: With its large LCD panel, quartet of onboard buttons, and oversize silver electrodes, the Omron BCM-500 is an eye-catching masterwork of brutalist design. If your bathroom is decked out in concrete and wrought iron, this scale will fit right in. The Bluetooth unit syncs with Omron’s HeartAdvisor app (Android, iOS), but it provides all six of its body metrics directly on the scale, cycling through them with each weigh-in (for up to four users). It can be difficult to read the label for each of the data points, in part because the LCD isn’t backlit, but the app is somewhat easier to follow, offering front-page graphs of weight, skeletal muscle, and body fat. On the other hand, the presentation is rather clinical, and the app is surprisingly slow to sync. For a scale without a Wi-Fi connection, it’s also rather expensive.

Renpho MorphoScan Lite

Renpho MorphoScan Lite for $95: This new entry-level offering in the MorphoScan line is specifically designed for new GLP-1 users. It's a simpler device, ditching the handheld display and, critically, Wi-Fi connectivity. It’s also one of the flimsiest scales I’ve tested—too lightweight for you to extend the handlebars without inadvertently dragging the scale across the floor. If this were a mega-bargain in line with foot-only scale pricing, I’d be sold, but the meager savings compared to other MorphoScan scales don’t justify considering it.

Tanita RD-545 InnerScan Pro

Tanita RD-545 InnerScan Pro for $480: This monstrous, industrial scale looks more like it belongs in the mailroom than the bathroom, and its level of complexity only provides more supportive evidence. The Bluetooth-only scale is confusing to set up and difficult to use correctly, and I was only able to get successful measurements by first opening the mobile app and ensuring the scale was connected before carefully stepping onto it. Then, I had to wait for a prompt to pick up the handles (while balanced on the device). Testing feels like it takes forever, and that’s even if you get it right the first time. For $480, the scale is a questionable value at best, despite its 40 measurements offered. No Wi-Fi at this price, really?

Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition

Wired October 10, 2026

Astronomers have obtained the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed.

Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant. With this resolution, researchers can now see that these filaments are not continuous as they had previously appeared. Instead, they’re shaped more like beads on a string, made up of pearl-like knots of gas of relatively uniform size.

These “cosmic pearls” are, in fact, enormous. According to the study published in The Astrophysical Journal, each bead measures about four light-days in diameter. “The planetary region of our solar system could fit in each knot about 10 times with room to spare,” Ilaria Caiazzo, a coauthor of the study, said in a press release. “The knots are quite strikingly uniform. We are excited to try to model them.”

How exactly the pearls formed is not yet entirely clear, though it’s assumed they are concentrations of material ejected during the explosion. What’s strange, however, is their regularity. In the aftermath of a supernova, astronomers expected to find much more oddly shaped accumulations, but the knots are similar in size and appear aligned along the filaments. This peculiar order is a new feature that could help researchers gain a deeper understanding of stellar death.

This image, obtained with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph, shows that the ejecta from the remnant—with its unmistakable fireworks-like shape—form a cascading structure resembling a knot.

The Pa 30 nebula is also particularly unusual because the central star isn’t exactly dead. Instead, it’s considered a “zombie star.” Typically, a thermonuclear supernova is the violent death of a star, which is completely destroyed in the explosion. But in rare cases, part of the star may survive, and scientists do not yet fully understand how or why this happens. The unusual structures of Pa 30 could help astronomers reconstruct more precisely how these kinds of detonations occur and how zombie stars can live on afterward.

All of this has been discovered because scientists seem to have a bit of a crush on Pa 30. Few astronomical structures connect modern observation so directly with human accounts from more than eight centuries ago. The nebula matches the records left by Chinese and Japanese astronomers in 1181, who described the appearance of a new star in the sky that remained visible for several months. At the time, it was impossible to know that they were witnessing the aftermath of a massive stellar explosion. Centuries later, scientists linked that event to the supernova that gave rise to Pa 30.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

How This Tiny Startup Built the World’s Safest Bike Helmet

Wired October 10, 2026

For decades, researchers judged cycling helmets on how well they protected against direct impacts. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) still does, even though research shows the danger isn't just how hard your head hits the ground, but how violently it twists. That rotational movement can make the brain twist and stretch inside the skull, increasing the risk of concussion and other brain injuries.

Not waiting for the CPSC to catch up, the cycling industry got to work. Multidirectional Impact Protection System, or MIPS, hit the market in 2007 and is now a common feature on premium helmets. At the same time, Virginia Tech turned helmet safety into something of a competition for manufacturers. In 2018, it launched helmet STAR ratings (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk), testing beyond the legal minimum and measuring both linear and rotational impacts.

Only four of the first 30 helmets earned five stars, but by 2025, 167 of 272 achieved five stars, and Virginia Tech had to tighten its grading. That only drove competition and improved helmet technology. Suddenly, hitting the number one spot was good for business and brains.

Sitting comfortably ahead of the competition, with a 4.61 score (10.1 or lower earns a five-star rating; lower is better), is the Pikio Si Oblik road cycling helmet, featuring a new safety system called Oblik. Inspired by the headbanging, concussion-proof woodpecker, this new design has wiped the floor with the competition. For context, Pikio's 4.61 score is 2.21 points lower than the previous best Canyon Deflectr’s 6.82. That’s about 32 percent lower, a massive shift when many of the highest-rated helmets score only between 7 and 10 points.

How has this relatively obscure Vancouver startup gotten it right the first time? As founder Daniel Abram explains, it “comes from 18 years researching impact protection and helmet design.” After studying mechanical engineering, he moved into helmet research at Simon Fraser University, where he helped develop BrainShield, a system designed to reduce rotational forces during impacts. He later founded helmet technology company BiaGuard, before MIPS paid around $1 million for the patents and intellectual property in 2022.

Most bike helmets use a thin plastic shell over expanded polystyrene (EPS) foam, which crushes on impact to absorb energy before it reaches your skull. Oblik takes that familiar foam structure and breaks it into independently mounted sections rather than one continuous block.

Each section attaches to the base EPS layer with flexible connection points, allowing them to move separately or detach if the helmet takes a serious impact. Combined with dual-density foam that absorbs direct impact, the movement helps to minimize the twisting force transmitted to the head. Abram explained how, “Rather than compressing material in one direction, the system is able to deform, deflect, and detach depending on the impact's intensity, location, and direction, helping manage both linear and rotational impact energy.”

Other helmet technologies approach the problem very differently. The now-ubiquitous MIPS remains the dominant commercial system, using a low-friction layer that can move 10 to 15 millimeters during the first 5 to 10 milliseconds of an impact. MIPS Spherical uses two nested liners that rotate relative to each other, while 6D’s Omni-Directional Suspension (ODS) suspends one liner inside another. WaveCel uses an engineered cellular structure that flexes, crumples, and glides under angled impacts.

Pikio's closest rival, the Release Layer System (RLS), featured on Canyon’s Deflectr and the third-placed, 3D-printed Hexr Miden RLS, tackles rotation from the outside, using external shell panels floating on tiny polycarbonate ball bearings that can roll and detach, redirecting rotational energy before it reaches the head.

Lab testing is one thing, but real-world data is something else. If your Pikio helmet is called into serious action, you will need to replace it—as with most EPS foam designs—but the company is offering a 30 percent discount on a replacement if it can get its hands on your damaged helmet.

“So far we’ve had four helmets returned and replaced,” Abram says. “Each has proven invaluable, not least because they’ve done their job and kept riders safe.”

At $379, the Pikio is a premium choice—a cool $219 more expensive than the second-best STAR-tested Canyon Deflectr RLS. Much of the cost stems from a vastly more complicated manufacturing process. Abram says a standard cycling helmet has around eight to 10 parts, but the Pikio Si uses around 80 individual components. The separate foam sections, intricately engineered flexible connection points, and dual-density construction all add to the cost.

It’s a small price to pay if it saves your life, but how does it fare day to day? I’ve been riding with the Si Oblik for the past month and have been impressed by how few compromises there have been in the pursuit of protection.

At 279 grams (in medium size), it's respectably light, though not class-leading, and the dial-to-fit cradle hugs my head neatly without pinch points. It’s a little bulky for a road lid, but is extremely comfortable; the 17 air vents keep my head refreshingly cool, and nobody has laughed at me for wearing it (yet). I would have preferred Pikio to use a magnetic Fidlock fastening under the chin as they’re brilliant, but it is a minor complaint—which Abram quickly quashed: “Fidlock weighs around 13 grams; a buckle is just four grams.”

It’s a great helmet loaded with unique, deliberately safety-first tech. Abram was keen to point out he is not interested in what he called “crown-like cycle helmet” aesthetics, and that “form always follows function.” The Pikio lacks a little of the cool factor you’ll find with a POC or Giro helmet, but it’s certainly not ugly.

For a company most cyclists have never heard of, taking the top spot at Virginia Tech is an extraordinary result. The harder part may be persuading people to trust an unknown name with something as consequential as head protection. MIPS faced a similar problem before turning an independent safety technology into something licensed across much of the helmet industry, and Oblik could conceivably follow the same path.

Whether Pikio becomes a major helmet brand—a second design is due early in the new year—a technology supplier, or both remains to be seen. But for now, it has given the cycling industry a new number to chase.

Tesla’s ‘Full Self-Driving’ Becomes ‘Assisted Driving’ in Europe

Wired October 09, 2026

Tesla’s most advanced driver-assistance feature is named Full Self-Driving (Supervised), but it can’t actually drive itself. While the feature can handle tasks like accelerating, braking, steering, and parking, the automaker requires drivers to stay alert and intervene at all times. Now, the company has officially renamed it to Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD) in Europe as it works to convince regulators to allow its use on public roads.

Tesla offered to change the name, according to a statement by the German Transport Ministry. The statement says that German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger found the “FSD” name “somewhat misleading.” After discussions with Tesla last month, Bilger said he would now advocate for European regulators to approve the feature “as quickly as possible.” The EU will likely vote on its approval by the end of the year.

On Friday, Tesla began using the Tesla Assisted Driving language on its European sales website. The automaker didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tesla has resisted changing the feature’s name for years, even defending it in court. Last year, California’s Department of Motor Vehicles concluded that Tesla’s use of the terms “Full Self-Driving” and “Autopilot” (an older and less advanced driver-assistance feature) was misleading and violated state law. After the agency threatened to suspend Tesla’s manufacturing and dealer licenses in the state, the automaker stopped using the term “Autopilot.” It has also continued to append “(Supervised)” to the official name of its Full Self-Driving tech.

Tesla drivers say FSD has improved tremendously since its introduction in 2020, and fans online say they’ve been able to take entire trips without intervening in their Tesla’s driving. But FSD has faced plenty of scrutiny. In March, the US federal government opened a probe into the system after nine incidents in which FSD allegedly failed to respond because of reduced visibility and didn’t warn its drivers to take over. Tesla recalled an older version of the software in 2023, after the US government found that it didn’t follow some traffic laws.

Tesla and CEO Elon Musk have pushed for other global markets to approve its driver assistance technology for years. That would likely create a lucrative, software-based funding stream for the world’s most valuable automaker. (Currently, Tesla charges $99 per month for a Full Self-Driving (Supervised) subscription in the US.) Australia and New Zealand approved it last year. The Netherlands became the first European government to give Tesla provisional permission to launch FSD this past spring. A version of the feature became available to Chinese customers in May.

This week, Reuters reported that Tesla presented misleading safety data to European regulators as it lobbied for FSD approval. Safety researchers have accused the automaker of also using misleading statistics to promote its tech in the US.

Book Publishers Are Quietly Using More AI. Staff Are Revolting

Wired October 09, 2026

In headline after headline this year, American book publishers have appeared to be fighting back against generative AI, from suing Google for copyright infringement to canceling books by authors suspected of using LLMs.

But behind the scenes, at least three of the Big Five US book publishers—HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette—have been quietly incorporating AI tools into their publishing processes without public disclosures or author consent.

According to interviews with more than two dozen workers, all of whom spoke under the condition of anonymity to avoid jeopardizing their employment, publishers are now using LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT to email literary agents, write publicity and back-cover copy, design cover art, and generate marketing materials, often at the direction of their executives.

At the same time, multiple editorial staffers say the widely publicized cases of authors accused of using LLMs to help write their books—like Hachette’s horror novel Shy Girl or Macmillan’s crime thriller Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body—are just the tip of the iceberg. “Every single imprint has a story of someone very esteemed who had a book canceled because of blatant AI use” without ever making the news, one editor says.

At HarperCollins senior leaders purchased Claude licenses from Anthropic months ago “but very quickly realized they didn’t know how to implement them,” according to a current employee. Dozens of junior- and senior-level staff were then “voluntold” to become “AI Champions” and were tasked with discovering use cases in monthly brainstorming sessions with staff across the company.

This spring, when some HarperCollins employees expressed concerns about the legal, ethical, and environmental impacts of AI at one of these brainstorming sessions, a person leading the meeting dismissed their qualms as “the cost of doing business,” according to someone who attended the meeting. Soon after, a statement was added to the new AI section of the HarperCollins online employee portal, noting that “while AI does have an environmental impact, it’s a small part of most individuals’ total digital carbon footprint.”

Some HarperCollins staffers were unnerved by the brainstorming sessions. “It was such a slap in the face,” says one employee. “We’ve been making valid business cases for years to be paid a healthy salary, and instead they spent that money on software that most of us don’t really want.” (The average entry-level salary for New York City publishing employees at the Big Five and Scholastic was $47,583 in 2023.) In addition to Claude, staffers say HarperCollins has also purchased licenses for ChatGPT and Jasper, an agentic platform that promises “to run end-to-end marketing workflows.”

At least one HarperCollins division has been “all in” on AI since gaining software licenses, according to one staffer, including AI-generated marketing videos. But according to workers at HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette, one of the most common use cases for LLMs so far is generating publicity copy.

Readers encounter publicity copy everywhere from Amazon and Goodreads to back covers, and it’s used to pitch books to booksellers, journalists, content creators, and critics. However, “using AI to generate publicity copy is short-sighted,” a Big Five publicist tells me. “Publicists have a duty to engage in good faith with readers and our colleagues in the media, who I’m sure have a low threshold for tolerating AI-generated pitches.”

On the other hand, Meg Reid, publisher of the independent Hub City Press, says LLM-written marketing and publicity unfortunately “feels pretty inevitable” for the Big Five. “That’s one place we’re probably going to see a bigger shift between corporate publishers looking for efficiencies and smaller publishers insisting that the humans involved are the whole point.”

Meanwhile, earlier this year, literary agents began suspecting specific Big Five editors were using AI to write rejection letters. “Among colleagues, we compared emails on different books from the same editors, and they all had the same classic signs of AI writing, like ‘not this, but that’ and the rule of three,” one agent says. Employees at Simon & Schuster, HarperCollins, and Hachette tell WIRED they believe the agents’ suspicions were correct.

A spokesperson for Hachette says the company “support[s] the use of AI tools for operational purposes, when they help our authors’ books reach more readers,” but that it “[does] not support creative uses of AI, including communicating with our authors and partners.”

Wibke Grutjen, global chief marketing and communications officer at Simon & Schuster, says “employees across all functions have access to a limited number of enterprise-level AI tools,” but using them is not mandatory. Grutjen said the company prohibits the use of any AI tool “that has not been vetted and approved” and that “the goal is always to free up more time for our employees to spend on deeper focus and creative work on behalf of and alongside our authors.”

HarperCollins did not respond to requests for comment.

Months ago, workers at Simon & Schuster attended a workshop with representatives from OpenAI. “The person leading the workshop genuinely had no idea what we did,” an attendee says, but one of the AI company’s recommendations for how to use ChatGPT in the book trade was, in fact, composing emails to literary agents. The practice has also grown among editors at HarperCollins and Hachette, employees say.

In May 2024, staffers say Simon & Schuster held a contest among employees to come up with the best use cases for AI, with a $10,000 prize for the winner and $5,000 each for two runners-up. Since then, the company has “rolled back some of the AI-pushing because employees kept complaining about it in town halls,” says one employee. According to several staffers, AI assets are also cropping up in cover art, with some foreign presses distributed by Simon & Schuster openly acknowledging AI use when sharing designs.

All of the agents I spoke with expressed fears that publishers might paste text from their authors’ manuscripts into the LLMs in order to generate things like rejection letters and publicity descriptions. “We’ve added AI clauses to our contracts saying ‘this material can’t be run through an LLM,’” says one agent, who did not want to be named to avoid professional repercussions. “Ostensibly, that was meant to protect authors from tech companies, but it also applies to the company buying and publishing the book. If they're not using a closed-loop model, they could be feeding an LLM with an author’s unpublished writing.” Unlike the LLMs most people use online (Google Gemini, ChatGPT, et al.), a closed-loop model operates on an individual computer or network that’s “air-gapped” so it can’t share data with the AI company’s cloud servers. One source at HarperCollins says multiple editors have asked managers if they could paste a full manuscript into an open-loop LLM and were told not to by the company’s legal team.

Hachette employees are also bracing for the company’s AI policies to “evolve” under new chief information officer Carl Hixson, due to his previous role as chief technology officer at SRMG, a Saudi state-backed company that has publicly embraced agentic AI.

Some staffers across the Big Five say they’re reluctantly experimenting with LLMs only because executives gutted their teams through layoffs and subsequently tripled their workloads.

“It’s skeleton crews everywhere you look,” says one employee. “Large teams have been reduced to just five or six people, give or take, and we’re doing double or triple the number of books. No wonder people are taking shortcuts. I don’t judge them for that. I judge the company for shoving the shortcuts down our throats and saying, ‘Do this or we fall behind.’”

In just the past few weeks, word spread among Simon & Schuster workers that the company was conducting an experimental trial with Skan AI “at the apparent urging of KKR”—the investment firm that purchased Simon & Schuster in 2023. According to its own website, Skan AI “gives leaders the evidence base they need to reduce costs, prioritize automation, and meet board-level transformation mandates.”

In response, Simon & Schuster employees began gathering signatures on an open letter to their CEO, Greg Greeley, expressing their “strong opposition” and “seeking a commitment to not bring Skan AI or other similar software into S&S workflows, either now or in the future.” Beyond the software’s surveillance capabilities, many workers were also concerned with Skan AI’s “automation discovery” tools being used to shadow and replace them.

News of the open letter was published in New York magazine’s Book Gossip newsletter on October 6. On the same day, Greeley sent a memo to Simon & Schuster employees confirming that the company has been exploring Skan AI’s Blueprint product but that “no decision has been made to use Blueprint or any other productivity-monitoring or workflow-analysis tool,” and that he “had not seen the materials relating to this early-stage exploration” before concerns were raised to him the day before. Pangram, which, for better or worse, has become the go-to AI-detection platform, indicates that at least some of Greeley’s memo was written by AI.

Almost two years ago at the UBS Global Media and Communications Conference, HarperCollins CEO Brian Murray said AI presents “more opportunities than risks” for book publishers and that he saw AI playing a role in increasing the number of translated books and audiobooks published by HarperCollins in the future. Since then, multiple editors say they’ve seen LLM-translated manuscripts with AI-use disclosures at the annual Frankfurt and London book fairs, where US publishers buy international publishing and translation rights from foreign literary agencies.

In August, Michael Reynolds, executive publisher at Europa Editions, an independent press in New York best known for publishing Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan Quartet of novels, told a room full of booksellers at the New Voices New Rooms conference in Baltimore he was excited about the possibilities for AI in translation and “seemed baffled by critiques of it,” according to attendees. Europa Editions is already controversial among literary circles for leaving the names of its human (for now) translators off the covers of its books.

“The C-suites at Big Five publishing companies have more in common with the C-suites at other major American companies than they do with the editors and publicists and translators who work for them,” says Dan Sinykin, author of Big Fiction: How Conglomeration Changed the Publishing Industry and American Literature. “They’re always looking for ways to maximize profit, and right now they’re trying to see what they can get away with before there’s a revolt.”

Most of the industry professionals I spoke with just want publishers to provide clear AI usage guidelines and disclosures, at the very least, to help mitigate the current chaos. “We need publishers to be clear about what is being used and when,” says Emma Dries, an agent at Triangle House Literary who previously worked in editorial at HarperCollins and Penguin Random House. A current HarperCollins staffer, meanwhile, says there has been no direction “about what to say to authors or agents about any of this, because I think they know it would start a shitstorm.”

“Short of these tools being banned, which would frankly be my preference,” Dries continues, “everybody should be communicating more.”

NASA Just Made Nearly 1 TB of Artemis II Data Available to the Public

Wired October 09, 2026

NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.

The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.

In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.

Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.

For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.

For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.

Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.

The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.
